docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Beginner

Short, plain-English definitions of the words this playbook uses. When a page uses a word you don't know, look here first.

docs.title: HTML
docs.text: Element One piece of a page, written as an opening tag, content and a closing tag: <p>Hello</p>. Some elements have no content or closing tag (<img>, <input>). Attribute Extra information on an opening tag: <a href="/cart">. href is the attribute name, /cart its value. Semantic HTML Choosing the element that matches the meaning (<button>, <nav>, <h2>) instead of a generic <div>. Browsers, search engines and screen readers all understand it for free. Landmark A region screen-reader users can jump to: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer>, <form role="search">. Data attribute A custom attribute starting with data- (data-price="18900") that holds information for JavaScript. Read it with element.dataset.price. Accessible name What a screen reader announces for a control: the button's text, a <label>, or an aria-label. Every button, link and input needs one. ARIA Attributes (aria-label, aria-current, aria-hidden, aria-live…) that add accessibility information HTML can't express on its own. First rule of ARIA: use a native element if one exists. DOM Document Object Model: the browser's live tree of elements built from your HTML. JavaScript reads and changes the DOM, not the HTML file.

docs.title: CSS
docs.text: Selector The part before { that picks which elements a rule applies to: .product-card, nav a, [aria-current="page"]. Specificity How the browser decides which of two conflicting rules wins. Roughly: id > class / attribute / pseudo-class > element. Equal specificity → the later rule wins. Cascade The full set of rules (origin, @layer, specificity, order) that decides the final value of every property. Box model Every element is a box: content, then padding, then border, then margin. box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border. Custom property / CSS variable / design token A named value, --brand: #0c831f, used with var(--brand). A design token is a custom property that stores a design decision (colour, spacing, radius). rem, em, px, %, vw, dvh, ch, fr Units. rem = root font size (16 px by default). em = this element's font size. vw = 1 % of the window width. dvh = 1 % of the visible screen height on phones. ch = width of a "0". fr = one share of the free space in a grid. Flexbox A layout mode for items in one direction (a row or a column): display: flex. Grid A layout mode for rows and columns at the same time: display: grid. auto-fill / auto-fit With repeat(auto-fill, minmax(160px, 1fr)) the grid makes as many columns as fit. auto-fit additionally stretches the items when there are fewer than fit. Media query CSS that applies only when a condition is true, usually the screen width: @media (width >= 768px) { … }. Breakpoint A width at which the layout changes (768 px, 900 px…). Choose them where your design breaks, not by device names. Mobile first Write the phone CSS first (no media query), then add @media (width >= …) rules for bigger screens. Container query Like a media query, but asks about the width of a parent element instead of the screen: @container (width > 400px). Stacking context / z-index Which element is drawn on top. z-index only works on positioned elements (and flex/grid items), and only within the same stacking context. Pseudo-class / pseudo-element :hover, :focus-visible, :has(), :nth-child() select elements in a state. ::before, ::after, ::backdrop style a part that isn't in the HTML. BEM A class-naming convention: block__element--modifier (.btn--outline). Keeps CSS flat and predictable.

docs.title: JavaScript and the browser
docs.text: Event Something that happens (click, input, change, keydown). You react with element.addEventListener("click", fn). Event delegation One listener on a parent handles events from all its children, using event.target.closest(…) to find which child was hit. State The data your UI is drawn from (the cart Map in the e-commerce tab). Change the state, then re-render; never let the screen become the only copy of the data. defer On <script defer>: download the script without blocking the page and run it once the HTML is parsed. XSS Cross-site scripting: an attacker's HTML/JS runs on your page because you inserted untrusted text with innerHTML. Use textContent for data.

docs.title: Performance and quality
docs.text: Core Web Vitals Google's three user-experience metrics: LCP (how fast the main content appears), INP (how fast the page responds to taps), CLS (how much the layout jumps). Lazy loading Loading something only when it's needed: <img loading="lazy"> waits until the image is about to scroll into view. Responsive images srcset + sizes let the browser download the smallest image that looks sharp on the current screen. WCAG Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Level AA is the usual legal and industry target (for example, 4.5 : 1 contrast for normal text). Progressive enhancement Build a version that works with plain HTML, then add CSS and JavaScript on top. If the JS fails, the page still works (the filters <details> in the e-commerce tab still opens without JS).

docs.title: E-commerce words
docs.text: PLP / PDP Product Listing Page (a grid of products with filters) / Product Detail Page (one product, full information). SKU Stock-keeping unit: one sellable item variant (e.g. "Shimla Apple, 1 kg"). CTA Call to action: the one button you want people to press ("Shop now", "Add to cart"). Minor units Storing money as whole numbers of the smallest unit (paise, cents) to avoid floating-point rounding errors. Mini cart / cart drawer A panel that shows the cart without leaving the current page. Empty state What a component shows when it has no data ("Your cart is empty"). Always design it.

docs.title: Every page follows the same pattern
docs.text:
1. Use: one sentence on what the thing is for.
  2. Code: a minimal, complete example you can copy.
  3. Output: the same code, rendered live on the page in a box labelled Output.
  4. Notes: common mistakes, and a Senior note with accessibility, performance or architecture advice.
<button type="button">Save</button>
Save

Senior note

Always set type on a <button>. Inside a <form>, a button with no type defaults to type="submit" and will submit the form when someone clicks it.

About the Output boxes

Output boxes sit inside this documentation site, so they pick up a little of its base styling (font, link colour). That's intentional: it shows you how elements look inside a real styled page, not in a bare browser. For a completely unstyled view, paste the code into a blank .html file.

docs.title: Try code yourself
docs.text:
For a full tour of the browser's tools, see Debugging with DevTools.

  • Create test.html, paste any example, and open it in a browser.
  • Open DevTools (F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I, Cmd+Option+I on macOS). In the Elements panel, click the flex or grid badge next to an element to see its layout overlay.
  • Toggle device mode (Ctrl+Shift+M) to test responsive layouts at phone widths.

docs.title: Senior & Architect Track
docs.text:
At 0–5 years, the question is "how do I build this?" At 5–15+ years, it becomes:

  • "Can everyone use this?" → Accessibility
  • "Is it fast on a ₹8,000 Android phone on a 3G connection?" → Performance
  • "Can 50 engineers keep adding to this CSS for 5 years without it rotting?" → CSS Architecture at Scale
  • "Can I explain and defend these decisions?" → Interview Questions

docs.title: What changes as you get more senior
docs.text: Mid-level Senior Staff / Principal Scope A feature A product area Many teams / the platform CSS concern "Does it look right?" "Will it break somewhere else?" "What system makes the wrong thing hard to do?" Accessibility Adds labels and alt text Audits flows; fixes focus management Builds accessible primitives into the design system; sets CI gates Performance Optimises images Owns Core Web Vitals for a product Sets budgets; chooses rendering architecture (SSR, streaming, islands) Browser support Tests in Chrome Tests on real devices Defines the support policy using Baseline; plans feature rollouts Review Gets reviewed Reviews code Reviews designs and architecture before code exists Mentoring Pairs occasionally Mentors juniors Grows other seniors; writes the team's playbook

docs.title: The senior review checklist
docs.text:
Use this on any UI pull request:

  • Semantics: correct elements (button vs link, headings in order, lists, landmarks)?
  • Keyboard: everything reachable and operable with Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, arrows? Focus visible? Focus moved correctly on open/close?
  • Screen reader: accessible names on every control? Dynamic changes announced?
  • Responsive: works at 320px, at 200% zoom, in landscape?
  • Content resilience: long words, long names, missing images, empty states, RTL?
  • Theming: dark mode, high-contrast / forced-colours mode?
  • Motion: respects prefers-reduced-motion?
  • Performance: images sized and lazy-loaded (except LCP), no layout shift, animations on transform/opacity?
  • CSS: uses tokens, no magic numbers, low specificity, no !important, no global leaks?
  • Browser support: new features behind @supports or with an acceptable fallback?

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
About 1 in 6 people worldwide lives with a significant disability (WHO, 2023). Add temporary and situational limits (a broken arm, bright sunlight, a baby in one arm) and accessibility affects everyone. In many countries it's also a legal requirement: the European Accessibility Act has applied to most consumer digital products since June 2025, and India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act covers many digital services.

The standard is WCAG 2.2, level AA.

Hands-on

To practise testing, work through the Accessibility Testing Walkthrough: a page with 10 planted problems, tested with axe, the keyboard, the accessibility tree and a screen reader.

docs.title: The four principles: POUR Intermediate
docs.text: Principle Means Examples Perceivable Users can sense the content Alt text, captions, contrast, no info by colour alone Operable Users can operate the UI Keyboard access, enough time, no seizure triggers, target size Understandable Users can understand it Clear labels, predictable behaviour, helpful errors Robust Works with assistive tech Valid HTML, correct name/role/value

docs.title: The 15 checks that catch most problems Intermediate
docs.text: # Check WCAG How 1 Every image has appropriate alt (empty for decorative) 1.1.1 Inspect / axe 2 Video has captions 1.2.2 <track kind="captions"> 3 Headings form a logical outline 1.3.1 HeadingsMap extension 4 Form fields have visible labels, programmatically linked 1.3.1, 3.3.2 <label for> 5 Inputs have autocomplete tokens for personal data 1.3.5 6 Text contrast ≥ 4.5:1 (≥ 3:1 for large text) 1.4.3 DevTools colour picker 7 UI component and focus ring contrast ≥ 3:1 1.4.11 8 Works at 320px wide / 400% zoom without horizontal scroll 1.4.10 Zoom the browser 9 Text spacing can be increased without breaking 1.4.12 Text spacing bookmarklet 10 Everything works with the keyboard alone 2.1.1 Unplug the mouse 11 No keyboard traps 2.1.2 Tab through modals 12 Focus is always visible and not hidden under sticky headers 2.4.7, 2.4.11 Tab through the page 13 Targets at least 24×24 CSS px 2.5.8 14 Errors are described in text and linked to the field 3.3.1 aria-describedby 15 Custom controls expose name, role, state 4.1.2 Accessibility tree in DevTools

docs.title: Semantic HTML first Beginner
docs.text:
Native elements come with keyboard support, roles and states built in. Compare:

<!-- ❌ 1 line of HTML that needs ~20 lines of JS to become accessible -->
<div class="btn" onclick="save()">Save</div>

<!-- ✅ Accessible by default -->
<button type="button" onclick="save()">Save</button>

What the <div> version is missing: focusability (tabindex="0"), a role (role="button"), Enter and Space key handlers, disabled state, form submission behaviour, and the "button" announcement.

docs.title: Focus management Advanced
docs.text:
/* Never remove outlines without a replacement. This is a strong, accessible default: */
:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #3f51b5;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

/* Keep focused elements visible under sticky headers (WCAG 2.4.11) */
html { scroll-padding-top: 5rem; }

Rules for dynamic UI:

  • Opening a dialog: move focus into it (showModal() does this). Closing: return focus to the button that opened it (<dialog> does this too).
  • Navigating in a single-page app: move focus to the new page's <h1> (with tabindex="-1") or announce the route change.
  • Deleting an item from a list: move focus to the next item, or to the list heading.
  • Off-canvas menus: make the background inert.

docs.title: Colour and contrast Intermediate
docs.text:
<p style="color:#999;background:#fff">#999 on white: 2.8:1 ✗ fails</p>
<p style="color:#767676;background:#fff">#767676 on white: 4.5:1 ✓ passes AA</p>
<p style="color:#595959;background:#fff">#595959 on white: 7:1 ✓ passes AAA</p>

#999 on white: 2.8:1 ✗ fails

#767676 on white: 4.5:1 ✓ passes AA

#595959 on white: 7:1 ✓ passes AAA

Never use colour alone to convey meaning. A red border for an error also needs an icon and text.

docs.title: Forced colours (Windows High Contrast) Advanced
docs.text:
In forced-colours mode, the OS replaces your colours. Backgrounds and box-shadows disappear, so anything that relies on them for meaning (custom checkboxes, focus rings drawn with box-shadow) vanishes.

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .btn { border: 2px solid ButtonText; }        /* system colour keywords */
  .custom-check:checked { background: Highlight; }
}
/* Use outline (not box-shadow) for focus: outlines survive forced colours. */

docs.title: Live regions Advanced
docs.text:
Announce changes that happen without a page load:

<div aria-live="polite" id="cart-status"></div>   <!-- "2 items in cart" -->
<div role="alert">Payment failed. Check your card details.</div>  <!-- assertive -->

The live region must exist in the DOM before you change its content, or screen readers may not announce it.

docs.title: Testing toolkit Intermediate
docs.text:
Tool Catches axe DevTools / Lighthouse ~30–40% of issues automatically (contrast, missing labels, ARIA misuse) Keyboard only Focus order, traps, missing focus styles, unreachable controls Screen readers: NVDA (Windows, free), VoiceOver (macOS/iOS, built in), TalkBack (Android) Names, roles, announcements, reading order Zoom to 400% Reflow and overlap bugs DevTools → Rendering → Emulate vision deficiencies Colour-only meaning @axe-core/playwright in CI Regressions on every PR

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

Automated tools can't tell you if alt text is meaningful, if focus order is logical, or if an error message is helpful. Budget for manual testing of every critical flow (sign-up, checkout, search) with a keyboard and at least one screen reader, and include disabled users in research. Bake accessible primitives (dialog, menu, tabs, combobox) into the design system once, so product teams don't re-implement them badly.

docs.title: CSS Architecture at Scale
docs.text: CSS is easy to write and hard to maintain. Every selector is global by default, and the cascade means a change in one file can break a page you've never seen. Architecture is about making the safe thing easy.

docs.title: The problems you're solving Advanced
docs.text:
1. Global namespace: two teams both write .card.
  2. Specificity creep: someone adds #app .page .card to win; the next person adds !important.
  3. Dead code: nobody dares delete CSS because nobody knows what uses it.
  4. Inconsistency: 47 shades of grey and 23 different paddings.
  5. Ordering bugs: styles depend on which file loaded last.

docs.title: The main approaches Advanced
A layered architecture that scales Expert
docs.text:
/* main.css */
@layer reset, tokens, base, layouts, components, utilities, overrides;

@import url("reset.css")       layer(reset);
@import url("tokens.css")      layer(tokens);       /* custom properties only */
@import url("base.css")        layer(base);         /* element defaults: body, a, h1… */
@import url("layouts.css")     layer(layouts);      /* .stack, .cluster, .sidebar, .grid */
@import url("components/*.css") layer(components);  /* (bundled) */
@import url("utilities.css")   layer(utilities);    /* .visually-hidden, .text-center */
/* third-party CSS goes in 'base' or its own low layer, so your components always win */
Layer Contains Specificity Rule reset Normalisation :where() → 0 Never edited per project tokens :root { --… } — The only place raw values live base Element selectors Low No classes layouts Layout primitives One class No colours or typography components One block per component One or two classes Uses tokens only utilities Single-purpose helpers One class Allowed to override components (layer order, not !important)

docs.title: Layout primitives Advanced
docs.text:
Reusable layout classes, independent of components (from the Every Layout approach):

.stack   > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--stack-space, 1rem); }
.cluster { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: var(--cluster-space, 1rem); align-items: center; }
.center  { box-sizing: content-box; max-inline-size: var(--measure, 65ch); margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: 1rem; }
.auto-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(var(--min, 15rem), 100%), 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
.switcher { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.switcher > * { flex-grow: 1; flex-basis: calc((40rem - 100%) * 999); }   /* row ↔ column at 40rem, no media query */

Components then focus on looks, not layout.

docs.title: Enforcing it Expert
Interview Questions (graded by level)
docs.text: Click a question to reveal a model answer. Answers are short on purpose: in an interview, lead with the core idea, then add depth if asked.

docs.title: 🟢 Beginner (0–2 years)
docs.text:
What's the difference between an element and a tag?

A tag is the markup text (<p>, </p>). An element is the whole thing: opening tag, content and closing tag, which becomes a node in the DOM.

Why do we need <!doctype html>?

It switches the browser into standards mode. Without it, browsers use "quirks mode", which emulates old browser bugs (for example, a different box model).

What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?

Using elements for their meaning (<nav>, <button>, <article>) instead of generic <div>s. It gives accessibility (roles, keyboard support), SEO and maintainability for free.

<button> vs <a>?

Links navigate (change the URL). Buttons perform actions (submit, open, toggle). Using the wrong one breaks keyboard and screen reader expectations.

Block vs inline vs inline-block?

Block: new line, full width, respects width/height. Inline: flows in text, ignores width/height and vertical margins. Inline-block: flows in text but respects width/height/margins.

Explain the box model.

Content → padding → border → margin. With the default box-sizing: content-box, width sets the content only; with border-box, width includes padding and border, which is why every reset uses border-box.

How do you centre a div?

display: grid; place-items: center on the parent. Or flexbox with justify-content: center; align-items: center. For horizontal centring of a block with a width: margin-inline: auto.

rem vs em vs px?

px is fixed. em is relative to the element's own font size (compounds when nested). rem is relative to the root font size and respects the user's browser setting. Use rem for font sizes and most spacing.

What does the viewport meta tag do?

width=device-width, initial-scale=1 tells mobile browsers to use the real device width. Without it, they lay out at ~980px and zoom out, so media queries don't work as expected.

What's the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden?

display: none removes the element from layout and the accessibility tree. visibility: hidden hides it but keeps its space.

docs.title: 🟡 Intermediate (2–5 years)
docs.text:
Explain specificity. Which wins: #nav a or .menu .item a:hover?

Specificity is (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types). #nav a = (1,0,1). .menu .item a:hover = (0,3,1). IDs are compared first, so #nav a wins.

Flexbox vs Grid: when do you use each?

Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts where content size drives layout (navbars, toolbars, button groups). Grid for two-dimensional layouts where you define tracks and place items (page layouts, card grids, dashboards). They're often nested.

Why won't my z-index: 9999 go on top?

z-index only competes within the same stacking context. If an ancestor creates a stacking context (via opacity < 1, transform, filter, position + z-index, isolation…) that sits below another, nothing inside it can escape. Fix the ancestor's stacking, or use the top layer (<dialog>, popover).

What is margin collapse?

Adjacent vertical margins of block elements in normal flow merge into the larger one. It doesn't happen in flex/grid containers, or when padding, a border or a new BFC separates them.

What's the difference between auto-fill and auto-fit?

Both create as many tracks as fit. With few items, auto-fill keeps the empty tracks; auto-fit collapses them so items stretch to fill the row.

How does position: sticky work, and why does it sometimes fail?

It's relative until the element hits its offset (top: 0) within its nearest scrolling ancestor, then it sticks. It fails when there's no offset, when an ancestor has overflow: hidden/auto, or when the parent isn't taller than the sticky element (common in stretched flex/grid items: add align-self: start).

How do you implement dark mode?

Define colours as custom properties, switch them under @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark), set color-scheme: light dark so native controls adapt, and add a [data-theme] override for a manual toggle stored in localStorage. light-dark() shortens this.

How do responsive images work?

srcset with width descriptors lists candidate files, sizes tells the browser how wide the image will display, and the browser picks the best file for the screen's width and pixel density. <picture> with <source media> is for art direction (different crops), and <source type> for format fallbacks (AVIF → WebP → JPEG).

defer vs async?

Both download in parallel without blocking parsing. defer executes in order after parsing finishes. async executes as soon as it downloads, in any order. Modules are deferred by default.

Which CSS properties are cheap to animate, and why?

transform and opacity: the compositor handles them on the GPU without re-running layout or paint. Animating width, height, top or margin triggers layout on every frame.

docs.title: 🟠 Advanced (5–10 years)
docs.text:
Explain the full cascade order.

Origin and importance (transitions > !important user-agent > !important user > !important author > animations > normal author > user > user-agent) → context (shadow DOM) → element-attached styles → cascade layers → specificity → order of appearance.

What problem does @layer solve? How does !important interact with layers?

It orders groups of styles by intent, so a later layer wins regardless of specificity. That makes integrating resets, third-party CSS and utilities predictable without !important. Unlayered styles beat all layers. For !important declarations the layer order reverses, so earlier layers win, which lets low layers protect critical rules.

Media queries vs container queries?

Media queries respond to the viewport; container queries respond to an ancestor's size (or custom-property style). Use media queries for page-level layout and container queries for reusable components that can appear in slots of different widths.

What can :has() replace, and what are its performance considerations?

Parent and previous-sibling styling that used to need JavaScript: form-level error states, layout changes based on content, toggles without JS. Broad selectors like body:has(.x) can trigger expensive style invalidation on DOM changes; keep the anchor element close and the argument specific (.card:has(> img)).

How do you make a custom component (e.g. a dropdown) accessible?

First check for a native element (<select>, <details>, popover). If custom: correct roles and states following the ARIA Authoring Practices pattern, full keyboard support (arrows, Home/End, Escape, typeahead), focus management, an accessible name, aria-expanded/aria-controls, and testing with real screen readers.

How do you diagnose and fix a poor CLS score?

Find the shifting elements (DevTools Performance → Layout Shifts, or the web-vitals attribution build). Typical fixes: width/height or aspect-ratio on media, reserved space for ads and embeds, font metric overrides or font-display: optional, not inserting content above existing content, and animating with transform instead of layout properties.

What creates a containing block for position: fixed?

Normally the viewport. But an ancestor with transform, perspective, filter, backdrop-filter, contain: paint/layout, or will-change naming one of these becomes the containing block, so the "fixed" element scrolls with it.

How would you build a fully accessible modal today?

<dialog> + showModal(): it gives you the top layer, inert background, Escape to close, and focus moved inside and returned on close. Add aria-labelledby to its heading, style ::backdrop, lock page scroll with html:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden }, and use @starting-style for the entry animation.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert (10–15+ years)
docs.text:
How would you structure CSS for a 50-engineer product with a shared design system?

Tokens as the single source of truth (generated for web, iOS, Android and Figma). A cascade-layer architecture (reset, tokens, base, layouts, components, utilities). Scoped component styles (CSS Modules, @scope, or zero-runtime CSS-in-JS). Accessible primitives built once in the design system. Stylelint rules for tokens, specificity and !important; visual regression and axe in CI; Storybook docs; ADRs for each major decision; and a deprecation process for old components.

How do you decide which new CSS features a team may use?

Use Baseline as the default policy ("widely available" is free to use; "newly available" with @supports fallbacks). Cross-check with your own analytics (which browsers your users actually have). Require progressive enhancement: the experience must work without the feature. Document approved features and their fallbacks in the team's guidelines, and review the list every quarter.

Utility-first CSS vs component CSS: how do you choose?

Utilities: fast iteration, guaranteed token use, no dead CSS, great for app teams owning their own UI. Component CSS: cleaner markup, better for a design system consumed by many teams and frameworks, easier to theme at the component level. Many orgs combine them: a component library styled internally, with utilities for layout glue. The deciding factors are team size and structure, how many consumers there are, and whether you need framework independence.

A page's INP is 450 ms on mid-range Android. Walk through your approach.

Measure first with RUM attribution to find the slow interactions and their phase (input delay, processing, presentation). Typical causes: long main-thread tasks from hydration or third-party scripts, heavy event handlers, huge DOM style recalculations. Fixes: break up long tasks (scheduler.yield()), defer non-critical JS, replace JS widgets with native elements, use content-visibility and containment to shrink rendering work, cut DOM size, and move work off the main thread. Verify with field data after release, not just lab data.

How do you make accessibility sustainable rather than a one-off audit?

Shift left: accessible primitives in the design system, accessibility acceptance criteria in tickets, design reviews that check focus order and contrast, automated checks in CI as a floor (not a ceiling), manual keyboard and screen-reader testing on critical flows each release, accessibility champions in each team, and including disabled users in research. Track issues as bugs with severity, not as "nice to have".

Explain the trade-offs of Shadow DOM for a cross-framework design system.

Pros: true style encapsulation, framework-agnostic custom elements, slots for composition. Cons: global styles (resets, fonts, utilities) don't reach inside; theming needs custom properties and ::part; SSR needs declarative shadow DOM; form participation needs ElementInternals; ARIA ID references can't cross shadow boundaries yet (reference target is still being standardised). Many teams use light-DOM components with @scope or CSS Modules instead, unless they truly need to serve multiple frameworks.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Speed is a feature. Slow pages lose users and rank lower in search. Google's Core Web Vitals are the shared yardstick.

docs.title: Core Web Vitals Intermediate
docs.text:
Metric Measures Good HTML/CSS levers LCP: Largest Contentful Paint When the main content (hero image or headline) appears ≤ 2.5 s Preload / fetchpriority="high" on the hero image, never lazy-load it, inline critical CSS, fast fonts INP: Interaction to Next Paint How quickly the page responds to taps and clicks ≤ 200 ms Less JS; native elements (dialog, details, popover) instead of heavy widgets; content-visibility to shrink rendering work CLS: Cumulative Layout Shift How much things jump around while loading ≤ 0.1 width/height on images and iframes, aspect-ratio, reserved space for ads/embeds, font-display + metric overrides

Measured at the 75th percentile of real users. Check yours with PageSpeed Insights (field data) and DevTools Performance panel (lab data).

docs.title: The critical rendering path Advanced
docs.text:
flowchart LR HTML --> DOM CSS --> CSSOM DOM --> RT[Render tree] CSSOM --> RT RT --> Layout --> Paint --> Composite JS -. "blocks parsing<br/>(unless defer/async/module)" .-> DOM
  • CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't paint until it has the CSS. Keep the critical CSS small; split the rest.
  • Classic <script> is parser-blocking. Use defer or type="module".
  • Every change to layout properties (width, top, font-size) re-runs Layout → Paint → Composite. Changes to transform and opacity only re-run Composite.

docs.title: HTML wins Intermediate
docs.text:
<!-- Hero image: high priority, no lazy loading, explicit size -->
<img src="hero.avif" alt="…" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async">

<!-- Below-the-fold images: lazy -->
<img src="card.avif" alt="…" width="400" height="300" loading="lazy" decoding="async">

<!-- Iframes (maps, videos): lazy -->
<iframe src="…" title="…" loading="lazy" width="560" height="315"></iframe>

<!-- Early connections to critical third-party origins -->
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com" crossorigin>

<!-- Preload the main web font -->
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

<!-- Speculative prefetch/prerender of likely next pages (Chromium) -->
<script type="speculationrules">
  { "prerender": [{ "where": { "href_matches": "/product/*" }, "eagerness": "moderate" }] }
</script>

docs.title: CSS wins Advanced
docs.text:
/* Skip rendering work for off-screen sections until they're near the viewport */
.section {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: auto 800px;   /* placeholder height so the scrollbar is stable */
}

/* Isolate a widget so its changes don't trigger page-wide layout */
.widget { contain: layout paint; }

/* Animate only compositor-friendly properties */
.card { transition: transform .2s, opacity .2s; }

/* Reserve space for late-loading content */
.ad-slot { min-height: 250px; }
.embed { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
  • Avoid @import in production CSS: each import is a sequential request.
  • Remove unused CSS: the DevTools Coverage tab shows how much of each file is used.
  • Avoid huge DOMs: over ~1,500 nodes slows style recalculation and layout. Virtualise long lists.
  • Fonts: WOFF2 only, subset to the characters you need, variable fonts instead of 6 separate weights, font-display: optional or swap with metric overrides.

docs.title: Images Intermediate
docs.text: Do Why AVIF → WebP → JPEG via <picture> AVIF is often ~50% smaller than JPEG srcset + sizes Phones don't download desktop-sized images width + height attributes Prevents CLS loading="lazy" below the fold Saves bandwidth SVG for icons and logos Tiny and sharp at any size <video> instead of GIF 5–20× smaller

docs.title: Budgets Expert
docs.text:
Set limits, then enforce them in CI (Lighthouse CI, size-limit, bundlewatch):

Resource Example budget (mid-range mobile) Critical CSS (inlined) ≤ 14 KB compressed (fits in the first TCP round trip) Total CSS ≤ 60 KB compressed JS on initial load ≤ 150 KB compressed Hero image ≤ 150 KB Web fonts ≤ 2 files, ≤ 100 KB total LCP (lab, Moto G Power, slow 4G) ≤ 2.5 s

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

The biggest performance wins are usually architectural, not micro-optimisations: ship less JavaScript (server-render, islands, native HTML features), cache aggressively at the CDN with immutable hashed assets, and measure real users (RUM via the web-vitals library) rather than trusting a fast laptop. Make performance visible: a dashboard of p75 LCP/INP/CLS per page type, reviewed every sprint.

docs.title: Learning Roadmap: 0 to 15+ Years
docs.text:
Frontend skill doesn't grow in a straight line. It grows in layers: first you make things appear, then you make them work everywhere, then you make them fast and accessible, then you make it possible for fifty other people to do the same without breaking each other's work.

flowchart LR A["🟢 Beginner<br/>0–2 yrs<br/>Make it appear"] --> B["🟡 Intermediate<br/>2–5 yrs<br/>Make it work everywhere"] B --> C["🟠 Advanced<br/>5–10 yrs<br/>Make it fast, accessible, robust"] C --> D["🔴 Expert<br/>10–15+ yrs<br/>Make it scale across teams"]

docs.title: 🟢 Beginner (0–2 years): make it appear
docs.text:
You can: build a static page from a design, using semantic HTML and a single stylesheet.

  • Write a valid HTML document from memory (<!doctype html>, lang, charset, viewport meta).
  • Choose the right element: <button> vs <a>, <ul> vs <ol>, <section> vs <div>.
  • Explain the box model and why box-sizing: border-box is everyone's default.
  • Use class selectors, descendant and child combinators, :hover and :focus-visible.
  • Use rem for font sizes and know why px font sizes hurt accessibility.
  • Build a navbar and a card row with Flexbox.
  • Build a responsive card grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(…)).
  • Write one mobile-first media query.
  • Build an accessible form: every input has a <label>.

Done looks like: you can rebuild the pricing table and sticky header recipes without looking.

docs.title: 🟡 Intermediate (2–5 years): make it work everywhere
docs.text:
You can: ship production UI that works on every screen size and browser your users have, and debug layout bugs quickly.

  • Explain the cascade in order: origin & importance → context → layers → specificity → order.
  • Debug stacking-context bugs (why z-index: 9999 "doesn't work").
  • Know when to pick Flexbox vs Grid, and use grid-template-areas.
  • Use custom properties for theming, and implement dark mode with prefers-color-scheme.
  • Serve responsive images with srcset/sizes and <picture>.
  • Use <dialog>, <details>, and the popover API instead of hand-rolled JS widgets.
  • Animate only transform and opacity, and honour prefers-reduced-motion.
  • Use the DevTools Layout, Computed and Rendering panels fluently.

Done looks like: you can rebuild the whole Layout Gallery from screenshots.

docs.title: 🟠 Advanced (5–10 years): make it fast, accessible and robust
docs.text:
You can: own the quality of a product's UI: performance budgets, WCAG compliance and resilient CSS.

  • Meet WCAG 2.2 AA: contrast, focus order, focus visibility, target size, reduced motion.
  • Know the first rule of ARIA (don't use ARIA if a native element does the job) and when ARIA is necessary.
  • Diagnose LCP, INP and CLS problems and fix them with HTML/CSS levers (fetchpriority, width/height, content-visibility, font loading).
  • Use container queries to build components that adapt to their slot, not the viewport.
  • Use @layer to make third-party and utility CSS predictable.
  • Use :has() to replace JS-driven state classes.
  • Write progressive enhancement: wrap newer features in @supports with a working fallback.

Done looks like: you can audit an existing page and produce a prioritised list of accessibility and performance fixes.

docs.title: 🔴 Expert (10–15+ years): make it scale across teams
docs.text:
You can: set the frontend direction for an organisation. Your decisions let dozens of engineers ship consistent UI without stepping on each other.

  • Design a token system (colour, space, type, radius, motion) and its naming.
  • Choose and justify a CSS architecture (utility-first, CSS Modules, @layer + BEM, CSS-in-JS) for a given team and product.
  • Set up linting, visual regression testing and accessibility checks in CI.
  • Plan browser support using Baseline, and roll out new CSS features safely.
  • Review designs for feasibility and accessibility before a line of code is written.
  • Mentor: explain any concept on this site to a beginner in two minutes.

Done looks like: you can write the CSS Architecture page for your own company, and other teams adopt it.

docs.title: Time budget
docs.text: Level Hours/week Focus split 🟢 8–10 40% HTML, 40% CSS, 20% layout 🟡 4–6 50% layout & responsive, 30% modern CSS, 20% DevTools 🟠 3–4 40% accessibility, 40% performance, 20% modern CSS 🔴 2–3 Architecture, standards tracking, mentoring

docs.title: Cascade order (who wins)
docs.text:
1. Origin & importance: transitions → !important (user-agent > user > author) → animations → normal author → user → user-agent
  2. Context: outer (light DOM) vs shadow DOM
  3. Inline style=""
  4. Cascade layers: later @layer wins (reversed for !important); unlayered beats all layers
  5. Specificity: (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements)
  6. Order: last declared wins

docs.title: Responsive Design Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Full guide: Responsive Design.

docs.title: The essentials
docs.text:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

img, video { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }          /* media never overflows */
.container { width: min(100% - 2rem, 75rem); margin-inline: auto; }

Mobile-first: write the phone layout as the base, then add min-width queries for bigger screens.

docs.title: Breakpoints
docs.text:
Token min-width Typical screen sm 40em (640px) Large phone, landscape md 48em (768px) Tablet portrait lg 64em (1024px) Tablet landscape, small laptop xl 80em (1280px) Laptop / desktop 2xl 96em (1536px) Large desktop

Add breakpoints where your content breaks, not for specific devices. Use em so breakpoints respect the user's font size.

docs.title: Media query syntax
docs.text:
@media (width >= 48em) { }                       /* range syntax */
@media (40em <= width < 64em) { }                /* between */
@media (min-width: 48em) { }                     /* classic */
@media (max-width: 47.99em) { }                  /* below */
@media screen and (orientation: landscape) { }   /* and */
@media (width < 40em), (orientation: portrait) { }  /* comma = or */
@media not print { }                             /* not */
.card { @media (width >= 48em) { padding: 2rem; } }  /* nested */

docs.title: Media features
Container queries
docs.text:
.slot { container: card / inline-size; }       /* name / type */

@container card (width >= 30rem) { .card { grid-template-columns: 10rem 1fr; } }
@container (width < 20rem) { .card .meta { display: none; } }
@container style(--variant: compact) { .card { padding: .5rem; } }   /* style query */

.card h2 { font-size: clamp(1rem, 4cqi, 1.75rem); }   /* container units */
container-type Allows queries on inline-size Width (most common) size Width and height (the container needs an explicit height) normal Style queries only

Media query = page layout. Container query = component layout.

docs.title: Intrinsic layouts (no breakpoints at all)
docs.text:
/* Cards that reflow from 1 to N columns */
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(15rem, 100%), 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }

/* Sidebar that drops above content when there's no room */
.with-sidebar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.with-sidebar > :first-child { flex: 1 1 15rem; }
.with-sidebar > :last-child  { flex: 999 1 0; min-inline-size: 60%; }

/* Row ↔ column switch at a container width of 40rem */
.switcher { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.switcher > * { flex-grow: 1; flex-basis: calc((40rem - 100%) * 999); }

/* Wrapping cluster of tags/buttons */
.cluster { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: .5rem; align-items: center; }

docs.title: Fluid type & space
docs.text:
:root {
  --step-0: clamp(1rem, .93rem + .36vw, 1.2rem);       /* body */
  --step-1: clamp(1.2rem, 1.09rem + .54vw, 1.5rem);     /* h4 */
  --step-2: clamp(1.44rem, 1.28rem + .8vw, 1.88rem);    /* h3 */
  --step-3: clamp(1.73rem, 1.5rem + 1.15vw, 2.34rem);   /* h2 */
  --step-4: clamp(2.07rem, 1.75rem + 1.63vw, 2.93rem);  /* h1 */
  --space-s: clamp(.75rem, .6rem + .6vw, 1rem);
  --space-m: clamp(1rem, .8rem + 1vw, 1.5rem);
  --space-l: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
}

• LCP image: fetchpriority="high", not lazy, preloaded if it's a CSS background

docs.title: Coding Interview: 12 Frontend Machine-Coding Problems
docs.text:
Frontend interviews include a machine-coding round: build a layout or widget in 45–60 minutes, then explain your choices. Interviewers check four things: it works at every screen size, it's accessible (keyboard, screen readers), the code is modern and simple (Grid, Flexbox, <dialog>, custom properties rather than hacks), and you can write the core JavaScript utilities (debounce, Promise.all, deep clone) from memory.

Every solution here is a self-contained file you can open, read and resize. More importantly, every one is verified in a real browser: coding-interview/run-tests.mjs uses Playwright and Chromium to measure real layout geometry at several viewport widths, press real keys, check focus and ARIA state, and test the JavaScript utilities with mock timers. That's 42 checks, run by CI on every change. Each page shows the live demo and its real check report.

Writing those checks exposed four real bugs in the first drafts, and the pages keep them as lessons: - invisible radio inputs stealing clicks from the star rating - screen-reader text hidden with hidden - an IntersectionObserver feed that stalls on tall screens - a colour transition that fooled a test

Each page follows the same structure:

  1. Problem: the statement as an interviewer would give it.
  2. Key idea: the shape of the solution before any code, with a diagram.
  3. Solution: the complete, runnable code (included from the repository, so it is exactly what CI ran).
  4. Walkthrough: the important lines and why they are written that way.
  5. Complexity: time and space for each approach.
  6. Run it: the command and its real output.
  7. Common mistakes and follow-up questions with answers.

docs.title: How to answer a coding round
docs.text:
1. Clarify the target: breakpoints, browsers, whether it must work without JavaScript, and accessibility expectations. Ask before you code.
  2. Semantic HTML first (<dialog>, <button>, radio inputs, landmarks). Native elements give you keyboard and screen-reader support for free.
  3. Layout with Grid or Flexbox, mobile first, and add complexity at larger breakpoints. Avoid fixed heights and magic numbers.
  4. Then the JavaScript: small, event-driven, with no layout thrashing (batch DOM writes, use observers instead of scroll handlers).
  5. Demonstrate it: resize the window, use only the keyboard, turn on dark mode. Say what you would test and how.

docs.title: 1. Center Anything: Three Ways
docs.text: L1 ★☆☆ · Grid place-items, Flexbox, absolute + translate

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Center an element horizontally and vertically inside a container, three ways, and explain when you would use each.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Grid (display: grid; place-items: center) is the shortest. Flexbox (justify-content + align-items) is natural when there are several items in a row. Absolute positioning (inset: 50% auto auto 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%)) takes the element out of the flow, which is what you want for overlays, badges and spinners on top of other content.

flowchart LR Q{"Is the element in the normal flow?"} -->|yes, single child| G["grid + place-items: center"] Q -->|yes, several items in a row| F["flex + justify-content + align-items"] Q -->|no: overlay / badge| A["position: absolute + translate(-50%, -50%)"]

docs.title: Solution
Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 01-centering.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why .grid { display: grid; place-items: center; } place-items is shorthand for align-items plus justify-items. One line, both axes. .flex { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; } Main axis plus cross axis. Swap them mentally if flex-direction: column. inset: 50% auto auto 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%); Moves the top-left corner to the centre, then shifts back by half the element's own size. No need to know its width. .box { position: relative; } The containing block for the absolutely positioned child. Forgetting it centres the item on the page instead. check: item centre == box centre (±1.5 px) at 1200 and 375 px Verified by measuring getBoundingClientRect() in Chromium at two widths.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• margin: auto without a width or a flex/grid parent. It centres horizontally only, and only block elements with a width.
  • text-align: center on a block element. That centres its inline content, not the box.
  • top: 50%; left: 50% without the translate, which centres the corner rather than the element.
  • line-height tricks for vertical centring. They break as soon as the text wraps.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you center a fixed-size modal without JavaScript?

Use <dialog> (problem 5): the browser centres it with margin: auto in the top layer. For a plain element: position: fixed; inset: 0; margin: auto; width: …; height: fit-content.

What does margin: auto do in Flexbox and Grid?

It absorbs all free space in that direction. margin-left: auto on the last nav item pushes it to the far right, and margin: auto on a single flex child centres it on both axes.

docs.title: 2. Holy Grail Layout with Grid Areas
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · grid-template-areas, mobile first, 100dvh, source order

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build a page with a header, footer, left navigation, main content and right sidebar. On desktop the three columns sit side by side and the footer stays at the bottom even when the content is short. On mobile everything stacks in reading order.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Name the regions with grid-template-areas, then redraw the "map" at each breakpoint. The HTML keeps semantic source order (header, nav, main, aside, footer), which is also the mobile and screen-reader order. min-height: 100dvh with a 1fr main row keeps the footer at the bottom without any position tricks.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reordering the DOM for the desktop design, or using order:/areas to put content in an illogical place. Keyboard and screen-reader order follow the DOM.
  • Fixed pixel heights on main or sidebar. Content overflows on small screens or large fonts.
  • Floats and calc(100% - 440px) for columns. Grid handles it with 200px 1fr 240px.
  • Forgetting <nav aria-label=…> and the landmark elements. They're how screen-reader users jump around the page.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Grid or Flexbox for page layout?

Grid for two-dimensional layouts (rows and columns aligned together, such as page skeletons and dashboards). Flexbox for one-dimensional flows (a toolbar, a row of buttons, centring). They nest happily: the page uses grid, the header uses flex.

How would you make the sidebar collapsible?

Toggle a class on .page that changes grid-template-columns to 0 1fr 240px (or redraws the areas), and animate with transition: grid-template-columns, which modern browsers support. Keep the toggle a real <button aria-expanded>.

docs.title: 3. Responsive Card Grid (No Media Queries)
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · repeat(auto-fit, minmax()), min(), subgrid-free alignment

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Show product cards in as many columns as fit (each at least 260 px), with no media queries, no horizontal scroll on a 320 px phone, and the "Buy" buttons aligned at the bottom of every card in a row even when descriptions differ in length.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(260px, 100%), 1fr)) creates as many columns as fit and stretches them to fill the row. min(260px, 100%) stops a 260 px minimum from overflowing a narrower screen. Inside each card, a grid with a 1fr row for the text pushes the button to the bottom. Because the grid row stretches every card to the same height, the buttons line up.

flowchart LR W["container width"] --> C{"how many 260px+ columns fit?"} C -->|"1200 px"| C4["4 columns"] C -->|"700 px"| C2["2 columns"] C -->|"375 px"| C1["1 column"] C -->|"320 px"| CM["1 column, min(260px, 100%) → no overflow"]

Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 03-card-grid.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(260px, 100%), 1fr)) auto-fit collapses empty tracks so the cards stretch. auto-fill would keep empty columns, which suits fixed-width cards. min(260px, 100%) A defensive minimum. Without it, a 260 px minimum on a 300 px-wide container with padding forces horizontal scroll. grid-template-rows: auto auto 1fr auto; Image, title, flexible text, then the button. The 1fr row absorbs the extra height. aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; Images reserve their space before loading (no layout shift, good for CLS) and crop instead of stretching. check: 4 / 2 / 1 columns at 1200 / 700 / 375 px; equal button bottoms; no overflow at 320 px Measured in Chromium by grouping the cards' top values.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Media queries for every breakpoint (@media (min-width: 768px) { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr) }), which breaks at sizes nobody tested.
  • Flexbox with flex-wrap and percentage widths. The last row's cards stretch to odd sizes.
  • Fixed card heights to align the buttons. Text overflows as soon as it wraps or the user zooms.
  • Images without dimensions or aspect-ratio, so the content jumps when they load.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you align titles across cards too, not just buttons?

Use subgrid: make each card grid-row: span 4; display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; inside a parent grid with grid-auto-rows: auto auto 1fr auto. Every card then shares the same row tracks, so titles and text blocks align across the row.

Container queries: when would you use them here?

When the card's own width should change its layout (image beside the text once the card is wider than 400 px), regardless of the viewport. Set container-type: inline-size on the card wrapper and use @container (min-width: 400px) { … }.

docs.title: 4. Sticky Header & Sticky Table Header
docs.text: L1 ★★☆ · position: sticky, scroll containers, scroll-padding-top

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Make the site header stay visible while scrolling, make a table's header row stay visible inside its own scrollable box, and make in-page anchor links land below the sticky header instead of underneath it.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
position: sticky; top: 0 behaves like relative until its scroll container scrolls it to top: 0, then it sticks. The nearest scrolling ancestor is the reference, so the same declaration on th sticks inside .scroll, not the page. scroll-padding-top on html offsets anchor jumps and scrollIntoView by the header's height.

flowchart TB V["viewport scrolls"] --> H["header: sticky, top 0 → pinned to the viewport"] S[".scroll box scrolls"] --> T["th: sticky, top 0 → pinned inside the box"] A["#faq link / scrollIntoView"] --> P["html { scroll-padding-top: 56px } → lands below the header"]

Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 04-sticky-header.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.text: Code Why .site-header { position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 10; } top is required: sticky does nothing without an offset. z-index keeps it above content that scrolls under it. background: rgb(255 255 255 / .9); backdrop-filter: blur(8px); A frosted header: content stays readable as it scrolls underneath. th { position: sticky; top: 0; } Sticky inside .scroll because that's the nearest scroll container. border-collapse: separate avoids rendering glitches with sticky cells. html { scroll-padding-top: 56px; } Without it, #faq scrolls under the header. The check verifies the heading lands below it. .scroll { tabindex=0 aria-label=… } A scrollable region must be focusable so keyboard users can scroll it, and labelled so screen readers announce it.

  ✔ table header sticks inside its own scroll container
  ✔ jump links land below the header (scroll-padding-top)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• overflow: hidden (or auto) on an ancestor. That ancestor becomes the scroll container, and sticky silently stops working on the page.
  • Forgetting top: 0.
  • Using position: fixed plus a hard-coded padding-top on the body. The header leaves the flow and the padding gets out of sync with its height.
  • Scroll listeners that toggle classes on every scroll event, which causes jank. Use sticky, or IntersectionObserver for "is it stuck?" styling.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you style the header differently once it's stuck?

Put a 1 px sentinel just above the header and observe it with IntersectionObserver. When the sentinel leaves the viewport, add a .stuck class (for example to add a shadow). Scroll-driven animations (animation-timeline: scroll()) can also do it in pure CSS.

Why might sticky not work inside a flex or grid parent?

If the sticky item stretches to the full height of its parent (the default align-items: stretch), there's no room to stick. Give it align-self: start.

docs.title: 5. Accessible Modal Dialog
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · showModal(), ::backdrop, focus management, method=dialog

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build a confirmation modal: it blocks the rest of the page, focus moves into it, Esc closes it, clicking the backdrop cancels, focus returns to the button that opened it, and the result (confirmed or cancelled) is reported.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
The native <dialog> with showModal() does the hard parts. It renders in the top layer (no z-index wars), makes the rest of the page inert (no focus or clicks outside), closes on Esc, and supports autofocus. A form with method="dialog" closes it and puts the clicked button's value in dialog.returnValue. You add backdrop-click handling and returning focus to the opener.

sequenceDiagram participant U as user participant B as "Delete account…" button participant D as dialog U->>B: click B->>D: showModal() → top layer, page inert, focus → input (autofocus) U->>D: Esc / backdrop click / Cancel / Delete D-->>D: close(returnValue) D->>B: focus() (return focus)

Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 05-modal-dialog.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why dialog.showModal() Not show(), which opens a non-modal dialog without inertness or a backdrop. <dialog aria-labelledby="confirm-title" aria-describedby="confirm-desc"> Screen readers announce the title and description when it opens. <form method="dialog"> … <button value="delete"> Submitting closes the dialog and sets returnValue. No preventDefault and no manual close(). formnovalidate on Cancel skips validation. if (e.target === dialog) dialog.close("cancel") Clicks on the ::backdrop are dispatched to the dialog element itself. Clicks inside hit the form or its children. opener.focus() Returning focus is part of the pattern. Otherwise keyboard users are dropped at the top of the document. check: page.waitForFunction(result !== "") The close event fires asynchronously. The first version of the check read the result too early and was flaky, so it now waits.

  ✔ Escape closes it and focus returns to the opener
  ✔ clicking the backdrop cancels
  ✔ typing DELETE and confirming deletes

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building a modal from <div>s, which means hand-writing the focus trap, inertness, Esc handling, ARIA roles and z-index.
  • Not returning focus to the opener on close.
  • Animating with display changes that remove the closing animation, or ignoring prefers-reduced-motion.
  • Putting critical content only in the modal for mobile users, where small viewports clip it. Use width: min(420px, 100% - 32px) and let the content scroll.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you prevent the page behind from scrolling?

Modern CSS: body:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }. Watch for layout shift as the scrollbar disappears. scrollbar-gutter: stable on html reserves its space.

Dialog vs the Popover API?

<dialog> with showModal() is for modal interactions that must be answered. The popover attribute (popover, popovertarget) is for non-modal overlays such as menus and tooltips that light-dismiss. It's also in the top layer, but it doesn't make the page inert.

docs.title: 6. Accessible Tabs (Roving Tabindex)
docs.text: L2 ★★★ · WAI-ARIA tabs pattern, aria-selected, arrow / Home / End keys

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build tabs that work with a mouse and keyboard and screen readers. The tab list is one Tab stop, arrow keys move between tabs (wrapping around), Home and End jump to the ends, and only the selected panel is visible.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Follow the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern: role="tablist", role="tab" with aria-selected and aria-controls, and role="tabpanel" with aria-labelledby. Use a roving tabindex: the selected tab has tabindex="0" and the others -1, so Tab enters the list once and the next Tab goes to the panel. Arrow keys change the selection and move focus.

stateDiagram-v2 direction LR Profile --> Security: ArrowRight Security --> Billing: ArrowRight Billing --> Profile: ArrowRight (wrap) Profile --> Billing: End / ArrowLeft (wrap) Billing --> Profile: Home

docs.title: Solution
Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 06-tabs.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why <button role="tab" aria-controls="panel-security" aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1"> Real buttons are focusable and clickable. tabindex=-1 removes the inactive tabs from the Tab order. t.tabIndex = on ? 0 : -1 The roving tabindex. The check confirms that exactly one tab has tabindex=0 after any number of key presses. { ArrowRight: i + 1, ArrowLeft: i - 1, Home: 0, End: tabs.length - 1 }[e.key] A lookup table instead of a switch, with modulo for wrap-around. e.preventDefault() Stops Home and End from scrolling the page. role="tabpanel" tabindex="0" Makes the panel itself focusable, so the next Tab after the tab list lands on the content. The check asserts this order.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Every tab in the Tab order. Keyboard users then press Tab several times just to get past the tabs.
  • Using <div>s with click handlers and no keyboard support or roles.
  • Hiding panels with opacity: 0. They stay focusable and readable. Use hidden.
  • Forgetting aria-selected, so screen readers can't tell which tab is active.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Automatic vs manual activation?

Automatic (this solution): arrow keys move focus and select. That's good when panels render instantly. Manual: arrows move focus only, and Enter or Space selects. Use it when showing a panel is expensive, for example when it fetches data.

When should tabs be links instead?

When each "tab" is really a separate page or URL (site sections). Then use a <nav> with links and aria-current="page", not the tabs pattern.

docs.title: 7. Star Rating with Zero JavaScript
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Radio inputs, row-reverse + ~, visually-hidden pattern, content: "★" / ""

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build a 5-star rating input. Hovering previews the rating, clicking sets it, it works with the keyboard and screen readers, it submits with a form, and it uses no JavaScript.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Use radio inputs for the semantics: keyboard arrows, form value and screen-reader names all come for free. CSS can only select later siblings (~), so put the stars in DOM order 5→1 and display them with flex-direction: row-reverse. "Checked and all stars below it" then becomes input:checked ~ label. Hide the inputs visually (the clip pattern), never with display: none, hidden or a full-size opacity: 0.

flowchart LR DOM["DOM order: s5 s4 s3 s2 s1"] --> RR["row-reverse → shows 1 2 3 4 5"] CK["s4:checked"] --> SIB["s4 ~ label → labels of s4, s3, s2, s1"] SIB --> LIT["4 stars lit"]

docs.title: Solution
Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 07-star-rating.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why .rating { flex-direction: row-reverse; } Visual order is reversed, so the sibling combinator selects the stars to the left of the checked one. .rating input:checked ~ label { color: #f59e0b; } The checked star and every later sibling (the lower ratings) light up. The check counts exactly 4 amber stars after clicking the 4th. .rating input { width: 1px; height: 1px; clip-path: inset(50%); } Bug found by the checks: the first draft used opacity: 0 at full size, and the five invisible inputs stacked over the first star and intercepted clicks. Clipping keeps them focusable without taking space. <span class="sr-only">4 stars</span> Bug found by the checks: the first draft used <span hidden>, which hides the text from screen readers too, so the radios had no names. The check asserts getByRole('radio', { name: '4 stars' }). content: "★" / ""; Alternative text for generated content. The decorative star isn't read aloud as "black star".

docs.text: Approach Time Space interaction O(1), pure CSS -

  ✔ clicking the 4th star checks 4 and lights up exactly 4 stars
  ✔ each star has an accessible name and the stars ARE native radios
  ✔ arrow keys change the rating (keyboard support for free)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• display: none on the inputs, which removes them from the keyboard and accessibility tree. The rating becomes mouse-only.
  • Building it from <span>s with click handlers: no keyboard support, no form value, no semantics.
  • Forgetting a group label (<fieldset> + <legend>), so screen readers don't know what the stars rate.
  • Hover-only previews with no focus styling for keyboard users (:focus-visible + label).

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you support half stars?

Use ten radio inputs (0.5 steps) whose labels each cover half a star (clip-path or a half-width ::before), or use a native <input type="range" step="0.5"> styled as stars. The range input announces its value and supports arrow keys.

How do you show a read-only average like 3.7?

Don't use inputs. Render the text 3.7 out of 5 for assistive technology and draw the stars with a background gradient or mask whose width is calc(3.7 / 5 * 100%).

docs.title: 8. Dark Mode with Custom Properties
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Design tokens, prefers-color-scheme, data-theme override, no flash

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Support light and dark themes. Follow the OS setting by default, let the user override it with a toggle, remember the choice, and avoid a flash of the wrong theme on load. Components must not contain colour values.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Components use tokens only (var(--bg), var(--fg)). A theme is just a different set of token values: light on :root, dark inside @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) unless the user forced light, and dark again under [data-theme="dark"]. A tiny inline script in <head> applies the saved choice before first paint. Setting color-scheme makes form controls and scrollbars match too.

flowchart TD L["page load"] --> S{"saved choice in localStorage?"} S -->|yes| D["set data-theme before first paint"] S -->|no| O["follow prefers-color-scheme"] D & O --> T["tokens: --bg --fg --card --accent"] T --> C["components use var(--…) only"] B["toggle click"] --> W["data-theme = opposite; save; aria-pressed"]

docs.title: Solution
Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 08-theme-toggle.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { … } } Dark by OS preference, unless the user explicitly chose light. :root[data-theme="dark"] { … } Dark by explicit choice, even when the OS is light. <script> try { … localStorage.getItem("theme") … } catch (e) {} </script> in <head> Runs before the body renders, so there's no flash. try covers private modes where storage throws. color-scheme: dark; The browser also darkens native UI: scrollbars, form controls, <dialog> backgrounds. check: assert on --bg, not body background Lesson from the checks: body has a 0.2 s colour transition, so getComputedStyle(body).backgroundColor read just after the click was still dark. The token isn't transitioned, so assert on it.
