docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hard-coded colours in components (color: #333). Every component then needs a dark override.
  • Applying the saved theme in a script at the end of <body>, which flashes light, then dark.
  • A toggle with only two states that ignores the OS. Users who change the OS theme at night expect the site to follow unless they chose otherwise.
  • Forgetting aria-pressed (or a clear label) on the toggle.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How would you offer light, dark and system?

Use a three-option control (radio group or select). "System" removes data-theme and the saved value, so the media query takes over again. Listen to matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').onchange only if JavaScript needs to know the theme.

What about the new light-dark() function?

color: light-dark(#0f172a, #e2e8f0) picks a value based on the element's color-scheme. Combined with color-scheme: light dark on :root (and color-scheme: dark for a forced theme), it removes most media-query duplication.

docs.title: 9. Debounce & Throttle from Scratch
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Timers, closures, this, leading/trailing edges, mock timers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement debounce(fn, wait, { leading, trailing }) and throttle(fn, wait). Preserve this and the latest arguments, and provide cancel(). Test them without waiting in real time.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Debounce restarts a timer on every call and runs only when calls stop for wait ms (search boxes, resize end). Throttle runs at most once per wait ms while calls keep coming: immediately, then the latest pending call at the end of each window (scroll, mousemove). Both are closures over timer state. Node's mock.timers (with Date) makes the tests instant and exact.

sequenceDiagram participant E as events (every 10 ms) participant D as debounce 200 ms participant T as throttle 50 ms E->>D: j, ja, jav, java, javas Note over D: timer restarts each time D-->>D: 200 ms of quiet → fn("javas") E->>T: 0, 1, 2 … 10 T-->>T: fn(0) now, fn(4) at 50 ms, fn(9) at 100 ms, fn(10) at 150 ms

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => { … fn.apply(lastThis, lastArgs) }, wait) The core of debounce: each call cancels the pending run, and only the last one survives. lastArgs = args; lastThis = this; The trailing call uses the latest arguments and the correct this, so it works as an object method (obj.inc). const callNow = leading && timer === null; Leading edge: fire on the first call of a burst, and don't fire again at the end unless more calls came in. const remaining = wait - (now - last); if (remaining <= 0) { …call now… } else { …schedule trailing… } Throttle: call immediately when the window has passed, otherwise remember the latest arguments and schedule one trailing call. assert.deepEqual(calls, [0, 4, 9, 10]) Lesson from the checks: the first expectation ([0, 5, 10]) was wrong. Throttle's trailing call carries the latest arguments in each window. The check also asserts at most one call per 50 ms.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space each call O(1) O(1)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd coding-interview && npm test   # runs every check; this problem's report is below

09-debounce-throttle: 4 checks, 0 failures
  ✔ debounce: 5 rapid calls -> 1 call with the LAST arguments
  ✔ debounce leading: fires immediately, then once more at the end
  ✔ debounce keeps `this` and cancel() drops the pending call
  ✔ throttle: calls every 10 ms -> first call, then the LATEST call at each 50 ms window end

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using arrow functions for the returned wrapper, so this is lost when it's used as a method.
  • Calling fn(...args) from the first call instead of the latest one on the trailing edge, which searches for "j" instead of "javas".
  • Creating a new debounced function on every render (React) so the timer never accumulates. Memoise it with useMemo/useRef.
  • Testing with real setTimeout and arbitrary sleeps, which gives slow, flaky tests.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Which would you use for a search box, window resize and infinite scroll?

Search box: debounce (about 300 ms), plus cancelling stale requests (AbortController). Resize: debounce for expensive recalculation, or ResizeObserver. Scroll position: throttle or requestAnimationFrame. Infinite scroll: neither, use IntersectionObserver (problem 12).

How would you add a maxWait to debounce?

Track when the first call of the burst happened. If now - firstCall >= maxWait, run immediately even though calls continue. That's lodash's maxWait, and it turns debounce into a guaranteed-progress throttle.

docs.title: 10. Promise.all, allSettled & a Concurrency Pool
docs.text: L2 ★★☆ · Promise construction, input order, first rejection, async worker pool

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement promiseAll and promiseAllSettled without the built-ins, and a pool(tasks, limit) that runs async tasks with at most limit in flight, returning results in input order.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
all creates one outer promise, subscribes to every input (wrapped in Promise.resolve so plain values and thenables work), stores each result at its index, and resolves when the countdown reaches zero, or rejects on the first rejection. allSettled maps every input to an outcome object, then reuses all. A pool starts limit workers that each pull the next index from a shared counter until the list is exhausted.

flowchart LR T["12 tasks"] --> W1["worker 1: next++"] T --> W2["worker 2: next++"] T --> W3["worker 3: next++"] W1 & W2 & W3 --> R["results[i] = await tasks[i]() (input order)"] R --> D["promiseAll(workers) → done"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why Promise.resolve(item).then((value) => { results[i] = value; if (--remaining === 0) resolve(results); }, reject) Index-based storage keeps input order even though completion order differs. Rejecting on the first failure matches the spec. if (remaining === 0) return resolve(results); all([]) must resolve immediately, a classic edge case. (value) => ({ status: "fulfilled", value }), (reason) => ({ status: "rejected", reason }) allSettled never rejects. Every input becomes a descriptive object, with the same shape as the built-in, and the check compares against it. const i = next++; results[i] = await tasks[i](); Safe without locks: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time, and await is the only point where another worker can run. Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, tasks.length) }, worker) Exactly limit workers. The check measures the maximum concurrency as 3.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space promiseAll O(n) O(n) pool O(n) tasks, ≤ limit concurrent O(n) results

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd coding-interview && npm test   # runs every check; this problem's report is below

10-promise-utils: 5 checks, 0 failures
  ✔ promiseAll keeps input order, not completion order
  ✔ promiseAll rejects with the first rejection; [] resolves immediately
  ✔ promiseAllSettled reports every outcome
  ✔ matches the built-ins on the same inputs
  ✔ pool never exceeds the limit and returns results in order

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Pushing results with results.push(value), which gives completion order instead of input order.
  • Forgetting that inputs can be plain values, not only promises.
  • A "pool" that starts every task at once with tasks.map(t => t()) and only awaits them in batches. The concurrency isn't actually limited.
  • promiseAll that keeps running other work after a rejection and leaks errors as unhandled rejections. (The other promises still run; all just stops listening. Use AbortController to really cancel.)

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
Implement Promise.race and Promise.any.

race: resolve or reject with the first settled input (items.forEach(p => Promise.resolve(p).then(resolve, reject))). any: resolve with the first fulfilled input. Reject only when all inputs reject, with an AggregateError of the reasons, counting down rejections the way all counts fulfilments.

How do you add a timeout to a promise?

Promise.race([p, new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej(new Error('timeout')), ms))]). For fetch, prefer AbortSignal.timeout(ms), which actually cancels the request instead of just ignoring it.

docs.title: 11. deepClone & deepEqual (Cycles, Map, Set, Date)
docs.text: L3 ★★★ · Recursion, WeakMap for cycles, prototypes, Reflect.ownKeys, Object.is

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Write deepClone(value) that copies nested objects and arrays plus Date, RegExp, Map, Set and symbol keys, keeps class prototypes, and survives cycles and shared references. Write a matching deepEqual.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Recurse by type, and keep a WeakMap from original to copy. Register the copy before recursing, so a cycle finds the half-built copy instead of looping forever, and shared references stay shared. Copy with Object.create(prototype) and Reflect.ownKeys (string and symbol keys). deepEqual mirrors the structure, with Object.is for primitives (NaN equals NaN) and a WeakMap of pairs already being compared, again for cycles.

flowchart TD V{type of value} -->|primitive / function| P[return as-is] V -->|seen before| S["return seen.get(value) (cycle / shared ref)"] V -->|Date / RegExp| D[new Date / new RegExp] V -->|Map / Set| M[new Map/Set, register, clone entries] V -->|array / object| O["Object.create(proto), register, clone own keys"]

docs.title: Solution
Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why if (seen.has(value)) return seen.get(value); Cycles (a.self = a) and shared references (left === right) map to the same copy. The check asserts c.self === c and c.left === c.right. seen.set(value, copy); // register BEFORE recursing If you register after recursing, a cycle recurses forever. Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value)) Class instances keep their methods. The check calls deepClone(new Money(1250)).format(). for (const key of Reflect.ownKeys(value)) Includes symbol keys, which Object.keys and for…in skip. if (Object.is(a, b)) return true; NaN equals NaN (unlike ===), and +0 and -0 are distinct. !deepEqual({ a: 1 }, { a: 1, b: undefined }) Key sets must match. A missing key isn't the same as an undefined value.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space deepClone / deepEqual O(nodes) O(nodes) for the WeakMap + recursion depth

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd coding-interview && npm test   # runs every check; this problem's report is below

11-deep-clone: 5 checks, 0 failures
  ✔ clones nested objects, arrays, Date, RegExp, Map, Set and symbol keys
  ✔ mutating the clone never affects the original
  ✔ handles cycles and shared references
  ✔ keeps the prototype (class instances stay instances)
  ✔ deepEqual: NaN, different types, missing keys, Map values

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)). It loses Date (becomes a string), Map/Set (become {}), undefined, functions and prototypes, and throws on cycles.
  • Registering the copy in seen after recursing, which gives infinite recursion on cycles.
  • for…in without hasOwnProperty, which copies inherited enumerable properties onto the clone.
  • Comparing typeof a === 'object' without excluding null.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
What about structuredClone?

structuredClone(value) is built in and handles cycles, Date, Map, Set, typed arrays and more. It doesn't keep prototypes (class instances become plain objects), and it throws on functions and DOM nodes. In interviews, mention it first, then write your own to show you understand the algorithm.

How would you avoid stack overflow on very deep structures?

Replace recursion with an explicit stack of [source, target, key] work items. Iterate, creating containers and pushing their children, so the depth is limited by heap memory rather than the call stack.

docs.title: 12. Infinite Scroll with IntersectionObserver
docs.text: L2 ★★★ · Sentinel + rootMargin, in-flight guard, DocumentFragment, end of feed

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Load posts 20 at a time as the user scrolls, starting before they reach the bottom. Never fire two requests at once, stop at the end (75 posts), announce progress to screen readers, and avoid scroll listeners.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Put an empty sentinel after the list and observe it with IntersectionObserver using rootMargin: "300px", so loading starts 300 px before it scrolls into view. A loading flag stops duplicate requests, a DocumentFragment appends a page in one reflow, and the observer disconnects at the end. Because the observer only fires on changes, check again after each load in case the sentinel is still visible (tall screens).

sequenceDiagram participant IO as IntersectionObserver participant L as loadMore() participant API as fetchPage(offset) IO->>L: sentinel within 300 px L->>L: loading = true (guard) L->>API: offset 0 API-->>L: 20 posts L->>L: append fragment, loading = false L->>L: sentinel still visible? → loadMore() again IO->>L: user scrolls → next page … until < 20 returned → disconnect

docs.title: Solution
Live demo
docs.text: Open it full-size: 12-infinite-scroll.html. Resize the window to watch it respond.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Code Why new IntersectionObserver(cb, { rootMargin: "300px" }) The browser computes visibility off the main thread. No scroll listener, no getBoundingClientRect on every scroll event. if (loading \|\| done) return; The observer can fire again while a request is in flight. Without the guard you get duplicate pages. The check asserts 75 unique posts. const frag = document.createDocumentFragment(); … feed.append(frag); One DOM insertion per page instead of 20, so a single layout. if (sentinel.getBoundingClientRect().top < innerHeight + 300) loadMore(); Bug found by the checks: on a 4000 px-tall screen the sentinel never left the viewport, so the observer never fired again and the feed stalled at 20. This re-check fixes it. <p id="status" role="status"> A live region: "40 posts loaded" and "All 75 posts loaded" are announced to screen-reader users.

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space per page O(page size) DOM work O(items rendered)

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd coding-interview && npm test   # runs every check; this problem's report is below

12-infinite-scroll: 4 checks, 0 failures
  ✔ first page of 20 loads on open
  ✔ scrolling to the bottom loads the next page; never loads twice at once
  ✔ keeps going to the end: 75 unique posts, then stops
  ✔ a very tall screen keeps loading without any scroll (observer only fires on change)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• window.addEventListener('scroll', …) measuring positions on every event, which causes jank and layout thrashing.
  • No in-flight guard, so the same page loads several times.
  • Never stopping, which fires empty requests forever at the end of the feed.
  • Keeping 10,000 DOM nodes. For very long feeds, virtualise (render only the visible window) and keep a "Load more" button as a fallback.

docs.title: Follow-up questions
docs.text:
How do you keep the footer reachable and the back button working?

Offer a "Load more" button instead of auto-loading after a few pages, or put the footer content elsewhere. Store the loaded page in the URL (?page=3) or history.state, and restore the scroll position on back navigation.

Cursor or offset pagination for the API?

Use a cursor (opaque next token from the last item). New posts inserted at the top then don't shift pages and cause duplicates or gaps, and deep pages stay fast on the database.

docs.title: CSS & CSS3: How It Works
docs.text: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML looks: colours, spacing, fonts, layout, animation.

Part Example Meaning Selector .card Which elements to style Declaration block { … } The styles Declaration padding: 1rem; One property + value Property padding What to change Value 1rem What to change it to

docs.title: Three ways to add CSS Beginner
docs.text:
<!-- 1. External stylesheet (best: cached, reusable) -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

<!-- 2. Internal <style> (single page, critical CSS) -->

  h1 { color: #e4572e; }
</style>

<!-- 3. Inline style attribute (one element; dynamic values) -->

Hello

docs.title: What "CSS3" means Intermediate
docs.text:
timeline 1996 : CSS1 : fonts, colours, margins 1998 : CSS2 : positioning, z-index, media types 2011 : CSS2.1 : the stable base everyone implemented 2011–2017 : "CSS3" modules : rounded corners, shadows, gradients, transforms, transitions, animations, media queries, flexbox, grid 2018–2026 : Living modules : custom properties, is() where() has() selectors, nesting, @layer, container queries, subgrid, view transitions, anchor positioning

After CSS2.1, CSS was split into independent modules (Selectors, Color, Flexbox, Grid…), each with its own level number. "CSS3" is just a marketing label for that first wave. There will never be a "CSS4"; the CSS Working Group publishes yearly snapshots instead, and developers track Baseline to see what's safe to use.

Baseline

Baseline marks a web feature as:

  • Newly available: works in the latest Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.
  • Widely available: has been newly available for 30+ months, so it's safe for almost every audience.

Throughout this playbook, newer features are labelled with their Baseline year.

docs.title: A modern starter stylesheet Beginner
docs.text:
Copy this into every new project. Every line is explained in the following chapters.

/* 1. Predictable sizing */
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

/* 2. Remove default margins, keep sensible text */
* { margin: 0; }
html { -webkit-text-size-adjust: none; text-size-adjust: none; color-scheme: light dark; }
body {
  min-block-size: 100dvh;
  line-height: 1.5;
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif;
  -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;
}

/* 3. Media is responsive by default */
img, picture, video, canvas, svg { display: block; max-inline-size: 100%; height: auto; }

/* 4. Form controls inherit fonts */
input, button, textarea, select { font: inherit; }

/* 5. Avoid text overflow and ugly line breaks */
p, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6 { overflow-wrap: break-word; }
h1, h2, h3 { text-wrap: balance; line-height: 1.15; }
p { text-wrap: pretty; }

/* 6. Visible keyboard focus */
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #e4572e; outline-offset: 2px; }

/* 7. Respect reduced-motion preferences */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: .01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: .01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

docs.text: Hover over and click the demos on this page; they're live.

docs.title: transform Beginner
docs.text:
Transforms move, rotate, scale or skew an element without affecting layout: neighbours don't move.

transform: translate(20px, 10px);
transform: rotate(15deg);
transform: scale(1.2);
transform: skew(10deg, 0);
transform: translateY(-4px) rotate(5deg) scale(1.05);  /* order matters: right to left */

/* Individual properties (Baseline 2022): easier to animate separately */
translate: 20px 10px;
rotate: 15deg;
scale: 1.2;

transform-origin: top left;
none translate rotate scale skew

docs.text:
.scene { perspective: 600px; }
.card  { transition: transform .6s; transform-style: preserve-3d; }
.scene:hover .card { transform: rotateY(180deg); }
.face  { backface-visibility: hidden; position: absolute; inset: 0; }

docs.title: transition Beginner
docs.text:
Animates between two states (e.g. normal → :hover).

.btn {
  background: #e4572e;
  transition: background-color .2s ease, translate .2s ease, box-shadow .2s ease;
  /* transition: property duration timing-function delay; */
}
.btn:hover {
  background: #c43d17;
  translate: 0 -2px;
  box-shadow: 0 6px 16px rgb(0 0 0 / .2);
}
Hover me

docs.title: Timing functions Intermediate
docs.text:
Hover the track to see each curve.

transition-timing-function: linear;
transition-timing-function: ease;          /* default */
transition-timing-function: ease-in;
transition-timing-function: ease-out;      /* good for entering elements */
transition-timing-function: ease-in-out;
transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(.34, 1.56, .64, 1);   /* overshoot / spring */
transition-timing-function: steps(5);
transition-timing-function: linear(0, 1.2 60%, .9 80%, 1);     /* bounce (Baseline 2023) */
linear ease ease-in ease-out cubic-bezier steps(5)

docs.title: Transition display and entry states Advanced Baseline 2024
docs.text:
.toast {
  transition: opacity .3s, translate .3s, display .3s allow-discrete;
  @starting-style { opacity: 0; translate: 0 1rem; }   /* where it animates FROM when it appears */
}
.toast[hidden] { display: none; opacity: 0; }

@starting-style and transition-behavior: allow-discrete finally allow fade-in/fade-out when toggling display: none, including for <dialog> and popovers.

docs.title: @keyframes and animation Beginner → Intermediate
docs.text:
@keyframes spin    { to { rotate: 360deg; } }
@keyframes pulse   { 50% { scale: 1.15; opacity: .7; } }
@keyframes bounce  { 0%, 100% { translate: 0 0; } 50% { translate: 0 -20px; } }
@keyframes shimmer { to { background-position: -200% 0; } }

.spinner  { animation: spin 1s linear infinite; }
.pulse    { animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite; }
.bounce   { animation: bounce .8s ease-in-out infinite; }
.skeleton {
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, #eee 25%, #f8f8f8 50%, #eee 75%) 0 0 / 200% 100%;
  animation: shimmer 1.4s linear infinite;
}
Property Values animation-name the @keyframes name animation-duration 1s, 300ms animation-timing-function as transitions animation-delay 0.2s, negative values start mid-way animation-iteration-count 1, 3, infinite animation-direction normal, reverse, alternate, alternate-reverse animation-fill-mode none, forwards (keep end state), backwards, both animation-play-state running, paused animation-composition replace, add, accumulate animation-timeline auto, scroll(), view() (see below)

docs.title: Scroll-driven animations Advanced Chromium 115+, Safari 26
docs.text:
Link an animation's progress to scrolling, with no JavaScript.

/* Reading progress bar */
.progress {
  position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: 4px; background: #e4572e;
  transform-origin: left;
  animation: grow linear both;
  animation-timeline: scroll(root);
}
@keyframes grow { from { scale: 0 1; } to { scale: 1 1; } }

/* Fade cards in as they enter the viewport */
.card {
  animation: reveal linear both;
  animation-timeline: view();
  animation-range: entry 0% entry 100%;
}
@keyframes reveal { from { opacity: 0; translate: 0 2rem; } }

Scroll inside the box (in a supporting browser):

Scroll me ↓ — the orange bar tracks progress, and each block fades in as it enters.

Block 1Block 2Block 3Block 4Block 5Block 6

Wrap them in @supports (animation-timeline: view()) { … } so other browsers simply show the content without the effect.

docs.title: View transitions Advanced Same-document: Baseline 2025
docs.text:
Animate between two DOM states (or two pages) with a cross-fade or morph.

// Same-document (SPA): wrap the DOM change
document.startViewTransition(() => updateTheDOM());

/* Cross-document (MPA): opt in on both pages */
@view-transition { navigation: auto; }

/* Morph a thumbnail into a hero image across pages */
.thumb, .hero { view-transition-name: product-photo; }

::view-transition-old(root), ::view-transition-new(root) { animation-duration: .3s; }
Shuffle layout 1 2 3 4

docs.title: Accessibility: reduced motion Intermediate
docs.text:
Some people get dizzy or nauseous from motion (vestibular disorders). Respect their OS setting:

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .card { transition: translate .3s; }     /* only add motion if the user is OK with it */
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .hero-video { display: none; }
  * { animation-duration: .01ms !important; transition-duration: .01ms !important; }
}

docs.title: Performance rules Advanced
docs.text:
flowchart LR S[Style] --> L[Layout] --> P[Paint] --> C[Composite] Animating… Triggers Cost transform, opacity (+ translate, rotate, scale, filter in many cases) Composite only ✅ Cheap: runs on the GPU compositor thread color, background, box-shadow, border-radius Paint + composite ⚠️ Moderate width, height, top, left, margin, padding, font-size Layout + paint + composite ❌ Expensive: whole page may re-layout every frame

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

  • Animate transform/opacity. To "animate height", use a grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr transition, interpolate-size: allow-keywords with height: auto, or scale.
  • will-change: transform promotes an element to its own layer. Add it just before an animation and remove it after; leaving it on hundreds of elements wastes GPU memory.
  • Keep UI transitions between 150–300ms. Entering: ease-out. Exiting: ease-in. Anything over 500ms feels sluggish for UI feedback.

docs.title: Colour formats Beginner → Advanced
docs.text:
color: tomato;                        /* named (148 names) */
color: #e4572e;                       /* hex: RRGGBB */
color: #e4572e80;                     /* hex + alpha (80 = 50%) */
color: rgb(228 87 46);                /* modern space-separated syntax */
color: rgb(228 87 46 / 50%);          /* with alpha */
color: hsl(14 77% 54%);               /* hue, saturation, lightness */
color: hwb(14 18% 11%);               /* hue, whiteness, blackness */
color: lab(56% 52 51);                /* perceptual lightness, a, b */
color: lch(56% 73 44);                /* lightness, chroma, hue */
color: oklab(0.64 0.15 0.11);         /* improved Lab */
color: oklch(64% 0.19 37);            /* ← recommended for design systems */
color: color(display-p3 0.9 0.35 0.2);/* wide-gamut P3 */
color: currentColor;                  /* = the element's current `color` */
color: transparent;
named hex hex 50% rgb hsl hwb lab lch oklch display-p3

docs.title: Why OKLCH? Advanced
docs.text:
In HSL, hsl(60 100% 50%) (yellow) and hsl(240 100% 50%) (blue) have the same "lightness" but look completely different in brightness. OKLCH is perceptually uniform: the same L looks equally light for every hue. That makes it ideal for generating accessible palettes: keep L fixed, rotate H.

/* Same lightness and chroma, different hues: all look equally bright */
.s1 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 30); }
.s2 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 140); }
.s3 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 250); }
.s4 { background: oklch(70% 0.15 320); }
H 30 H 140 H 250 H 320 hsl 30 hsl 140 hsl 250 hsl 320

Top row: OKLCH, consistent brightness. Bottom row: HSL with the same lightness, but the green looks much brighter than the blue.

docs.title: color-mix() Intermediate Baseline 2023
docs.text:
--brand: #e4572e;
--brand-light: color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 40%);
--brand-dark:  color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), black 30%);
--brand-faded: color-mix(in srgb, var(--brand) 20%, transparent);
light brand dark faded

docs.title: Relative colour syntax Advanced Baseline 2024
docs.text:
Take an existing colour, change one channel:

--hover: oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.1) c h);   /* 10% darker */
--muted: oklch(from var(--brand) l calc(c * 0.4) h);   /* less saturated */
--alpha: rgb(from var(--brand) r g b / 50%);           /* 50% opacity */

docs.title: light-dark() Intermediate Baseline 2024
docs.text:
:root { color-scheme: light dark; }
body {
  background: light-dark(#ffffff, #121212);
  color:      light-dark(#1f2329, #e6e8ec);
}

Uses the first value in light mode and the second in dark mode, following color-scheme.

docs.title: Absolute
docs.text: Unit Meaning Use px CSS pixel (1/96 inch, scaled by zoom and device pixel ratio) Borders, shadows, small fixed details pt, cm, mm, in Physical units Print stylesheets only

docs.title: Relative to font size
Relative to the viewport
docs.text:
Unit 1 unit = 1% of… vw / vh Viewport width / height vmin / vmax Smaller / larger dimension svh / svw Small viewport (mobile URL bar visible) lvh / lvw Large viewport (URL bar hidden) dvh / dvw Dynamic: changes as the URL bar shows/hides vi / vb Inline / block axis of the viewport 
.hero { min-height: 100vh; }   /* ❌ on mobile, taller than the visible area */
.hero { min-height: 100svh; }  /* ✅ always fits with the URL bar shown */
.app  { height: 100dvh; }      /* ✅ tracks the real visible height (can cause reflow on scroll) */

docs.title: Relative to a container Advanced Baseline 2023
docs.text:
cqw, cqh, cqi, cqb, cqmin, cqmax: 1% of the nearest size container (see container queries).

.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; }
.card h2 { font-size: clamp(1rem, 5cqi, 2rem); }  /* scales with the card, not the page */

docs.title: Others
docs.text: Unit Use % Relative to the parent (for width), or the element itself (for translate) fr Fraction of free space in a grid deg, turn, rad Angles s, ms Time dpi, dppx, x Resolution (image-set, media queries)

docs.title: Maths functions IntermediateResize the window: I scale smoothly
docs.text:
width: calc(100% - 2rem);
width: min(100%, 60rem);        /* the smaller: "max 60rem, but never overflow" */
width: max(50%, 300px);         /* the larger */
font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.8rem + 1.5vw, 2rem);  /* min, preferred, max */
padding: round(up, 13px, 4px);  /* 16px */

clamp() is the backbone of fluid design: one line instead of three media queries.

<h2 style="font-size: clamp(1.2rem, 1rem + 3vw, 3rem)">Resize the window: I scale smoothly</h2>

Other functions: abs(), sign(), mod(), rem(), pow(), sqrt(), sin(), cos(), tan(), atan2(), exp(), log(), hypot(). Trig functions are handy for circular layouts.

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

For fluid type, mix rem into the middle value (1rem + 2vw, not 4vw alone). A pure vw value doesn't grow when the user zooms, which fails WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text). Tools like Utopia generate a full fluid type and space scale for you.

docs.title: The basics Beginner
docs.text:
Custom properties (often called CSS variables) store a value once and reuse it everywhere.

:root {
  --brand: #e4572e;
  --radius: 12px;
  --space: 1rem;
}
.btn {
  background: var(--brand);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
  padding: calc(var(--space) / 2) var(--space);
}
.btn--ghost {
  background: transparent;
  color: var(--brand);
  border: 2px solid var(--brand);
}
Primary Ghost
  • Names start with -- and are case-sensitive.
  • Fallback: var(--accent, royalblue) uses royalblue if --accent isn't set.
  • They inherit and cascade like normal properties, and they're live: change one in JS or a media query and everything using it updates.

docs.title: Scoping: the real superpower Intermediate
docs.text:
Unlike Sass variables, custom properties can be overridden for one part of the page:

.btn { background: var(--btn-bg, #e4572e); }
.danger-zone { --btn-bg: crimson; }       /* every .btn inside turns red */
.card[data-tone="calm"] { --btn-bg: seagreen; }
Default Inside .danger-zone Inside [data-tone=calm]

docs.title: Passing values from HTML Intermediate
docs.text:
<div class="bar" style="--value: 72%"></div>

.bar { background: #eee; border-radius: 99px; height: 12px; }
.bar::after { content: ""; display: block; height: 100%; width: var(--value); background: #e4572e; border-radius: inherit; }

docs.title: Dark mode Intermediate
docs.text:
Use the system setting, and let users override it with a toggle.

:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --fg: #1f2329;
  --surface: #f4f5f7;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root { --bg: #121417; --fg: #e6e8ec; --surface: #1d2129; }
}
/* Manual override (set data-theme on <html> from JS / localStorage) */
:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; --bg: #ffffff; --fg: #1f2329; --surface: #f4f5f7; }
:root[data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark;  --bg: #121417; --fg: #e6e8ec; --surface: #1d2129; }

body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg); }
.card { background: var(--surface); }

Shorter, with light-dark() (Baseline 2024):

:root { color-scheme: light dark; }
:root[data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; }
:root[data-theme="dark"]  { color-scheme: dark; }
body  { background: light-dark(#fff, #121417); color: light-dark(#1f2329, #e6e8ec); }
Dark mode Card titleColours come from variables that switch with the theme.

docs.title: Design tokens Advanced
docs.text:
Tokens are named design decisions. Organise them in tiers:

:root {
  /* Tier 1: primitive tokens (the raw palette; never used directly in components) */
  --orange-500: oklch(64% 0.19 37);
  --orange-600: oklch(56% 0.19 37);
  --gray-50: oklch(98% 0 0);
  --gray-900: oklch(22% 0.01 260);
  --space-1: .25rem; --space-2: .5rem; --space-3: 1rem; --space-4: 1.5rem; --space-5: 2rem;
  --radius-sm: 4px; --radius-md: 8px; --radius-lg: 16px;

  /* Tier 2: semantic tokens (what components use) */
  --color-bg: var(--gray-50);
  --color-text: var(--gray-900);
  --color-accent: var(--orange-500);
  --color-accent-hover: var(--orange-600);

  /* Tier 3: component tokens (optional, for highly configurable components) */
  --button-bg: var(--color-accent);
  --button-radius: var(--radius-md);
}

Dark mode or a new brand only changes tier 2; no component CSS changes.

docs.title: Typed custom properties with @property Advanced Baseline 2024
docs.text:
Normal custom properties are untyped strings, so the browser can't animate them. Register a type and it can:

@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}
.spin-border {
  background: conic-gradient(from var(--angle), #e4572e, #f3a712, #3f51b5, #e4572e);
  animation: rotate 3s linear infinite;
}
@keyframes rotate { to { --angle: 360deg; } }
Animated gradient border

docs.title: Reading and writing from JavaScript Intermediate
docs.text:
const root = document.documentElement;
getComputedStyle(root).getPropertyValue('--brand');   // " #e4572e"
root.style.setProperty('--brand', 'royalblue');

// Follow the pointer
document.addEventListener('pointermove', e => {
  root.style.setProperty('--x', e.clientX + 'px');
  root.style.setProperty('--y', e.clientY + 'px');
});

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

Source your tokens from one place (a JSON file in the W3C Design Tokens format) and generate CSS, iOS, Android and Figma outputs with Style Dictionary or Terrazzo. Changing a token on the root invalidates style for the whole document. That's fine for theme switches, but avoid updating root-level variables on every pointermove on large pages; set them on the smallest element that needs them.

docs.title: Backgrounds, Borders & Effects
docs.text: These are the features most people mean by "CSS3": the things that used to need images and Photoshop.

docs.title: border-radius Beginner
docs.text:
.r1 { border-radius: 8px; }
.r2 { border-radius: 50%; }              /* circle (on a square) */
.r3 { border-radius: 999px; }            /* pill */
.r4 { border-radius: 24px 0; }           /* top-left+bottom-right / others */
.r5 { border-radius: 60% 40% 30% 70% / 60% 30% 70% 40%; }  /* blob */

New in 2025 (Chromium): corner-shape: squircle | bevel | notch | scoop changes the shape of rounded corners.

docs.title: Borders and outlines Beginner
docs.text:
border: 2px solid #e4572e;
border-style: dotted | dashed | double | groove | ridge | inset | outset;
border-inline-start: 4px solid royalblue;    /* left in LTR */
outline: 2px dashed royalblue;               /* doesn't take space */
outline-offset: 4px;
solid dashed dotted double inline-start outline + offset

docs.title: box-shadow Beginner
docs.text:
Syntax: offset-x offset-y blur spread color, plus optional inset. Comma-separate several shadows.

.s1 { box-shadow: 0 1px 3px rgb(0 0 0 / .12), 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / .24); } /* small */
.s2 { box-shadow: 0 10px 30px -5px rgb(0 0 0 / .25); }                        /* large, soft */
.s3 { box-shadow: inset 0 2px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .3); }                          /* inset */
.s4 { box-shadow: 0 0 0 4px #e4572e; }                                        /* ring (no layout shift) */
.s5 { box-shadow: 0 0 20px 4px rgb(228 87 46 / .7); }                         /* glow */

docs.title: text-shadow Beginner
docs.text:
.t1 { text-shadow: 2px 2px 0 #e4572e; }
.t2 { text-shadow: 0 0 8px #3f51b5; }
.t3 { text-shadow: 0 2px 4px rgb(0 0 0 / .5); }   /* legible text over images */

Retro

Neon

docs.title: Gradients Beginner → Intermediate
docs.text:
.g1 { background: linear-gradient(135deg, #e4572e, #f3a712); }
.g2 { background: radial-gradient(circle at 30% 30%, #fff, #3f51b5); }
.g3 { background: conic-gradient(#e4572e 0 40%, #f3a712 0 70%, #3f51b5 0); } /* pie chart */
.g4 { background: repeating-linear-gradient(45deg, #eee 0 10px, #ddd 10px 20px); } /* stripes */
.g5 { background: linear-gradient(in oklch 90deg, #e4572e, #3f51b5); }  /* smoother interpolation */

docs.title: Background properties Beginner
docs.text:
.hero {
  background-image: linear-gradient(rgb(0 0 0 / .5), rgb(0 0 0 / .5)),   /* overlay */
                    url("hero.jpg");                                      /* photo */
  background-size: cover;          /* fill, crop the excess  | contain: fit, may letterbox */
  background-position: center;
  background-repeat: no-repeat;
  background-attachment: fixed;    /* parallax-ish; disabled on iOS */
  background-clip: padding-box;
  background-origin: content-box;
  background-blend-mode: multiply;
}
Text over an image with an overlay

Multiple backgrounds stack: the first one listed is on top.

docs.title: opacity and filter Beginner
docs.text:
opacity: .5;
filter: blur(3px);
filter: grayscale(1);
filter: brightness(1.3) contrast(1.2) saturate(1.5);
filter: sepia(1);
filter: hue-rotate(90deg);
filter: invert(1);
filter: drop-shadow(0 4px 6px rgb(0 0 0 / .4));   /* follows the shape (PNG/SVG alpha) */
original blur grayscale sepia hue-rotate invert

docs.title: backdrop-filter (glassmorphism) Intermediate
docs.text:
Applies a filter to whatever is behind the element.

.glass {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / .2);
  backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.5);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(12px) saturate(1.5);
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / .35);
  border-radius: 16px;
}
Glass cardThe photo behind me is blurred.

docs.title: clip-path and mask Intermediate
docs.text:
.c1 { clip-path: circle(50%); }
.c2 { clip-path: polygon(50% 0, 100% 100%, 0 100%); }           /* triangle */
.c3 { clip-path: polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 80%, 0 100%); }      /* slanted section edge */
.c4 { clip-path: inset(10% round 20px); }
.m1 { mask-image: linear-gradient(black 60%, transparent); }     /* fade out */

docs.title: Blend modes Advanced
docs.text:
.knockout { mix-blend-mode: multiply; }     /* blend with what's behind */
.duotone  { background-blend-mode: screen; }  /* blend background layers */
isolation: isolate;   /* limit blending to this stacking context */

docs.title: object-fit and aspect-ratio Beginner
docs.text:
.thumb {
  inline-size: 160px;
  aspect-ratio: 1;          /* square box, any image */
  object-fit: cover;        /* fill and crop | contain: fit inside | fill: stretch */
  object-position: top;
}
.video-wrap { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; }
fill (stretched) contain cover

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

filter, backdrop-filter, big blurred box-shadows and mix-blend-mode are paint-heavy. Animating them, or stacking many glass cards on a scrolling page, can drop frames on low-end Android phones. Profile with DevTools → Rendering → "Paint flashing", and prefer animating a pseudo-element's opacity over animating a shadow directly.

docs.title: The cascade Beginner → Advanced
docs.text:
When two rules set the same property on the same element, the cascade decides who wins. It checks these in order and stops at the first difference:

flowchart TD A["1 · Origin & importance<br/>transitions > !important user-agent > !important user > !important author > animations > author > user > user-agent"] --> B B["2 · Context<br/>Shadow DOM: outer vs inner styles"] --> C C["3 · Element-attached styles<br/>style="…" attribute"] --> D D["4 · Cascade layers<br/>later @layer wins (reversed for !important); unlayered beats layered"] --> E E["5 · Specificity<br/>(id, class, type)"] --> F F["6 · Order of appearance<br/>last one wins"]

For day-to-day work, the three that matter are layers → specificity → order.

<p class="note" id="intro">Which colour am I?</p>

<style>
  p        { color: green; }   /* (0,0,1) */
  .note    { color: blue; }    /* (0,1,0) */
  #intro   { color: crimson; } /* (1,0,0) wins: highest specificity */
  .note    { color: orange; }  /* same specificity as .note above; later, but still loses to #intro */
</style>

Which colour am I?

docs.title: Specificity Beginner
docs.text:
Specificity is a score of three numbers: (IDs, classes, types). Compare left to right; the first higher number wins. 1,0,0 beats 0,15,0.

Selector Score Why * 0,0,0 Universal adds nothing li 0,0,1 1 type ul li 0,0,2 2 types .nav 0,1,0 1 class a:hover 0,1,1 pseudo-class counts as a class [type="email"] 0,1,0 attribute counts as a class li::before 0,0,2 pseudo-element counts as a type #main .nav a 1,1,1 :is(#a, .b) p 1,0,1 :is() takes its most specific argument :where(#a, .b) p 0,0,1 :where() is always 0 :not(.x) 0,1,0 takes its argument's specificity style="…" beats all selectors !important jumps to a higher origin Use only to override third-party CSS or in utilities

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

Keep specificity low and flat: mostly single classes. Use :where() in resets and libraries so users can override them with a single class. Use @layer instead of specificity hacks to manage order between reset, base, components and utilities. See Modern CSS → @layer.

docs.title: Inheritance Beginner
docs.text:
Some properties pass down from parent to children: mostly text properties (color, font-*, line-height, letter-spacing, text-align, visibility, cursor, list-style). Box properties (margin, padding, border, background, width, display) do not.

.parent { color: purple; border: 2px solid purple; }
/* Children are purple text, but get no border. */
Parent

Child: purple text inherited, no border

Control inheritance with these keywords, which work on any property:

Keyword Means inherit Use the parent's value initial Use the spec's initial value (display: initial is inline!) unset inherit if the property inherits, otherwise initial revert Go back to the browser's default style revert-layer Go back to the value from the previous cascade layer

docs.title: The box model Beginner
docs.text:
Every element is a rectangular box made of four layers:

margin border padding contentwidth × height 
.box {
  width: 200px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 5px solid;
  margin: 10px;
}
box-sizing Total visible width content-box (default) 200 + 20×2 + 5×2 = 250px width = content only border-box 200px width includes padding + border

That's why every modern reset sets *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }.

<div class="cb">content-box</div>
<div class="bb">border-box</div>

.cb, .bb { width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid; }
.cb { box-sizing: content-box; }
.bb { box-sizing: border-box; }
content-box (250px) border-box (200px)

docs.title: Shorthand order Beginner
docs.text:
margin: 10px;                 /* all four */
margin: 10px 20px;            /* block (top/bottom) | inline (left/right) */
margin: 10px 20px 30px;       /* top | inline | bottom */
margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;  /* top | right | bottom | left: clockwise */
margin-inline: auto;          /* centre a block with a width */

docs.title: display Beginner
display: none vs visibility: hidden vs opacity: 0
Margin collapse Intermediate
docs.text:
Vertical margins between block elements in normal flow merge into the larger of the two. They don't add up.

h2 { margin-bottom: 30px; }
p  { margin-top: 20px; }
/* Gap between them = 30px, not 50px */

Margins don't collapse inside flex or grid containers, or across a parent with padding, a border, or display: flow-root. A common surprise: a child's top margin "leaking" out of its parent. Fix it with display: flow-root on the parent, or use gap instead of margins.

Senior note · 🟡 Intermediate

Many teams avoid margin collapse entirely by using one direction only (margin-block-end) or, better, layout gap and the "stack" pattern: .stack > * + * { margin-block-start: var(--space, 1rem); }.

docs.title: Logical properties Intermediate
docs.text:
Logical properties follow the writing direction, so layouts flip automatically for right-to-left languages and vertical writing modes.

Physical Logical width / height inline-size / block-size margin-left / margin-right margin-inline-start / margin-inline-end margin-top / margin-bottom margin-block-start / margin-block-end padding-left + padding-right padding-inline top / bottom / left / right inset-block-start / … / inset-inline-end text-align: left text-align: start border-top-left-radius border-start-start-radius

docs.title: Formatting contexts Expert
docs.text: A block formatting context (BFC) is an isolated layout region: floats inside it are contained, and its children's margins don't collapse with outside margins. These create one: the root element, floats, absolutely positioned elements, display: flow-root, inline-block, table cells, overflow other than visible/clip, flex and grid items, contain: layout | content | paint, and multi-column containers. Knowing this explains most "why does my margin/float behave differently in here?" bugs.

docs.title: Modern CSS (2023–2026)
docs.text:
Features that changed how professional CSS is written. Each section gives the Baseline status and a fallback.

Feature Status (Oct 2026) Replaces Nesting Baseline 2023 Sass nesting :has() Baseline 2023 JS "add class to parent" code Container queries (size) Baseline 2023 JS ResizeObserver hacks, many media queries @layer Baseline 2022 Specificity wars, !important Subgrid Baseline 2023 Fixed heights to align card internals @scope Baseline 2025 BEM naming, CSS Modules (partly) @property Baseline 2024 — (enables animating variables) light-dark(), relative colours, color-mix() Baseline 2023–24 Sass colour functions Popover API, @starting-style Baseline 2024 JS menu/tooltip libraries View transitions (same-document) Baseline 2025 Animation libraries for state changes Anchor positioning Chromium 125+, Safari 26, Firefox in progress Popper.js / Floating UI Scroll-driven animations Chromium 115+, Safari 26 Scroll listeners, IntersectionObserver Container style queries Chromium 111+, Safari 18 Modifier classes field-sizing: content Chromium 123+ Auto-grow textarea JS interpolate-size / calc-size() Chromium 129+ JS height animations if(), custom functions (@function) Chromium 137+ (experimental elsewhere) Preprocessor logic

docs.title: @layer (cascade layers) Advanced
docs.text:
Layers let you control the cascade by intent instead of specificity. Later layers win over earlier layers, regardless of specificity.

/* 1. Declare the order once, at the very top */
@layer reset, base, vendor, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  * { margin: 0; box-sizing: border-box; }
}
@layer base {
  a { color: royalblue; }
}
@layer vendor {
  @import url("datepicker.css") layer(vendor);   /* or import straight into a layer */
}
@layer components {
  .card a { color: inherit; }
}
@layer utilities {
  .text-red { color: crimson; }   /* single class, but beats .card a (0,1,1) because the layer is later */
}

/* Unlayered styles beat ALL layers */

<div class="card"><a class="text-red" href="#">Which colour?</a></div>
I'm crimson: the utilities layer wins over a more specific selector

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

@layer is the cleanest answer to "how do we integrate Tailwind, a component library and our own CSS without !important?" Put third-party CSS in a low layer, your components above it, utilities on top. Note the twist: for !important declarations the layer order is reversed, so an !important in reset beats an !important in utilities. That's deliberate: it lets low layers protect critical rules.

docs.title: Container queries Advanced
docs.text:
Media queries ask "how wide is the viewport?" Container queries ask "how wide is my container?" So a card can be stacked in a narrow sidebar and side-by-side in a wide main column, on the same screen.

.card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; container-name: card; }

.card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }

@container card (width > 400px) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }
}

Drag the bottom-right corner of the box to resize the container:

Container query cardNarrow container: stacked. Wider than 400px: side by side. Resize me ↘

Style queries (Chromium, Safari 18): query a custom property value on the container.

@container style(--variant: featured) {
  .card { border: 2px solid gold; }
}

docs.title: :has() Advanced
docs.text:
Covered in depth in Selectors. A few modern patterns:

/* Lock page scroll while a modal is open */
html:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden; }

/* Form-level error state */
form:has(:user-invalid) .submit-hint { display: block; }

/* Layout switches on content */
.grid:has(> :nth-child(5)) { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }

docs.title: Subgrid Advanced
docs.text:
Let a grid item's children line up with the parent's grid tracks. Perfect for card rows where titles, text and buttons should align across cards.

.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 1rem; }
.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;                /* card occupies 3 row tracks of the parent */
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;     /* its children use those tracks */
}
Short title

One line.

Buy A much longer title that wraps onto two lines

Some text that is a bit longer than the others, so it takes up more space.

Buy Medium title

Two short lines of text here.

Buy

All titles, texts and buttons line up across cards, even though their content lengths differ.

docs.title: @scope Advanced Baseline 2025
docs.text:
Limit styles to a DOM subtree, with an optional lower boundary ("donut scope").

@scope (.card) to (.card__content) {
  img { border-radius: 8px; }   /* images in .card, but NOT inside .card__content */
  :scope { padding: 1rem; }     /* :scope = the .card itself */
}

Also gives proximity: when two scopes' rules have equal specificity, the closer scope root wins. Useful for nested light/dark themes.

docs.title: Anchor positioning Advanced Chromium 125+, Safari 26
docs.text:
Tether a positioned element (tooltip, menu) to another element, with automatic flipping when it hits the viewport edge. Replaces Popper.js / Floating UI for most cases.

<button popovertarget="tip" class="anchor">Hover target</button>
<div id="tip" popover>Anchored tooltip</div>

.anchor { anchor-name: --btn; }
#tip {
  position-anchor: --btn;
  position-area: top;                  /* place above the anchor */
  margin: 0 0 8px;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block;  /* flip below if there's no room above */
}
Click me Anchored to the button ✨

In a browser without anchor positioning, the popover falls back to the centre of the screen: still usable.

docs.title: Feature queries with @supports Intermediate
docs.text:
Progressive enhancement: write the baseline, then upgrade where supported.

.cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; }              /* works everywhere */

@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .cards { display: grid; /* … subgrid version … */ }
}

@supports selector(:has(a)) {
  .card:has(img) { /* … */ }
}

@supports not (anchor-name: --a) {
  .tooltip { /* JS-positioned fallback */ }
}

docs.title: Other modern features worth knowing Advanced
position Beginner
Offsets with inset Beginner
docs.text:
.overlay { position: absolute; inset: 0; }          /* top:0; right:0; bottom:0; left:0 */
.corner  { position: absolute; inset: auto 1rem 1rem auto; }   /* bottom-right */
.bar     { position: fixed; inset-inline: 0; inset-block-end: 0; }  /* full-width bottom bar */

docs.title: sticky Intermediate
docs.text:
.section-title { position: sticky; top: 0; background: white; }

Scroll inside the box:

A — sticky

Apple

Apricot

Avocado

B — sticky

Banana

Blackberry

Blueberry

C — sticky

Cherry

Coconut

Cranberry

Why isn't my sticky sticking?

  1. You forgot an offset (top: 0).
  2. An ancestor has overflow: hidden | auto | scroll. Sticky sticks within the nearest scrolling ancestor. Use overflow: clip if you just need clipping.
  3. The parent is exactly as tall as the sticky element, so there's no room to stick.
  4. In a flex/grid container, the item is stretched to full height. Add align-self: start.

docs.title: z-index and stacking contexts Intermediate → Advanced
docs.text:
z-index controls which overlapping element is on top. It applies to positioned elements and to flex/grid items.

The catch: z-index only competes within the same stacking context. A child with z-index: 9999 can never escape a parent whose stacking context is below a sibling.

<div class="a" style="position:relative; z-index:1">
  A (z 1)
  <div style="position:absolute; z-index:9999">child of A (z 9999)</div>
</div>
<div class="b" style="position:relative; z-index:2">B (z 2): on top of A's child!</div>
A (z-index 1) child of A (9999) B (z-index 2): still on top of A's child

What creates a stacking context:

  • The root <html>
  • position: absolute | relative with a z-index other than auto
  • position: fixed | sticky (always)
  • Flex/grid items with a z-index
  • opacity < 1
  • transform, scale, rotate, translate, filter, backdrop-filter, perspective, clip-path, mask (any non-none value)
  • mix-blend-mode other than normal
  • isolation: isolate (the clean, intentional way)
  • contain: layout | paint, container-type: size | inline-size
  • will-change naming any of the above
  • Top-layer elements (dialog, popovers, fullscreen) sit above everything, no z-index needed

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

Define a z-index scale as tokens (--z-dropdown: 100; --z-sticky: 200; --z-modal: 300; --z-toast: 400) and use isolation: isolate on components to contain their internal z-indexes. Better yet, move modals, menus and toasts to the top layer with <dialog> and popover; then z-index wars mostly disappear.

docs.title: overflow Beginner
docs.text:
overflow: visible;   /* default: content spills out */
overflow: hidden;    /* clip, still programmatically scrollable; creates a scroll container */
overflow: clip;      /* clip, NOT a scroll container (sticky keeps working) */
overflow: scroll;    /* always show scrollbars */
overflow: auto;      /* scrollbars only when needed */
overflow-x: auto; overflow-y: hidden;
scrollbar-gutter: stable;        /* reserve space so content doesn't jump */
scrollbar-width: thin;
scrollbar-color: #e4572e transparent;
overscroll-behavior: contain;    /* stop scroll chaining from modals to the page */

docs.title: Scroll snap Intermediate
docs.text:
.carousel {
  display: flex; gap: 1rem; overflow-x: auto;
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;
  scroll-padding-inline: 1rem;
}
.carousel > * { flex: 0 0 80%; scroll-snap-align: center; }
Slide 1 (swipe / scroll →) Slide 2 Slide 3 Slide 4

docs.title: float and clear (legacy) Intermediate
docs.text:
Floats were built for wrapping text around images. For about a decade they were also abused for page layouts. Today use them only for text wrap.

.avatar { float: inline-start; margin: 0 1rem .5rem 0; shape-outside: circle(); }
.after-floats { clear: both; }

Text flows around the floated circle. Because of shape-outside: circle(), the lines follow the curve instead of the square box. This is the one job floats are still the best tool for: magazine-style text wrapping around images and pull quotes. For anything else, reach for Flexbox or Grid.

docs.title: Centering an absolutely positioned element Beginner
docs.text:
/* Modern */
.center { position: absolute; inset: 0; margin: auto; width: fit-content; height: fit-content; }

/* Classic */
.center { position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; translate: -50% -50%; }

More centering techniques: Layout Patterns → Centering.

docs.title: CSS Property Cheat Sheet
docs.text: The properties you'll use in real projects, grouped by job. Inh. = inherited by children by default.

Quantity queries Advanced

Style a list differently depending on how many items it has:

/* If there are 4 or more items, make them all smaller */
li:nth-last-child(n+4), li:nth-last-child(n+4) ~ li { font-size: .85em; }

/* Same idea, much easier, with :has() */
ul:has(> li:nth-child(4)) li { font-size: .85em; }

docs.title: Form-state pseudo-classes Intermediate
Logical pseudo-classes: :is(), :where(), :not(), :has() Intermediate → Advanced
docs.text:
/* :is(): shorter selectors. Specificity = most specific argument */
:is(h1, h2, h3):hover { color: #e4572e; }
article :is(h2, h3) { margin-top: 2em; }

/* :where(): same as :is() but specificity 0. Perfect for resets and libraries */
:where(ul, ol)[role="list"] { list-style: none; padding: 0; }

/* :not(): exclude. Accepts a selector list */
.btn:not(.primary, .danger) { background: #eee; }
li:not(:last-child) { border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd; }

docs.title: :has(), the "parent selector" Advanced Baseline 2023
docs.text:
:has() selects an element based on what's inside it or after it. It replaces a huge amount of JavaScript "add a class to the parent" code.

/* A card that contains an image gets a different layout */
.card:has(img) { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 80px 1fr; }

/* A form field whose input is invalid gets a red label */
.field:has(input:user-invalid) label { color: crimson; }

/* Highlight the h2 that's directly followed by a p */
h2:has(+ p) { margin-bottom: 0; }

/* Dark mode toggle with no JS */
:root:has(#dark:checked) { color-scheme: dark; }

/* Dim siblings of the hovered card */
.grid:has(.card:hover) .card:not(:hover) { opacity: .5; }
Card with an image → becomes a grid Card without an image → stays a block Hover any card: the others dim

Pseudo-elements style a part of an element, or insert generated content. They use two colons.

Pseudo-element Styles ::before / ::after Generated box before/after the content (needs content) ::first-letter First letter (drop caps) ::first-line First rendered line ::marker List bullet / number, summary triangle ::placeholder Input placeholder text ::selection Text the user selected ::file-selector-button The button inside input[type=file] ::backdrop The layer behind a modal dialog / popover / fullscreen element ::part(name) A shadow-DOM part exposed by a web component ::slotted() Slotted content (inside shadow CSS) ::cue Video captions ::details-content The collapsible part of <details> (2025) ::picker(select) The drop-down of a customizable select (2025) ::view-transition-* View transition snapshots ::scroll-marker, ::scroll-button() CSS carousels (Chromium 135+) 
.quote::before { content: "“"; font-size: 3em; color: #e4572e; line-height: 0; vertical-align: -.4em; }
.drop::first-letter { float: left; font-size: 3em; line-height: 1; padding-right: .1em; color: #3f51b5; }
.tick li::marker { content: "✔ "; color: seagreen; }
.sel::selection { background: #e4572e; color: white; }
.req::after { content: " *"; color: crimson; }

Design is how it works.

Once upon a time, the web was mostly text. Drop caps were one of the first typographic tricks that CSS made easy.

  • Semantic HTML
  • Accessible forms

Select this text to see a custom highlight.

Email

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

Text inside content on ::before/::after is read by most screen readers. For decorative icons, use the alt-text syntax content: "★" / ""; to give it an empty accessible name.

docs.title: Nesting Intermediate Baseline 2023
docs.text:
Native CSS nesting works like Sass nesting:

.card {
  padding: 1rem;

  & h3 { margin: 0; }          /* .card h3 */
  &:hover { box-shadow: 0 4px 12px #0002; }   /* .card:hover */
  &.featured { border: 2px solid gold; }      /* .card.featured */
  .theme-dark & { background: #222; }         /* .theme-dark .card */

  @media (width >= 600px) { padding: 2rem; }  /* media query inside */
}

The & is optional before a nested type selector in current browsers (h3 { } works), but keep it for clarity and older-browser safety.

docs.title: Selector performance Expert
docs.text: Browsers match selectors right to left: for .nav li a, they find every a, then check if it's inside an li, inside .nav. In practice, selector matching is rarely a bottleneck on modern engines. What actually costs time is style invalidation: a change that forces re-matching for many elements, such as toggling a class on <body> that a large :has() selector depends on. Keep :has() arguments narrow (.card:has(> img) rather than body:has(.x)), and use the DevTools Performance panel's "Selector stats" to find the expensive ones.

docs.title: Loading web fonts with @font-face Intermediate
docs.text:
@font-face {
  font-family: "Inter";
  src: url("/fonts/Inter-Variable.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 100 900;          /* variable font: the full range in one file */
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;            /* show fallback text immediately, swap when loaded */
  unicode-range: U+0000-00FF;    /* only download for these characters */
}
body { font-family: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif; }
font-display Behaviour auto Browser decides (usually block) block Invisible text up to ~3s, then fallback swap Fallback immediately, swap when ready (risk: layout shift) fallback ~100ms invisible, swap only if it loads within ~3s optional ~100ms; if not ready, use the fallback for this page view. Best for CLS.

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

To prevent layout shift when the web font swaps in, adjust the fallback font's metrics to match: @font-face { font-family: "Inter Fallback"; src: local("Arial"); size-adjust: 107%; ascent-override: 90%; }. Next.js and Fontaine generate these values automatically. Preload only the one or two most critical font files.

docs.title: Fluid type scale Advanced
docs.text:
:root {
  --step--1: clamp(0.83rem, 0.78rem + 0.24vw, 0.97rem);
  --step-0:  clamp(1.00rem, 0.93rem + 0.36vw, 1.20rem);
  --step-1:  clamp(1.20rem, 1.09rem + 0.54vw, 1.50rem);
  --step-2:  clamp(1.44rem, 1.28rem + 0.80vw, 1.88rem);
  --step-3:  clamp(1.73rem, 1.50rem + 1.15vw, 2.34rem);
  --step-4:  clamp(2.07rem, 1.75rem + 1.63vw, 2.93rem);
}
body { font-size: var(--step-0); }
h1 { font-size: var(--step-4); }
h2 { font-size: var(--step-3); }

Each step is a fixed ratio larger than the last (1.2 at small screens, 1.25 at large). The text is smaller on phones and larger on desktops, with no breakpoints.

docs.title: Debugging with DevTools
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

Every browser ships with developer tools (DevTools): a panel that shows you the live HTML, every CSS rule that applies to an element (and which ones lost), every network request, every JavaScript error, and lets you pause your code line by line. Learning DevTools well is the single biggest speed-up in frontend work: you stop guessing and start looking.

This page is a guided tour. Then the Bug Lab gives you a page with 7 real bugs to find, one per tool, and the Accessibility Testing Walkthrough shows how to test a page with axe, the keyboard, the accessibility tree and a screen reader.

Which browser?

The steps use Chrome. Edge has the same DevTools (both are built on Chromium). Firefox has the same panels with slightly different names (Inspector instead of Elements, Debugger instead of Sources); the ideas are identical. Menu names move a little between versions: if something isn't where this page says, use the Command Menu (below) and type its name.

docs.title: Opening DevTools
docs.text:
To… Windows / Linux macOS Open / close DevTools F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I Cmd+Option+I Open straight to the Console Ctrl+Shift+J Cmd+Option+J Pick an element on the page Ctrl+Shift+C, then click it Cmd+Shift+C Command Menu: run any DevTools command by name Ctrl+Shift+P (inside DevTools) Cmd+Shift+P Toggle the device toolbar (phone view) Ctrl+Shift+M Cmd+Shift+M

Or right-click anything on the page → Inspect. That opens the Elements panel with that element selected: the fastest way in.

docs.title: The panels you'll use daily
docs.text: Panel Answers the question… Typical bug Elements What does the page look like right now, and which CSS applies to this element? "My style isn't working", layout problems Console What went wrong in JavaScript? What is this value? Errors, wrong values Sources What is my code doing, step by step? Logic bugs with no error message Network What did the page request, and what came back? Missing data, 404s, slow loading Application What's saved in this browser? localStorage, cookies, stale data Lighthouse How good is this page overall? Performance, accessibility, SEO audits Rendering (a drawer tab) How does the page look in dark mode, with reduced motion, with colour blindness? Media-query and accessibility checks

docs.title: Elements: the live page and its CSS
docs.text: The Elements panel shows the DOM: the HTML as it is now, after JavaScript has changed it (not the original file). Select an element and the panes on the side explain how it's styled.

docs.title: Styles: which rules apply, and which lost
docs.text:
The Styles pane lists every rule that matches the selected element, most specific first:

  • A declaration that lost to another rule is shown struck through. Look for the winning rule above it.
  • An invalid declaration (a typo in the property name, or a value that isn't allowed) is struck through with a warning icon. The browser ignored it completely.
  • Hover a selector to see its specificity, for example (0,1,1).
  • Click any value to edit it live; tick or untick the checkbox next to a declaration to switch it off and on.
  • :hov forces states like :hover and :focus so you can style them without keeping the mouse there. .cls adds and removes classes.
  • + adds a new rule for the selected element. Nothing is saved to your files: copy what works back into your CSS.

docs.title: Computed: the final values, and the box model
docs.text:
The Computed tab shows the final value of every property, after the cascade. At the top is the box model diagram:

┌──────────────── margin ────────────────┐
│ ┌────────────── border ──────────────┐ │
│ │ ┌──────────── padding ───────────┐ │ │
│ │ │                                │ │ │
│ │ │      content   420 × 48        │ │ │
│ │ │                                │ │ │
│ │ └────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
│ └────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────┘

Hover each layer to highlight it on the page. Click a property in the Computed list and DevTools jumps to the rule that set it.

docs.title: Grid and Flexbox overlays
docs.text: Elements with display: grid or display: flex get a small grid or flex badge in the DOM tree. Click the badge to draw the layout on the page: column and row lines, gaps, track sizes and area names. The Layout pane lists every grid and flex container on the page with options for the overlay. If you expected three columns and the overlay shows one, the problem is in the container's CSS, not the items.

docs.title: Device toolbar: test on phone sizes
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+Shift+M (Cmd+Shift+M). Pick a device or type a width (try 320 and 375). Things to check:

  • Sideways scrolling: if you can drag the page left, something is wider than the screen. Find it with the find-overflow snippet.
  • Touch targets: buttons and links should be at least about 44 × 44 px.
  • Throttling: the toolbar can also slow the network and CPU to feel like a cheap phone on mobile data.

docs.title: Console: errors and quick questions
docs.text:
The Console shows every JavaScript error, warning and console.log, and lets you run JavaScript in the page.

  • Every error has a link on the right (bug-lab.html:125): click it to jump to the exact line in Sources.
  • $0 is the element currently selected in Elements. Select something, then type $0.textContent or $0.dataset.
  • $$("selector") is a shortcut for [...document.querySelectorAll("selector")]: an array you can map/filter.
  • copy(value) copies any value (an object, an element's HTML) to the clipboard.
  • console.table(array) draws an array of objects as a table.
  • The eye icon creates a Live expression that re-evaluates continuously, for example document.activeElement to see where keyboard focus is.

docs.title: Useful console snippets
docs.text:
Paste these into the Console (or save them in Sources → Snippets to run them on any page). They're tested against the Bug Lab on every change.

Find what makes the page scroll sideways
// Which elements stick out past the right edge of the screen? (the cause of sideways scrolling)
{
  const pageWidth = document.documentElement.clientWidth;
  const culprits = [...document.querySelectorAll("body *")].filter(
    (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().right > pageWidth + 1,
  );
  console.log(culprits.length ? culprits : "Nothing overflows 🎉");
}
Outline every element (run again to remove)
// Draw an outline around every element: makes margins, gaps and invisible boxes visible. Run it again to remove.
{
  const existing = document.getElementById("debug-outlines");
  if (existing) {
    existing.remove();
    console.log("outlines off");
  } else {
    const style = document.createElement("style");
    style.id = "debug-outlines";
    style.textContent = "* { outline: 1px solid rgb(255 0 0 / 0.5) !important; }";
    document.head.append(style);
    console.log("outlines on");
  }
}
Log every keyboard focus stop (then press Tab)
// Log every element that receives keyboard focus: press Tab around the page and read the order.
document.addEventListener("focusin", (event) => {
  const el = event.target;
  console.log("focus →", el.tagName.toLowerCase() + (el.id ? `#${el.id}` : "") + (el.className ? `.${String(el.className).split(" ").join(".")}` : ""), el);
});

The { } around the first two keeps their consts private, so you can paste them again without a "has already been declared" error.

docs.title: Sources: pause your code and look inside
docs.text:
console.log is fine for quick checks. For anything harder, pause the code at a line and look at every variable:

  1. Open Sources and find your file in the left tree (or press Ctrl+P / Cmd+P and type its name).
  2. Click a line number to add a breakpoint (a blue marker).
  3. Do whatever runs that line (click the button). The page freezes there.
  4. Hover any variable to see its value, or read them all in the Scope pane. The Call Stack pane shows how you got here.
  5. Step through:
Key Does F8 Resume until the next breakpoint F10 Step over: run this line, stop at the next F11 Step into the function called on this line Shift+F11 Step out of the current function

Other kinds of breakpoints, for when you don't know which line to stop on:

Breakpoint Set it from Stops when… Conditional Right-click a line number → Add conditional breakpoint (e.g. qty > 5) that line runs and the condition is true Logpoint Right-click a line number → Add logpoint never stops; logs a message, like a console.log you didn't have to write DOM Elements → right-click a node → Break on → subtree modifications / attribute modifications / node removal JavaScript changes that element. Answers "what is changing this?" Event listener Sources → Event Listener Breakpoints → e.g. Mouse → click any click handler starts running Exceptions Sources → Breakpoints pane → Pause on uncaught exceptions an error is about to be thrown, with all the variables still there debugger; Write it in your code that line runs while DevTools is open

The Watch pane keeps expressions you care about, such as typeof total or cart.size, visible while you step.

docs.title: Network: what the page asked for, and what came back
docs.text:
Open Network, then reload the page (requests made before DevTools was open aren't recorded). Each row is one request.

  • Filter with Fetch/XHR to see only your API calls, or Img, CSS, JS.
  • The Status column: anything that isn't 2xx is red. Click a row for Headers (URL, method, status), Payload (what you sent), Preview (the parsed JSON) and Response (the raw text).
  • Tick Disable cache while DevTools is open, so you always get your latest files.
  • Tick Preserve log to keep requests when the page navigates or reloads.
  • The throttling dropdown simulates slow mobile connections. Every loading state you build should be tested this way.
  • Right-click a request → Copy → Copy as fetch gives you working JavaScript to repeat it in the Console.
Status Means Usually 200 OK Worked 304 Not Modified Served from the browser cache Fine 400 Bad Request The server didn't understand what you sent Wrong body or parameters 401 / 403 Not logged in / not allowed Missing or expired token 404 Not Found Nothing at that URL A typo in the URL or path 500 Server Error The server crashed A backend bug; check its logs (failed) / CORS error No response at all, or the browser blocked it Server down, offline, or missing CORS headers

docs.title: Application: what the browser has saved
docs.text: Application → Storage shows Local storage, Session storage, Cookies and IndexedDB for the site. You can view, edit and delete entries. Storage → Clear site data wipes everything for the site: the quickest way to test "first visit".

docs.title: Rendering: emulate settings without changing your computer
docs.text:
Open it from the Command Menu (type Rendering). The most useful options:

  • Emulate CSS media feature prefers-color-scheme: test dark mode.
  • Emulate CSS media feature prefers-reduced-motion: check animations switch off.
  • Emulate vision deficiencies: see the page as someone with colour blindness or blurred vision would.
  • Layout Shift Regions: flashes the areas that jump while the page loads (what Core Web Vitals call CLS).

docs.title: Lighthouse and Performance
docs.text:
Lighthouse runs an automated audit and scores Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices and SEO from 0 to 100, with a list of specific problems (images without alt, low contrast, render-blocking files, missing width/height on images). Run it in an Incognito window, because browser extensions slow pages down and skew the score.

The Performance panel records everything the browser does while you interact (scripting, layout, painting) on a timeline. Use it when something feels slow: long yellow blocks are JavaScript keeping the browser busy.

docs.title: A debugging routine
docs.text:
When something is wrong, work through it in this order instead of changing code at random:

  1. Reproduce it. Find the exact steps and screen width that show the bug.
  2. Read the Console. Any red error? Click its link.
  3. Inspect the element. Is it in the DOM? What do Styles and Computed say?
  4. Check Network. Did the data arrive? With what status and what body?
  5. Pause the code. Breakpoint where the value is first wrong, and step.
  6. Fix it in DevTools first (edit the CSS live, try the expression in the Console), then copy the fix into your files.
  7. Check you didn't break something else: other screen widths, keyboard use, the Console stays clean.

Ready to practise? Open the Bug Lab → Then test a page the way people with disabilities use it in the Accessibility Testing Walkthrough →

docs.title: Accessibility Testing Walkthrough
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate Advanced

Accessibility explains what makes a page accessible. This page is about testing it: the four checks to run on every page, in order, and what each one finds. You'll practise on the A11y Lab, a small FreshCart page with 10 planted accessibility problems.

The most important lesson comes first, from a real run on that page:

Testing method Problems it found in the lab (of 10) 1. Automated scan (axe, the engine inside Lighthouse) 5 2. Keyboard only 3 more 3. Accessibility tree in DevTools confirms several, and 1 more 4. Screen reader the last 1, and how all of them feel

An automated scan is the start, not the finish. It found half the problems in seconds, and passed a page that a keyboard user couldn't use to add anything to the cart.

docs.title: The A11y Lab
docs.text: Open the A11y Lab in a new tab and test it as you read. It looks fine with a mouse. That's the point.

docs.title: Step 1: Automated scan (2 minutes)
docs.text:
Run one of these:

  • Lighthouse: DevTools → Lighthouse → tick Accessibility → Analyze page load.
  • axe DevTools (free browser extension from Deque): DevTools → axe DevTools → Scan all of my page. Same engine as Lighthouse, with more detail per issue.
  • In your tests: run axe in Playwright on every page in CI, as this site does:
await page.addScriptTag({ path: require.resolve("axe-core") });
const { violations } = await page.evaluate(() => axe.run());

The real result for the lab, produced by the site's test runner with axe-core 4.14.0:

a11y-lab.html (broken): 5 rules failed
  ✘ button-name     critical  1 element   Buttons must have discernible text
  ✘ color-contrast  serious   1 element   Elements must meet minimum color contrast ratio thresholds
  ✘ heading-order   moderate  1 element   Heading levels should only increase by one
  ✘ html-has-lang   serious   1 element   <html> element must have a lang attribute
  ✘ image-alt       critical  1 element   Images must have alternative text

Every one of these is a real problem: A1, A2, A3, A8 and A10 below. But look at what it didn't report: nothing about the ADD control, the focus ring, the dialog, the search label or the cart count. Automated tools can only check what can be decided from the code. Whether something is usable needs a person.

Check contrast by hand, too

In Elements, select the text, then click the colour swatch next to color in Styles. The colour picker shows the contrast ratio with ✓/✗ for AA (4.5 : 1 for normal text) and AAA. Drag the colour until it passes.

docs.title: Step 2: Keyboard only (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Put the mouse away. Use only:

Key Does Tab / Shift+Tab Next / previous focusable element Enter Activate a link or button Space Activate a button, tick a checkbox Arrow keys Move inside radios, selects, menus, tabs Esc Close a dialog or menu

Ask four questions at every step:

  1. Can I reach it? Every link, button and field gets focus, in a sensible order.
  2. Can I see where I am? A clear focus ring, never hidden.
  3. Can I use it? Enter / Space do what a click does.
  4. Can I get out? Dialogs close with Esc, and focus goes back where it was.

What the tests recorded on the lab when pressing Tab from the top:

Tab stops, in order Focus ring Broken logo → cart button → search box → Go → Delivery info none (outline: none) Fixed logo → cart button → search box → Go → ADD → Delivery info 3 px blue ring

The broken page has no way to add the apple to the cart from the keyboard, and you can't see where you are. axe reported neither problem.

docs.title: Step 3: The accessibility tree (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Screen readers don't read your HTML. They read the accessibility tree: the browser's summary of every element as a role (button, heading, link…), a name ("Add Shimla Apple to cart") and a state (checked, expanded…).

  • In Elements, select an element and open the Accessibility pane (next to Styles). It shows the element's computed Name and Role, and where the name came from (content, aria-label, <label>, alt).
  • Chrome can show the whole page as an accessibility tree: tick Enable full-page accessibility tree in that pane, then switch the Elements tree with the button that appears.
