<p>As the docs say, <q>prefer native elements over ARIA</q>.</p>
<p>A <dfn>pixel</dfn> is the smallest unit of a digital image.</p>

My favourite book is The Pragmatic Programmer.

As the docs say, prefer native elements over ARIA.

A pixel is the smallest unit of a digital image.

  • cite: the title of a creative work (not a person's name).
  • q: a short inline quote. The browser adds quote marks for the current lang.
  • dfn: the term being defined in this sentence.

docs.title: <time> and <data> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: human-readable text with a machine-readable value.

<p>Sale ends <time datetime="2026-12-31T23:59">New Year's Eve at midnight</time>.</p>
<p>Product: <data value="SKU-4821">Blue running shoes</data></p>

Sale ends New Year's Eve at midnight.

Product: Blue running shoes

docs.title: <span> Generic inline container Beginner
docs.text:
Use: an inline wrapper with no meaning, for styling a word or attaching JS.

<p>Status: <span class="badge">Active</span></p>

Status: Active

docs.title: <ins> and <del> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: edits to a document (inserted / deleted text), like track changes.

<p>Meeting moved to <del>Monday</del> <ins>Tuesday</ins>.</p>

Meeting moved to Monday Tuesday.

docs.title: <bdi>, <bdo>, <wbr> Advanced
docs.text:
<!-- bdi: isolate text whose direction is unknown (user names) -->
<p>User <bdi>إيان</bdi>: 3 posts</p>

<!-- bdo: force a direction -->
<p><bdo dir="rtl">This text is reversed</bdo></p>

<!-- wbr: a place the browser MAY break a long word -->
<p>https://example.com/<wbr>very/<wbr>long/<wbr>path/<wbr>to/<wbr>a/<wbr>resource</p>

User إيان: 3 posts

This text is reversed

https://example.com/very/long/path/to/a/resource

docs.title: <ruby>, <rt>, <rp> Advanced
docs.text:
Use: pronunciation annotations for East Asian text.

<ruby>漢<rp>(</rp><rt>kan</rt><rp>)</rp>字<rp>(</rp><rt>ji</rt><rp>)</rp></ruby>

漢(kan)字(ji)

<rp> holds fallback parentheses, shown only in browsers that don't support ruby.

docs.title: Quick decision table
docs.text: You want to… Use Show something is important strong Change the meaning by stress em Style a keyword without extra meaning b or span Highlight a search match mark Show a price that changed s + new price Show a date time datetime="…" Show code / keys / output code / kbd / samp

docs.title: Interactive Elements & Web Components
docs.text: Modern HTML can do things that used to need a JavaScript library: accordions, modals, menus and tooltips. Native versions handle focus, keyboard and screen readers for you.

docs.title: <details> and <summary> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a disclosure widget (show/hide), with no JavaScript.

<details>
  <summary>What is Flexbox?</summary>
  <p>A one-dimensional layout model for rows or columns.</p>
</details>

<details open>
  <summary>Open by default</summary>
  <p>The <code>open</code> attribute starts it expanded.</p>
</details>
What is Flexbox?

A one-dimensional layout model for rows or columns.

Open by default

The open attribute starts it expanded.

docs.title: Exclusive accordion with name Intermediate Baseline 2024
docs.text:
Give several <details> the same name and only one can be open at a time.

<details name="faq" open><summary>Shipping</summary><p>3–5 days.</p></details>
<details name="faq"><summary>Returns</summary><p>30 days, free.</p></details>
<details name="faq"><summary>Warranty</summary><p>2 years.</p></details>
Shipping

3–5 days.

Returns

30 days, free.

Warranty

2 years.

Style the marker:

summary { list-style: none; cursor: pointer; }           /* hide the triangle */
summary::-webkit-details-marker { display: none; }      /* older Safari */
summary::after { content: "+"; float: inline-end; }
details[open] > summary::after { content: "−"; }

/* Animate open/close height (Chromium 131+) */
details::details-content {
  block-size: 0; overflow: hidden;
  transition: block-size .3s, content-visibility .3s allow-discrete;
}
details[open]::details-content { block-size: auto; }
:root { interpolate-size: allow-keywords; }  /* lets 'auto' animate */

docs.title: <dialog> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: a modal or non-modal dialog. showModal() gives you, for free: a backdrop, focus moved inside, the rest of the page made inert, Esc to close, and rendering on the top layer above every z-index.

<button type="button" onclick="dlg.showModal()">Delete project…</button>

<dialog id="dlg" aria-labelledby="dlg-title">
  <h2 id="dlg-title">Delete project?</h2>
  <p>This can't be undone.</p>
  <form method="dialog">
    <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
    <button value="delete">Delete</button>
  </form>
</dialog>

dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(0 0 0 / .5); backdrop-filter: blur(2px); }
Delete project…
  • <form method="dialog"> closes the dialog on submit and sets dialog.returnValue to the clicked button's value.
  • show() opens it non-modally (no backdrop, page still interactive).
  • New: closedby="any" (Chromium 134+) lets a click on the backdrop close it.

docs.title: Delete project?
docs.text:
This can't be undone.

Cancel Delete

docs.title: The Popover API Intermediate Baseline 2024
docs.text:
Use: menus, tooltips, toasts and pickers that float on the top layer. Declarative: no JS needed to open and close.

<button popovertarget="menu">Open menu</button>

<div id="menu" popover>
  <a href="#">Profile</a>
  <a href="#">Settings</a>
  <a href="#">Sign out</a>
</div>
Open menu

Profile

Settings

Sign out

Feature popover (auto) popover="manual" popover="hint" Closes on outside click / Esc ✅ ❌ (you close it) ✅ Closes other auto popovers ✅ ❌ ❌ (closes other hints) Typical use Menus, pickers Toasts Tooltips

popovertargetaction="show | hide | toggle" controls what the button does. Pair popovers with CSS anchor positioning to attach them to their button.

dialog vs popover

Use <dialog> + showModal() when the user must respond before continuing (blocks the page). Use popover for lightweight, dismissable UI that doesn't block anything.

docs.title: <template> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: inert HTML that isn't rendered, ready to be cloned by JavaScript.

<ul id="list"></ul>

<template id="row">
  <li><strong class="name"></strong> — <span class="role"></span></li>
</template>

<script>
  const tpl = document.getElementById('row');
  for (const [name, role] of [['Asha', 'Design'], ['Ravi', 'Frontend']]) {
    const li = tpl.content.cloneNode(true);
    li.querySelector('.name').textContent = name;
    li.querySelector('.role').textContent = role;
    document.getElementById('list').append(li);
  }
</script>
  • —

docs.title: Custom elements, Shadow DOM and <slot> Advanced
docs.text:
Use: build your own reusable HTML tags (Web Components) with encapsulated styles. They work in any framework or none.

<user-card>
  <span slot="name">Asha Rao</span>
  <span slot="role">Design Lead</span>
</user-card>

<script>
  customElements.define('user-card', class extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
      super();
      this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).innerHTML = `
        <style>
          :host { display: inline-block; padding: 1rem; border-radius: 12px;
                  background: linear-gradient(135deg, #e4572e, #f3a712); color: white; }
          ::slotted([slot=role]) { opacity: .85; font-size: .9em; }
        </style>
        <strong><slot name="name">Anonymous</slot></strong><br>
        <slot name="role"></slot>`;
    }
  });
</script>
Asha RaoDesign Lead
  • Custom element names must contain a hyphen (user-card).
  • <slot> is where the light-DOM children get projected. Named slots match slot="…".
  • Styles inside the shadow root don't leak out; page styles don't leak in (except inherited properties like color and font, and ::part()).

docs.title: Declarative Shadow DOM Expert Baseline 2024
docs.text:
Server-render a shadow root without JavaScript:

<user-card>
  <template shadowrootmode="open">
    <style>:host { display:block; border:1px solid #ccc; padding:1rem; }</style>
    <slot></slot>
  </template>
  Rendered on the server, encapsulated, no JS required.
</user-card>

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

Web Components shine for design systems shared across frameworks (React, Angular, Vue, plain pages). Trade-offs: SSR needs declarative shadow DOM; form participation needs ElementInternals; ARIA references (aria-labelledby) can't cross shadow boundaries yet; and global CSS such as a reset doesn't reach inside the shadow root. Many teams use Lit to cut the boilerplate.

docs.title: <img> Image Beginner → Advanced
docs.text:
Use: embed an image.

<img src="https://picsum.photos/id/1015/320/180"
     alt="A river winding through a green valley"
     width="320" height="180"
     loading="lazy" decoding="async">
Attribute Why src Image URL (required) alt Text alternative (required). Describe the purpose. For purely decorative images use alt="" so screen readers skip them. width / height Intrinsic size. The browser reserves space before the image loads, which prevents layout shift (CLS). Always set them, then let CSS make the image responsive. loading="lazy" Don't load until it's near the viewport. Never lazy-load the hero / LCP image. decoding="async" Decode off the main thread. fetchpriority="high" Boost the LCP image's priority. srcset / sizes Responsive image candidates (below). 
/* The responsive image rule everyone uses */
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; }

docs.title: Writing good alt text
docs.text: Image Good alt Product photo in a shop alt="Blue Cloud Runner shoe, side view" Logo that links home alt="Acme home" (describe the link's purpose) Chart Short summary in alt, full data in a table or caption Decorative swirl alt="" Icon next to the text "Delete" alt="" (the text already says it)

docs.title: Responsive images with srcset and sizes Intermediate
docs.text:
<!-- Resolution switching: same image, different file sizes -->
<img
  src="photo-800.jpg"
  srcset="photo-400.jpg 400w, photo-800.jpg 800w, photo-1600.jpg 1600w"
  sizes="(min-width: 1024px) 50vw, 100vw"
  alt="…" width="800" height="533">

Read it as: "This image shows at 50% of the viewport on screens ≥ 1024px, otherwise full width. Here are three files and their real widths; browser, pick the smallest one that's sharp enough for this screen's pixel density."

docs.title: <picture> and <source> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: offer different formats (AVIF → WebP → JPEG) or different crops at different screen sizes (art direction).

<picture>
  <!-- Art direction: square crop on phones -->
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="hero-square.avif" type="image/avif">
  <!-- Modern formats first, browser picks the first it supports -->
  <source srcset="hero.avif" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="hero.webp" type="image/webp">
  <!-- Fallback + where alt, width, height live -->
  <img src="hero.jpg" alt="Team working together" width="1200" height="600">
</picture>

The <img> inside is required: it's what actually renders. <source> only swaps its src.

docs.title: <video> Beginner
docs.text:
<video controls width="320" preload="metadata"
       poster="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-images/flower.jpg">
  <source src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track kind="captions" src="flower-en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  Your browser doesn't support video. <a href="flower.mp4">Download it</a>.
</video>
Your browser doesn't support video. Attribute Use controls Show play/pause/volume controls autoplay Start automatically. Browsers only allow it with muted. muted, loop Self-explanatory playsinline Play inside the page on iOS instead of going fullscreen poster Image shown before playback preload none, metadata (recommended), auto

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

A background hero video should be autoplay muted loop playsinline, be paused when prefers-reduced-motion: reduce matches, and have a visible pause button (WCAG 2.2.2: anything moving for more than 5 seconds must be pausable).

docs.title: <audio> Beginner
docs.text:
<audio controls src="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-audio/t-rex-roar.mp3">
  <a href="t-rex-roar.mp3">Download audio</a>
</audio>

docs.title: <track> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: timed text for video/audio in WebVTT format: kind="captions | subtitles | descriptions | chapters | metadata".

flower-en.vtt
WEBVTT

00:00:00.000 --> 00:00:03.000
A bee lands on a pink flower.

docs.title: <iframe> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: embed another web page: maps, YouTube, payment widgets.

<iframe
  src="https://www.openstreetmap.org/export/embed.html?bbox=77.58,12.96,77.62,12.99"
  title="Map of central Bengaluru"
  width="100%" height="220"
  loading="lazy"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin"></iframe>

Always set a title (screen readers announce it). Use sandbox to restrict what embedded third-party content can do, and allow="…" to grant specific permissions (camera, fullscreen).

docs.title: <embed> and <object> Advanced
docs.text:
Legacy ways to embed plugins (Flash, Java applets). Today their main remaining use is embedding PDFs, where <iframe> works just as well. Prefer <iframe>, <video> or <img>.

<object data="guide.pdf" type="application/pdf" width="100%" height="400">
  <a href="guide.pdf">Download the guide (PDF)</a>
</object>

docs.title: <svg> Inline SVG Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: vector graphics that are crisp at any size and can be styled with CSS. Ideal for icons, logos and charts.

<svg width="120" height="120" viewBox="0 0 120 120" role="img" aria-label="Orange circle with a check mark">
  <circle cx="60" cy="60" r="54" fill="#e4572e"/>
  <path d="M35 62 l17 17 l33 -36" fill="none" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="10"
        stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/>
</svg>

Icons

Use fill="currentColor" in icon SVGs so they inherit the text colour, and they'll follow hover states and dark mode automatically. Decorative icons get aria-hidden="true".

docs.title: <canvas> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: a pixel drawing surface for JavaScript: games, charts with thousands of points, image editing. Not accessible on its own, so provide fallback content or an alternative.

<canvas id="c" width="240" height="100">A red-to-blue gradient bar.</canvas>
<script>
  const ctx = document.getElementById('c').getContext('2d');
  const g = ctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 240, 0);
  g.addColorStop(0, '#e4572e');
  g.addColorStop(1, '#3f51b5');
  ctx.fillStyle = g;
  ctx.fillRect(0, 20, 240, 60);
</script>
A red-to-blue gradient bar.

docs.title: <map> and <area> Advanced
docs.text:
Use: clickable regions on an image (image maps). Rare today; an inline SVG with <a> elements is usually easier to make responsive.

<img src="floor.png" alt="Office floor plan" usemap="#floor" width="400" height="200">
<map name="floor">
  <area shape="rect" coords="0,0,200,200" href="/rooms/a" alt="Meeting room A">
  <area shape="circle" coords="300,100,60" href="/rooms/b" alt="Lounge">
</map>

docs.title: Format cheat sheet Advanced
docs.text: Content Best format (2026) Fallback Photos AVIF WebP → JPEG Icons, logos SVG PNG Screenshots / UI WebP lossless or AVIF PNG Animation <video> MP4/WebM (AV1/H.264) Animated WebP; avoid GIF (10× larger) Fonts WOFF2 —

docs.title: Sectioning & Landmarks
docs.text: Sectioning elements describe the regions of a page. Screen readers expose them as landmarks, so users can jump straight to the navigation, the main content or the search box. They also give you meaningful CSS hooks instead of div.header.

docs.title: The page skeleton Beginner
docs.text:
<body>
  <a class="skip-link" href="#content">Skip to content</a>
  <header>
    <a href="/">Logo</a>
    <nav aria-label="Primary">…</nav>
    <search>…</search>
  </header>

  <main id="content">
    <article>
      <h1>Article title</h1>
      <section>
        <h2>Part one</h2>
        …
      </section>
    </article>
    <aside>Related links</aside>
  </main>

  <footer>© 2026 Acme</footer>
</body>
<header> logo · <nav> · <search> <main> <article> h1 <section> h2 <section> h2 <aside> <footer> Element Landmark role When it's a landmark <header> banner Only when it's a direct child of <body> (not inside article/section/main) <nav> navigation Always <main> main Always <aside> complementary At top level, or with an accessible name <footer> contentinfo Only when it's a direct child of <body> <section> region Only when it has an accessible name (aria-labelledby / aria-label) <search> search Always <form> form Only when it has an accessible name <article> article Always (not a landmark, but a document structure role)

docs.title: <header> BeginnerWhy Grid beats floats
docs.text:
Use: introductory content for the page or for a section: logo, title, nav, author info. A page can have several (one per article).

<article>
  <header>
    <h2>Why Grid beats floats</h2>
    <p>By Asha · <time datetime="2026-10-01">1 Oct 2026</time></p>
  </header>
  <p>…</p>
</article>

By Asha · 1 Oct 2026

…

docs.title: <nav> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a block of major navigation links: main menu, breadcrumbs, table of contents, pagination. Not every group of links needs <nav> (footer legal links usually don't).

<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol>
    <li><a href="/">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/docs">Docs</a></li>
    <li><a aria-current="page">Flexbox</a></li>
  </ol>
</nav>
  1. Home /
  2. Docs /
  3. Flexbox

Senior note · 🟡 Intermediate

With more than one <nav> on a page, give each an aria-label ("Primary", "Breadcrumb", "Pagination") so screen reader users can tell them apart. Use aria-current="page" on the link to the current page.

docs.title: <main> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: the dominant content of the page. Exactly one visible <main> per page. Not inside article, aside, header, footer or nav.

<a class="skip-link" href="#content">Skip to content</a>
<main id="content">…</main>

The skip link lets keyboard users jump past a long header. Hide it until it gets focus:

.skip-link { position: absolute; translate: 0 -200%; }
.skip-link:focus { translate: 0 0; }

docs.title: <article> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: self-contained content that makes sense on its own and could be syndicated: a blog post, a news story, a product card, a forum comment.

Test: "Would this still make sense in an RSS feed?" If yes, it's an <article>.

<article class="product">
  <img src="shoe.jpg" alt="Blue running shoe" width="120" height="80">
  <h3>Cloud Runner</h3>
  <p>₹4,999</p>
</article>

docs.title: <section> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a thematic grouping of content, with a heading. If you can't think of a heading for it, it's probably a <div>.

<section aria-labelledby="pricing-h">
  <h2 id="pricing-h">Pricing</h2>
  …
</section>

section vs article vs div

  • article: stands alone (a card, a post).
  • section: a chapter of something bigger, with a heading.
  • div: no meaning, styling only.

docs.title: <aside> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: content related to the surrounding content, but separate from it: sidebars, pull quotes, "related articles", ads.

<aside>
  <h3>Did you know?</h3>
  <p>Flexbox shipped in all major browsers in 2015.</p>
</aside>
Did you know?

Flexbox shipped in all major browsers in 2015.

docs.title: <footer> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: footer for the page or a section: copyright, author, related links, contact.

<footer>
  <p>© 2026 Acme Inc. · <a href="/privacy">Privacy</a></p>
</footer>

docs.title: <address> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: contact information for the nearest <article> or the whole page. Not for any postal address in the text.

<address>
  Written by <a href="mailto:asha@example.com">Asha</a>.<br>
  Acme Inc., Bengaluru
</address>
Written by Asha. Acme Inc., Bengaluru

docs.title: <hgroup> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: a heading grouped with a subtitle or tagline. Since 2023 the spec allows one heading plus <p> elements.

<hgroup>
  <h1>Web UI Frontend Playbook</h1>
  <p>From your first tag to frontend architect.</p>
</hgroup>
Web UI Frontend Playbook

From your first tag to frontend architect.

docs.title: <search> Intermediate new 2023
docs.text:
Use: wraps search or filter controls. It's the native version of <div role="search">. Baseline since 2023.

<search>
  <form action="/search">
    <label for="q">Search docs</label>
    <input id="q" name="q" type="search" placeholder="e.g. flexbox">
    <button>Search</button>
  </form>
</search>
Search docs Search

Senior note · 🔴 Expert

The "document outline algorithm" never shipped. HTML5 once proposed that <h1> inside a nested <section> would be treated as an <h2>. No browser or screen reader implemented it and it was removed from the spec in 2022. Always use explicit heading levels (h1–h6) that match the real nesting depth. Also, browsers are removing the default smaller font-size for h1 inside article/section, so set heading sizes explicitly in CSS.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: Use tables for tabular data only: things with rows and columns that relate to each other (prices, schedules, comparisons). Never use tables for page layout; that's what Flexbox and Grid are for.

docs.title: A complete, accessible table Beginner
docs.text:
<table>
  <caption>Plan comparison</caption>
  <colgroup>
    <col>
    <col span="2">
    <col class="highlight">
  </colgroup>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Feature</th>
      <th scope="col">Free</th>
      <th scope="col">Pro</th>
      <th scope="col">Team</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Projects</th>
      <td>3</td>
      <td>Unlimited</td>
      <td>Unlimited</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Storage</th>
      <td>1 GB</td>
      <td>100 GB</td>
      <td>1 TB</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Support</th>
      <td colspan="2">Community forum</td>
      <td>24/7 phone</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Price / month</th>
      <td>₹0</td>
      <td>₹499</td>
      <td>₹1,999</td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>
Plan comparison FeatureFreeProTeam Projects3UnlimitedUnlimited Storage1 GB100 GB1 TB SupportCommunity forum24/7 phone Price / month₹0₹499₹1,999

docs.title: Every table element
docs.text: Element Use <table> The table container <caption> The table's title. First child of <table>. Screen readers announce it. <colgroup> / <col> Style whole columns. Only background, border, width and visibility work on columns. <thead> Header rows. Repeats on each printed page. <tbody> Body rows. A table can have several, to group rows. <tfoot> Summary rows (totals) <tr> A table row <th> A header cell. scope="col" or scope="row" tells assistive tech what it labels. <td> A data cell

docs.title: Spanning cells Beginner
docs.text:
<table>
  <tr><th rowspan="2">Mon</th><td>9:00 Standup</td></tr>
  <tr><td>14:00 Design review</td></tr>
  <tr><th>Tue</th><td>10:00 Planning</td></tr>
</table>
Mon9:00 Standup 14:00 Design review Tue10:00 Planning

colspan="n" merges cells across columns; rowspan="n" merges down rows.

docs.title: Styling tables Intermediate
docs.text:
table {
  border-collapse: collapse;       /* single borders instead of doubled */
  inline-size: 100%;
  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;   /* digits line up in columns */
}
th, td {
  padding: .5rem .75rem;
  border-block-end: 1px solid #ddd;
  text-align: start;
}
td:is(:nth-child(n+2)) { text-align: end; }  /* right-align numbers */
tbody tr:nth-child(even) { background: #f6f7f9; }   /* zebra stripes */
tbody tr:hover { background: #fff1ea; }
thead th { position: sticky; inset-block-start: 0; background: white; }  /* sticky header */

docs.title: Responsive tables Intermediate
docs.text:
Tables don't shrink well. Two reliable patterns:

1. Horizontal scroll (simplest)2. Stack cells as cards on small screens 
<div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-labelledby="cap" tabindex="0">
  <table>
    <caption id="cap">Quarterly results</caption>
    …
  </table>
</div>

.table-scroll { overflow-x: auto; }

tabindex="0" makes the scroll area keyboard-scrollable; role="region" + label makes it announceable.

<td data-label="Storage">100 GB</td>

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  thead { display: none; }
  tr, td { display: block; }
  td::before { content: attr(data-label) ": "; font-weight: 700; }
}

Warning

Changing display on table elements can strip their table semantics in some browsers. Add role="table", role="row", role="cell" explicitly if you use this pattern.

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

For complex tables with multi-level headers, use id on each <th> and headers="id1 id2" on each <td>. Test with a screen reader in table mode (Ctrl+Alt+Right in VoiceOver/NVDA) to hear what each cell announces.

docs.title: Text Content
docs.text: Block-level elements that organise text: headings, paragraphs, lists, quotes and figures.

docs.title: <h1> – <h6> Headings BeginnerHeading 2
docs.text:
Use: section titles, from most important (h1) to least (h6).

<h1>Heading 1</h1>
<h2>Heading 2</h2>
<h3>Heading 3</h3>
<h4>Heading 4</h4>
<h5>Heading 5</h5>
<h6>Heading 6</h6>
Heading 1 Heading 3 Heading 4 Heading 5 Heading 6

Rules:

  • One <h1> per page, describing the page.
  • Don't skip levels (h2 → h4). Screen reader users navigate by heading level and a skip looks like missing content.
  • Pick the level for structure, then use CSS for size. Need a small-looking h2? Style it.

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

About 68% of screen reader users navigate long pages by headings first (WebAIM survey). A correct heading outline is one of the cheapest, highest-impact accessibility wins.

docs.title: <p> Paragraph Beginner
docs.text:
<p>The first paragraph.</p>
<p>The second paragraph, with space above it from the browser's default margin.</p>

The first paragraph.

The second paragraph, with space above it from the browser's default margin.

Common mistake: using empty <p></p> or <br><br> for spacing. Use CSS margin instead.

docs.title: <br> Line break Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a line break that's part of the content, such as in an address or a poem.

<p>221B Baker Street<br>London<br>NW1 6XE</p>

221B Baker StreetLondonNW1 6XE

docs.title: <hr> Thematic break Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a change of topic between paragraphs. It's semantic, not just a line, so screen readers announce it as a separator.

<p>End of chapter one.</p>
<hr>
<p>Chapter two begins.</p>

End of chapter one.

Chapter two begins.

docs.title: <pre> Preformatted text Beginner
docs.text:
Use: keeps whitespace and line breaks exactly as written, in a monospace font. Wrap code in <pre><code>.

<pre><code>function greet() {
  return "hi";
}</code></pre>

function greet() {
  return "hi";
}

docs.title: <blockquote> Block quotation Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a long quote from another source. cite holds the source URL (not shown on screen).

<figure>
  <blockquote cite="https://www.w3.org/standards/webdesign/accessibility">
    <p>The power of the Web is in its universality.</p>
  </blockquote>
  <figcaption>— Tim Berners-Lee</figcaption>
</figure>

The power of the Web is in its universality.

— Tim Berners-Lee

docs.title: <ul> Unordered list Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a list where order doesn't matter. Navigation menus are usually <ul> inside <nav>.

<ul>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
</ul>
  • Milk
  • Eggs
  • Bread

docs.title: <ol> Ordered list Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a list where order matters: steps, rankings.

Key attributes: start="5", reversed, type="1 | a | A | i | I". On <li>: value="10".

<ol type="i" start="3">
  <li>Preheat the oven</li>
  <li>Mix the batter</li>
  <li>Bake for 25 minutes</li>
</ol>

<ol reversed>
  <li>Bronze</li>
  <li>Silver</li>
  <li>Gold</li>
</ol>
  1. Preheat the oven
  2. Mix the batter
  3. Bake for 25 minutes
  1. Bronze
  2. Silver
  3. Gold

docs.title: <li> List item Beginner
docs.text:
Use: an item inside <ul>, <ol> or <menu>. Lists can nest: put a whole <ul> inside an <li>.

<ul>
  <li>Frontend
    <ul>
      <li>HTML</li>
      <li>CSS</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Backend</li>
</ul>
  • Frontend
    • HTML
    • CSS
  • Backend

Senior note · 🟠 Advanced

list-style: none makes Safari/VoiceOver stop announcing a list as a list. If the list semantics matter (a nav menu does), add role="list" to the <ul>. Or use list-style-type: "", which hides the bullets and keeps the semantics in current Safari.

docs.title: <dl>, <dt>, <dd> Description list Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: name–value groups: glossaries, metadata, FAQs, key-value specs.

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>Structure and meaning of content.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Presentation and layout.</dd>
  <dt>JS</dt>
  <dd>Behaviour.</dd>
</dl>
HTML Structure and meaning of content. CSS Presentation and layout. JS Behaviour.

You may wrap each dt/dd group in a <div> for styling (for example, a grid of cards).

docs.title: <div> Generic container Beginner
docs.text:
Use: a block container with no meaning. Use it for styling and layout hooks only, when no semantic element fits.

<div class="card">
  <h3>Plan A</h3>
  <p>For small teams.</p>
</div>
Plan A

For small teams.

docs.title: <figure> and <figcaption> Beginner
docs.text:
Use: self-contained content (image, chart, code, quote) with an optional caption. The figure could be moved to an appendix without breaking the text.

<figure>
  <img src="chart.svg" alt="Revenue grew 40% from Q1 to Q4" width="240" height="120">
  <figcaption>Figure 1: Revenue by quarter, 2026.</figcaption>
</figure>
Figure 1: Revenue by quarter, 2026.

docs.title: <menu> Intermediate
docs.text:
Use: a semantic alternative to <ul> for a list of commands (toolbar buttons). Browsers treat it like <ul>.

<menu>
  <li><button type="button">Copy</button></li>
  <li><button type="button">Cut</button></li>
  <li><button type="button">Paste</button></li>
</menu>
  • Copy
  • Cut
  • Paste

docs.title: <main> Beginner
docs.text: See Sectioning & Landmarks. One visible <main> per page, holding the page's primary content.

docs.title: JavaScript Basics: Start Here
docs.text:
Beginner

HTML is the content of a page, CSS is how it looks, and JavaScript is how it behaves: what happens when you click "ADD", type in a search box, or wait for products to load. This tab teaches the JavaScript you need for frontend work, from your first line to fetch(), using one running example: the FreshCart grocery store from the E-commerce Page tab.

docs.title: How to run JavaScript (pick one)
How each lesson is laid out
docs.text:
1. A short explanation of what and why.
  2. The code, then its console output right underneath.
  3. A line-by-line table for the lines that matter.
  4. Try it exercises with collapsed solutions (also run and checked by CI), and common mistakes.

Every output on these pages is real

The code lives in docs/javascript/examples/, and javascript/run-examples.mjs runs every example and saves what it prints. CI fails if an output on the site no longer matches the code. The page demos (lessons 6–8) are clicked through in a real browser by Playwright on every change.

Console output: browser vs this site

Outputs here come from Node.js. Your browser's console shows the same values, but draws objects and arrays as expandable trees (▶ {name: 'Apple'}) instead of text. Error messages can also be worded slightly differently between browsers.

docs.title: The lessons
docs.text:
# Lesson You learn 1 Variables, Types & Strings const/let, the 7 basic types, template literals, why money is stored in paise, converting "3" to 3 2 Operators & Decisions ===, && || !, truthy/falsy, ?? and ?., if/else, the ternary, switch 3 Functions Declarations and arrow functions, defaults, return, scope, callbacks, closures 4 Arrays & Objects Lists and records, destructuring, spread, references vs copies, Map, Set, JSON 5 Loops & Array Methods for, for…of, map, filter, find, reduce, sorting, and a full cart bill 6 The DOM: Changing the Page Finding elements, changing text, classes and attributes, building elements from data 7 Events: Reacting to Users Clicks, typing, forms, keyboard, event delegation 8 Async: Timers, Promises & fetch Why JS doesn't wait, promises, async/await, try/catch, loading data from a server 9 Errors, Debugging & Good Habits Reading error messages, throw, DevTools breakpoints, modules, clean-code habits

After lesson 9, rebuild the FreshCart cart in E-commerce lesson 6: every line of its JavaScript uses only what this tab teaches.

docs.title: How JavaScript runs, in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR H["HTML parsed"] --> D["DOM tree built"] D --> J["Your script runs (defer)"] J --> L["Listeners registered:<br/>click, input, submit…"] L --> W["Browser waits"] W -->|"user clicks / types"| E["Your function runs"] W -->|"timer ends / data arrives"| E E -->|"changes the DOM"| P["Browser redraws the page"] P --> W

Your script runs once at the start and sets things up. After that, almost all your code runs in response to events: a click, a keystroke, a timer, or data arriving from the server.

docs.title: 1. Variables, Types & Strings
docs.text:
Beginner

A program works with values (a price, a product name, "is the user logged in?"). A variable is a name you give to a value so you can use it later.

docs.title: Your first line
docs.text:
console.log("Hello, FreshCart!");
console.log(2 + 3);
console.log("Total:", 189 + 49);
Console output
Hello, FreshCart!
5
Total: 238
Code What it does console.log(…) Prints to the console. Your main tool for seeing what your code is doing. "Hello, FreshCart!" A string: text inside quotes. "…", '…' and `…` all work. 2 + 3 JavaScript works the sum out first, then prints 5. console.log("Total:", 189 + 49) Several values separated by commas are printed with spaces between them. ; Ends a statement. Optional in most cases, but this playbook always writes it. // … A comment: ignored by JavaScript, written for humans.

docs.title: const and let
docs.text:
const storeName = "FreshCart";   // const: this name will always point to the same value
let itemsInCart = 0;             // let: this value is going to change

itemsInCart = itemsInCart + 1;
itemsInCart += 2;                // short for: itemsInCart = itemsInCart + 2
console.log(storeName, "has", itemsInCart, "items in the cart");

storeName = "OtherCart";         // not allowed: storeName is const
Console output
FreshCart has 3 items in the cart
Uncaught TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
Code What it does const storeName = "FreshCart"; Creates a variable that can never be reassigned. Use const by default. let itemsInCart = 0; Creates a variable you will change. itemsInCart = itemsInCart + 1; Read the current value (0), add 1, store the result back. = means "store", not "equals". itemsInCart += 2; Shortcut for the line above with 2. Also -=, *=, and ++ (add 1). storeName = "OtherCart"; Error: you can't reassign a const. The program stops at this line, which is why it's the last thing printed.

Don't use var

Old tutorials use var. It ignores { } blocks and can be used before it's declared, which causes confusing bugs. Modern code uses only const and let.

Naming rules: letters, digits, _ and $; can't start with a digit; case-sensitive (total ≠ Total). Use camelCase and say what the value is: cartTotalPaise, not x or data2.

docs.title: Types: what kind of value is it?
docs.text:
console.log(typeof "Apple");      // text
console.log(typeof 189);          // whole numbers and decimals are both "number"
console.log(typeof true);         // yes / no
console.log(typeof undefined);    // "no value has been given yet"
console.log(typeof null);         // "deliberately empty" (typeof says "object": a famous old bug)
console.log(typeof { name: "Apple" });
console.log(typeof ["Apple", "Banana"]);
console.log(Array.isArray(["Apple", "Banana"]));  // the right way to test for an array
Console output
string
number
boolean
undefined
object
object
object
true
Type Example Used for string "Apple" Text number 189, 4.6 Whole numbers and decimals (one type for both) boolean true, false Yes/no: inStock, isLoggedIn undefined undefined "No value has been given yet" null null "Deliberately empty" (you set it) object { name: "Apple" }, ["a", "b"] Groups of values (lesson 4). Arrays are objects too, so check them with Array.isArray(). bigint, symbol 10n, Symbol() Rare in frontend code; you can skip them for now

typeof value tells you the type as a string. typeof null says "object": a bug from 1995 that can never be fixed without breaking old websites.

docs.title: undefined vs null
docs.text:
let deliverySlot;                 // declared, but no value yet
console.log(deliverySlot);

let coupon = null;                // we chose "no coupon"
console.log(coupon);

coupon = "FRESH50";
console.log(coupon);
Console output
undefined
null
FRESH50

undefined is what JavaScript gives you when nothing was set. null is what you write to say "empty on purpose" (no coupon, no address yet).

docs.title: Strings and template literals
docs.text:
const product = "Shimla Apple";
const qty = 2;
const price = 189;

// Template literal: backticks, and ${ } to insert any value or expression
const line = `${qty} × ${product} = ₹${qty * price}`;
console.log(line);

console.log(product.length);                 // number of characters
console.log(product.toUpperCase());
console.log(product.includes("Apple"));
console.log(product.split(" "));             // cut into an array of words
console.log("  milk  ".trim());              // remove spaces at both ends
console.log("ADD".padStart(6, "."));
Console output
2 × Shimla Apple = ₹378
12
SHIMLA APPLE
true
[ 'Shimla', 'Apple' ]
milk
...ADD
Code What it does `${qty} × ${product} = ₹${qty * price}` A template literal: backticks, and ${ } to insert any value or calculation. Much easier to read than qty + " × " + product. .length Number of characters (a property, so no ()). .toUpperCase() A method: a function that belongs to the string. Strings never change; methods return a new string. .includes("Apple") true if the text contains it. Case-sensitive. .split(" ") Cuts the text at each space into an array of parts. .trim() Removes spaces at both ends. Always trim what users type. .padStart(6, ".") Pads to 6 characters from the left. Useful for lining up columns.

docs.title: Numbers, and why money is stored in paise
docs.text:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);              // decimals are stored in binary, so this is not exactly 0.3
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);

// Fix: keep money in whole paise (1 rupee = 100 paise), and only divide when displaying
const applePaise = 18900;
const bananaPaise = 4900;
const totalPaise = applePaise + bananaPaise;
console.log(totalPaise);
console.log((totalPaise / 100).toFixed(2));

const rupees = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" });
console.log(rupees.format(totalPaise / 100));
console.log(rupees.format(123456789 / 100));   // Indian digit grouping: 12,34,567.89
Console output
0.30000000000000004
false
23800
238.00
₹238.00
₹12,34,567.89
Code What it does 0.1 + 0.2 Computers store decimals in binary, where 0.1 can't be written exactly, so tiny errors appear. In every language, not just JS. const applePaise = 18900; The fix used by real stores: keep money as whole numbers of the smallest unit (paise, cents). Whole numbers add up exactly. (totalPaise / 100).toFixed(2) Divide only when showing the price. toFixed(2) gives exactly two decimals (as a string). new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }) The browser's built-in formatter: adds ₹ and Indian digit grouping (12,34,567). Use "en-US"/"USD" for $1,234,567.89.

docs.title: Converting between types
docs.text:
const fromInput = "3";               // values from inputs and data-* attributes are ALWAYS strings

console.log(fromInput + 1);          // + with a string joins text
console.log(Number(fromInput) + 1);  // convert first, then add
console.log(Number("12abc"));        // NaN: "Not a Number"
console.log(Number.isNaN(Number("12abc")));
console.log(String(42) + "!");
console.log(parseInt("250g", 10));   // reads digits until the first non-digit
Console output
31
4
NaN
true
42!
250
Code What it does "3" + 1 → 31 If either side of + is a string, + joins text. The most common beginner bug: values from <input> and data-* attributes are always strings. Number("3") + 1 → 4 Convert first, then do maths. Number("12abc") → NaN "Not a Number": the conversion failed. Check with Number.isNaN(). String(42) Number to text. parseInt("250g", 10) → 250 Reads digits from the start and stops at the first non-digit. Always pass 10 (base ten).

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Make const variables for your favourite product's name, price in paise and pack size, and print "Shimla Apple (1 kg): ₹189.00" using one template literal and Intl.NumberFormat.
  2. In the browser console, type "5" * 2, "5" + 2 and "5" - 2. Which one surprised you, and why?
  3. Print the length of your own name, then print it reversed (hint: split(""), .reverse(), .join("")).

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

1. One template literal 
const productName = "Shimla Apple";
const pricePaise = 18900;
const packSize = "1 kg";

const rupees = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" });
console.log(`${productName} (${packSize}): ${rupees.format(pricePaise / 100)}`);
Console output
Shimla Apple (1 kg): ₹189.00
2. "5" * 2, "5" + 2, "5" - 2 
console.log("5" * 2);   // * only works on numbers, so "5" is converted to 5
console.log("5" + 2);   // + with a string JOINS text: the surprising one
console.log("5" - 2);   // - only works on numbers, so "5" is converted to 5
Console output
10
52
3

+ is the odd one out: it means both "add" and "join text", and any string on either side makes it join. *, - and / only do maths, so JavaScript converts "5" to the number 5 first. Convert input values with Number() yourself so you never rely on these rules.

3. Length and reverse 
const myName = "Asha";
console.log(myName.length);
console.log(myName.split("").reverse().join(""));
Console output
4
ahsA

Strings have no .reverse(), but arrays do: split("") turns the text into an array of characters, reverse() flips the array, and join("") glues it back into a string.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using let everywhere "just in case". Start with const; change it to let only when you really reassign it.
  • Adding prices as decimals (0.1 + 0.2). Use whole paise.
  • Forgetting that input values are strings: input.value + 1 gives "31", not 4.
  • Writing name and Name and wondering why one is undefined: names are case-sensitive.

docs.title: 2. Operators & Decisions
docs.text:
Beginner

Programs make decisions all the time: is delivery free? Is the item in stock? Is the user logged in? This lesson covers how to compare values and choose what happens next.

docs.title: Comparing values
docs.text:
console.log(5 > 3);
console.log(199 >= 200);
console.log("5" == 5);     // == converts types first: avoid it
console.log("5" === 5);    // === compares value AND type: always use this
console.log("5" !== 5);
Console output
true
false
true
false
true
Operator Means > < >= <= Greater than, less than, or equal === Strictly equal: same value and same type. "5" === 5 is false. !== Strictly not equal == / != Loose equality: converts types first ("5" == 5 is true). Causes surprises; don't use it.

docs.title: if / else if / else
docs.text:
const cartTotal = 15000;          // ₹150 in paise
const freeDeliveryFrom = 19900;   // ₹199

if (cartTotal >= freeDeliveryFrom) {
  console.log("Delivery is FREE");
} else if (cartTotal > 0) {
  const missing = (freeDeliveryFrom - cartTotal) / 100;
  console.log(`Add ₹${missing} more for free delivery`);
} else {
  console.log("Your cart is empty");
}
Console output
Add ₹49 more for free delivery
Code What it does if (cartTotal >= freeDeliveryFrom) { … } The code in { } runs only if the condition in ( ) is true. else if (cartTotal > 0) { … } Checked only if the first condition was false. Add as many as you need. const missing = (…) / 100; A variable created inside { } exists only inside those braces. else { … } Runs if none of the conditions above were true.

JavaScript checks the conditions top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.

docs.title: AND, OR, NOT
docs.text:
const isLoggedIn = true;
const hasAddress = false;

console.log(isLoggedIn && hasAddress);   // AND: true only if both are true
console.log(isLoggedIn || hasAddress);   // OR: true if at least one is true
console.log(!hasAddress);                // NOT: flips true/false

if (isLoggedIn && !hasAddress) {
  console.log("Please add a delivery address");
}
Console output
false
true
true
Please add a delivery address
Operator Reads as true when… a && b a and b both are true a || b a or b at least one is true !a not a a is false

docs.title: Truthy and falsy
docs.text:
if doesn't need a real true or false. Every value counts as one or the other:

// In an if, every value counts as true or false. These six are "falsy":
const falsy = [[false, "false"], [0, "0"], ["", '""'], [null, "null"], [undefined, "undefined"], [NaN, "NaN"]];
for (const [value, label] of falsy) {
  console.log(label, "→", value ? "truthy" : "falsy");
}
// Everything else is "truthy", even these:
console.log('"0"', "→", "0" ? "truthy" : "falsy");
console.log('"false"', "→", "false" ? "truthy" : "falsy");
console.log("[]", "→", [] ? "truthy" : "falsy");
Console output
false → falsy
0 → falsy
"" → falsy
null → falsy
undefined → falsy
NaN → falsy
"0" → truthy
"false" → truthy
[] → truthy

Only six values are falsy: false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including the string "0", the string "false", an empty array [] and an empty object {}.

That's why you can write if (searchText) { … } to mean "if the user typed something".

docs.title: Default values: || vs ??
docs.text:
const settings = { theme: "", itemsPerPage: 0 };

// || falls back on ANY falsy value, so "" and 0 are replaced too
console.log(settings.theme || "light");
console.log(settings.itemsPerPage || 20);

// ?? falls back only on null or undefined, so real 0 and "" are kept
console.log(settings.theme ?? "light");
console.log(settings.itemsPerPage ?? 20);
console.log(settings.language ?? "en");
Console output
light
20

0
en
Code What it does a || b "a, unless a is falsy, then b". Replaces 0 and "" too, which is often wrong: itemsPerPage: 0 became 20. a ?? b "a, unless a is null or undefined, then b". Keeps real 0 and "". Use ?? for defaults. settings.language ?? "en" language doesn't exist (undefined), so the default "en" is used.

docs.title: Optional chaining ?.
docs.text:
const user = { name: "Asha", address: null };

console.log(user.address?.city);              // stops at null and gives undefined, no crash
console.log(user.address?.city ?? "No city yet");
console.log(user.address.city);               // without ?. this crashes
Console output
undefined
No city yet
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'city')
Code What it does user.address?.city "If address is null or undefined, stop and give undefined; otherwise read .city." user.address?.city ?? "No city yet" ?. and ?? together: the classic pattern for data that may be missing. user.address.city Without ?., reading a property of null crashes the whole script. This is the most common error in frontend code.

docs.title: The ternary: if/else in one expression
docs.text:
const qty = 3;
const label = qty === 1 ? "1 item" : `${qty} items`;   // condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
console.log(label);

const stock = 0;
console.log(stock > 0 ? "ADD" : "Out of stock");
Console output
3 items
Out of stock

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse gives back a value, so you can put it in a variable or a template literal. Use it for short choices between two values; use if when each branch does several things.

docs.title: switch: one value, many cases
docs.text:
function statusMessage(status) {
  switch (status) {
    case "placed":
      return "Order placed";
    case "packed":
      return "Packing your items";
    case "out-for-delivery":
      return "On the way 🛵";
    case "delivered":
      return "Delivered. Enjoy!";
    default:
      return "Unknown status";
  }
}
console.log(statusMessage("packed"));
console.log(statusMessage("out-for-delivery"));
console.log(statusMessage("lost"));
Console output
Packing your items
On the way 🛵
Unknown status
Code What it does switch (status) Compares status (with ===) against each case. case "placed": return … If it matches, run this code. return leaves the function, so we don't need break. default: Runs if no case matched. Always include one.

Without return, use break

In a switch that isn't inside a function, end each case with break;. Without it, JavaScript "falls through" and runs the next case's code too.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Write an if/else if/else that prints "Morning slot", "Evening slot" or "Closed" for an hour from 0 to 23 (6–11 morning, 16–21 evening).
  2. Given const product = { stock: 0 }, print "ADD", "Only N left" (stock 1 to 3, with the real number) or "Out of stock" with a ternary inside a ternary. Then rewrite it with if. Which is easier to read?
  3. Predict, then check in the console: null ?? "x", 0 || "x", 0 ?? "x", "" && "x".

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

1. Morning, evening or closed 
function slotFor(hour) {
  if (hour >= 6 && hour <= 11) {
    return "Morning slot";
  } else if (hour >= 16 && hour <= 21) {
    return "Evening slot";
  } else {
    return "Closed";
  }
}

for (const hour of [5, 6, 11, 12, 16, 21, 22]) {
  console.log(hour, slotFor(hour));
}
Console output
5 Closed
6 Morning slot
11 Morning slot
12 Closed
16 Evening slot
21 Evening slot
22 Closed

Test the edges (5, 6, 11, 12, 16, 21, 22), not just one value in the middle: that's where < vs <= bugs hide.

2. Nested ternary vs if 
for (const stock of [0, 2, 3, 10]) {
  const product = { stock };

  // Nested ternary: works, but hard to read
  const label1 = product.stock === 0 ? "Out of stock" : product.stock <= 3 ? `Only ${product.stock} left` : "ADD";

  // The same with if: easier to read, so prefer it
  let label2;
  if (product.stock === 0) label2 = "Out of stock";
  else if (product.stock <= 3) label2 = `Only ${product.stock} left`;
  else label2 = "ADD";

  console.log(stock, label1, label2);
}
Console output
0 Out of stock Out of stock
2 Only 2 left Only 2 left
3 Only 3 left Only 3 left
10 ADD ADD

Both give the same answer, but the if version is easier to read and to extend (try adding a fourth case to each). Keep the ternary for one simple choice.

3. Predict ?? || && 
console.log(null ?? "x");   // null → use the default
console.log(0 || "x");      // 0 is falsy → || uses the default
console.log(0 ?? "x");      // 0 is not null/undefined → ?? keeps 0
console.log("" && "x");     // "" is falsy → && stops and gives ""
Console output
x
x
0

The last line looks blank because "" && "x" gives the empty string: && stops at the first falsy value and returns it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• if (x = 5): a single = assigns, so the condition is always truthy. Compare with ===.
  • Using == and getting surprised by "" == 0 being true.
  • count || 10 for a default when 0 is a valid count. Use ??.
  • Reading data.user.address.city from an API without ?. and crashing when one level is missing.

docs.title: 3. Functions
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

A function is a named, reusable piece of code. You write it once ("how to work out a line total") and use it wherever you need it. Every click handler, every calculation and every API call in a web app is a function.

docs.title: Declaring and calling a function
docs.text:
// Define once…
function lineTotal(pricePaise, qty) {
  return pricePaise * qty;
}

// …use many times
console.log(lineTotal(18900, 2));
console.log(lineTotal(4900, 6));
console.log(lineTotal(6800, 1));
Console output
37800
29400
6800
Code What it does function lineTotal(pricePaise, qty) { … } Defines a function called lineTotal. pricePaise and qty are parameters: placeholders for the values it will receive. Nothing runs yet. return pricePaise * qty; Sends the result back to whoever called the function. lineTotal(18900, 2) Calls the function. 18900 and 2 are the arguments: they fill the parameters in order. The call becomes the returned value, 37800.

docs.title: Three ways to write a function
docs.text:
// The same function written three ways
function addGst1(paise) {
  return Math.round(paise * 1.05);
}
const addGst2 = function (paise) {
  return Math.round(paise * 1.05);
};
const addGst3 = (paise) => Math.round(paise * 1.05);   // arrow function: one expression is returned automatically

console.log(addGst1(10000), addGst2(10000), addGst3(10000));
Console output
10500 10500 10500
Form When to use it function addGst1(paise) { … } A declaration. Good for the main, named functions of a file. const addGst2 = function (paise) { … }; A function expression stored in a variable. You'll see it in older code. const addGst3 = (paise) => Math.round(paise * 1.05); An arrow function. Short, and the standard choice for callbacks (list.map((p) => p.name)). With no { }, the single expression is returned automatically.

With { }, an arrow function needs an explicit return: (paise) => { return paise * 2; }.

docs.title: Default and rest parameters
docs.text:
function greet(name = "guest") {          // default value when nothing is passed
  return `Hello, ${name}!`;
}
console.log(greet("Asha"));
console.log(greet());

function sum(...prices) {                 // rest parameter: all the arguments as an array
  let total = 0;
  for (const p of prices) total += p;
  return total;
}
console.log(sum(18900, 4900, 3200));
console.log(sum());
Console output
Hello, Asha!
Hello, guest!
27000
0
Code What it does function greet(name = "guest") If the caller passes nothing (or undefined), name is "guest". function sum(...prices) ... collects all the arguments into an array called prices, however many there are. sum() → 0 No arguments: an empty array, so the loop never runs and the total stays 0.

docs.title: return ends the function
docs.text:
function deliveryFee(subtotalPaise) {
  if (subtotalPaise === 0) return 0;          // return ends the function immediately
  if (subtotalPaise >= 19900) return 0;
  return 2500;
}
console.log(deliveryFee(0), deliveryFee(9800), deliveryFee(28700));

function noReturn() {
  const x = 1 + 1;
}
console.log(noReturn());                      // a function without return gives undefined
Console output
0 2500 0
undefined

As soon as a return runs, the function stops; nothing after it in that call runs. Writing the special cases first and returning early (the "guard clause" pattern) keeps functions flat and readable. A function with no return gives back undefined.

docs.title: Scope: where a variable can be seen
docs.text:
const storeName = "FreshCart";                // global: visible everywhere below

function showBanner() {
  const message = `Welcome to ${storeName}`;  // local: lives only inside this function
  console.log(message);
}
showBanner();

if (true) {
  const insideBlock = "only inside these { }";
  console.log(insideBlock);
}
console.log(typeof insideBlock);               // not visible outside its block
console.log(message);                          // not visible outside the function
Console output
Welcome to FreshCart
only inside these { }
undefined
Uncaught ReferenceError: message is not defined
Code What it does const storeName (outside everything) Global scope: visible to all the code below it. const message (inside the function) Function scope: exists only while the function runs, and only inside it. const insideBlock (inside if { }) Block scope: const and let live only inside the nearest { }. typeof insideBlock → undefined Outside its block, the name doesn't exist. (typeof is the one safe way to ask about a name that doesn't exist.) console.log(message) → ReferenceError Using a name that isn't visible here is an error, and the script stops.

Keep variables in the smallest scope that works. Fewer globals means fewer accidental clashes.

docs.title: Callbacks: passing a function to a function
docs.text:
// A callback is a function you hand to another function, to be called later
function repeat(times, action) {
  for (let i = 1; i <= times; i++) action(i);
}
repeat(3, (n) => console.log(`Delivery partner ${n} assigned`));

setTimeout(() => console.log("…printed 100 ms later"), 100);
console.log("This prints first");
Console output
Delivery partner 1 assigned
Delivery partner 2 assigned
Delivery partner 3 assigned
This prints first
…printed 100 ms later
Code What it does function repeat(times, action) action is a parameter that will hold a function. action(i); Calls whatever function was passed in. repeat(3, (n) => console.log(…)) We pass an arrow function as the second argument. This is a callback: "call this back when it's time". setTimeout(() => …, 100) The browser calls our function back after 100 ms. Meanwhile, the next line runs straight away, which is why "This prints first" really does print first.

Callbacks are everywhere: addEventListener("click", callback), array.map(callback), setTimeout(callback, ms).

docs.title: Closures: functions that remember
docs.text:
// A closure: the inner function remembers variables from where it was created
function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;                  // private: nothing outside can touch it
  return () => {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}
const nextOrderNumber = makeCounter();
console.log(nextOrderNumber());
console.log(nextOrderNumber());
console.log(nextOrderNumber());

const otherCounter = makeCounter();   // a brand-new, separate count
console.log(otherCounter());
Console output
1
2
3
1
Code What it does let count = 0; inside makeCounter A variable that only the code inside makeCounter can see. return () => { count++; return count; }; Returns a new function. That inner function keeps access to count even after makeCounter has finished. This is a closure. nextOrderNumber() ×3 → 1, 2, 3 Each call updates the same remembered count. const otherCounter = makeCounter(); → 1 Every call to makeCounter creates a fresh, separate count.

Closures give you private state without classes. Event handlers use them constantly: a click handler created inside a loop remembers which product it belongs to.

docs.title: Pure functions
docs.text:
// Pure function: same input → same output, and it changes nothing outside itself. Easy to test.
const discount = (paise, percent) => Math.round((paise * (100 - percent)) / 100);
console.log(discount(23600, 20));

// Impure: depends on and changes something outside
let total = 0;
function addToTotal(paise) {
  total += paise;                  // side effect
  return total;
}
console.log(addToTotal(100), addToTotal(100));   // same input, different output
Console output
18880
100 200

A pure function only uses its inputs and only gives back a result: same inputs, same output, every time. Pure functions are easy to test and reuse. Write your calculations (totals, discounts, delivery fees) as pure functions, and keep the "impure" parts (changing the page, saving data) separate.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Write formatRupees(paise) that returns "₹189.00" for 18900, using Intl.NumberFormat. Test it with three values.
  2. Write deliveryFee(subtotalPaise) as an arrow function with a ternary: free from ₹199, otherwise ₹25.
  3. Write makeCart() that returns { add(paise), total() }, keeping the running total private in a closure.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

1. formatRupees 
const rupees = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" });

function formatRupees(paise) {
  return rupees.format(paise / 100);
}

console.log(formatRupees(18900));
console.log(formatRupees(4950));
console.log(formatRupees(12345600));
Console output
₹189.00
₹49.50
₹1,23,456.00

The formatter is created once, outside the function: building an Intl.NumberFormat is slower than using one.

2. deliveryFee as an arrow function 
const deliveryFee = (subtotalPaise) => (subtotalPaise >= 19900 ? 0 : 2500);

console.log(deliveryFee(9800));
console.log(deliveryFee(19900));
console.log(deliveryFee(50000));
Console output
2500
0
0

Exactly ₹199 (19900) is free, because the test is >=. Always check the boundary value.

3. makeCart with a private total 
function makeCart() {
  let totalPaise = 0;           // private: only add() and total() can reach it

  return {
    add(paise) {
      totalPaise += paise;
    },
    total() {
      return totalPaise;
    },
  };
}

const cart = makeCart();
cart.add(18900);
cart.add(4900);
console.log(cart.total());
console.log(cart.totalPaise);   // undefined: the variable is hidden inside the closure
Console output
23800
undefined

add and total are closures over totalPaise. The only way to change the total is through add(), so nothing else in the program can set it to a wrong value by accident.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting return, then wondering why the result is undefined.
  • Writing button.addEventListener("click", handleClick()): the () calls it immediately. Pass the function itself: handleClick.
  • An arrow function with { } but no return: (p) => { p.name } returns undefined. Remove the braces or add return.
  • Huge functions that do five things. If you can't name it clearly, split it.

docs.title: 4. Arrays & Objects
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

Real data comes in groups: a list of products, a product with a name, price and size. Arrays hold lists; objects hold named fields. Almost every API returns an array of objects.

docs.title: Arrays: ordered lists
docs.text:
const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"];

console.log(fruits[0]);              // positions (indexes) start at 0
console.log(fruits.length);
console.log(fruits.at(-1));          // last item

fruits.push("Grapes");               // add at the end
console.log(fruits);

const removed = fruits.shift();      // remove from the start
console.log(removed, fruits);

console.log(fruits.includes("Mango"));
console.log(fruits.indexOf("Grapes"));
console.log(fruits.join(" · "));
Console output
Apple
3
Mango
[ 'Apple', 'Banana', 'Mango', 'Grapes' ]
Apple [ 'Banana', 'Mango', 'Grapes' ]
true
2
Banana · Mango · Grapes
Code What it does ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"] An array literal: values in [ ], separated by commas. fruits[0] The first item. Positions (indexes) start at 0, so the last is fruits[fruits.length - 1]. fruits.at(-1) Negative positions count from the end: the easy way to get the last item. fruits.push("Grapes") Adds to the end. (unshift adds to the start.) fruits.shift() Removes and returns the first item. (pop removes the last.) .includes(…), .indexOf(…) "Is it there?" and "at which position?" (-1 if not found). .join(" · ") Joins all items into one string with a separator.

const fruits doesn't stop you changing the array's contents; it only stops you pointing fruits at a different array.

docs.title: Objects: named fields
docs.text:
const product = {
  id: "apple",
  name: "Shimla Apple",
  pricePaise: 18900,
  inStock: true,
  tags: ["fruit", "seasonal"],
};

console.log(product.name);           // dot notation
console.log(product["pricePaise"]);  // bracket notation (needed when the key is in a variable)

const key = "inStock";
console.log(product[key]);

product.pricePaise = 17900;          // change a property
product.rating = 4.6;                // add a new one
delete product.tags;                 // remove one
console.log(product);

console.log(Object.keys(product));
console.log("rating" in product);
Console output
Shimla Apple
18900
true
{
  id: 'apple',
  name: 'Shimla Apple',
  pricePaise: 17900,
  inStock: true,
  rating: 4.6
}
[ 'id', 'name', 'pricePaise', 'inStock', 'rating' ]
true
Code What it does { id: "apple", name: "Shimla Apple", … } An object literal: key: value pairs. Keys are names; values can be anything, including arrays and other objects. product.name Dot notation: read a property. product["pricePaise"], product[key] Bracket notation: needed when the key is in a variable or has spaces/dashes. product.pricePaise = 17900; Change a property. product.rating = 4.6; Assigning to a key that doesn't exist adds it. delete product.tags; Removes a property. Object.keys(product) An array of the keys. (Object.values and Object.entries exist too.) "rating" in product Does the key exist?

docs.title: An array of objects
docs.text:
// The shape almost every API returns: an array of objects
const products = [
  { id: "apple", name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900, category: "fruits" },
  { id: "milk", name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800, category: "dairy" },
  { id: "bread", name: "Whole Wheat Bread", pricePaise: 5000, category: "bakery" },
];

console.log(products.length, "products");
console.log(products[1].name);
console.log(products[2].pricePaise / 100);
Console output
3 products
Full Cream Milk
50

products[1].name reads left to right: "the array → item at position 1 → its name". Lesson 5 shows how to loop over, filter and total arrays like this one.

docs.title: Destructuring: unpack values into variables
docs.text:
const item = { name: "Brown Eggs", pricePaise: 8400, size: "6 pcs" };

const { name, pricePaise } = item;           // pull properties out into variables
console.log(name, pricePaise);

const { size: packSize, rating = "no rating" } = item;   // rename, and give a default
console.log(packSize, rating);

const [first, second] = ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"];    // arrays: by position
console.log(first, second);

function describe({ name, size }) {           // destructuring right in the parameters
  return `${name} (${size})`;
}
console.log(describe(item));
Console output
Brown Eggs 8400
6 pcs no rating
Apple Banana
Brown Eggs (6 pcs)
Code What it does const { name, pricePaise } = item; Creates two variables from the properties with the same names. Same as const name = item.name; const pricePaise = item.pricePaise; { size: packSize } Read size, but call the variable packSize. { rating = "no rating" } A default when the property is missing. const [first, second] = [...] Arrays destructure by position. function describe({ name, size }) Destructure right in the parameter list: very common in frameworks.

docs.title: Spread: copy and combine
docs.text:
const base = { name: "Milk", pricePaise: 6800 };

const updated = { ...base, pricePaise: 7200 };   // copy, then override one property
console.log(base);                               // the original is unchanged
console.log(updated);

const veg = ["Tomato", "Onion"];
const fruit = ["Apple"];
const all = [...veg, ...fruit, "Bread"];         // join arrays
console.log(all);
Console output
{ name: 'Milk', pricePaise: 6800 }
{ name: 'Milk', pricePaise: 7200 }
[ 'Tomato', 'Onion', 'Apple', 'Bread' ]
Code What it does { ...base, pricePaise: 7200 } Copies every property of base into a new object, then overrides pricePaise. The original stays unchanged. [...veg, ...fruit, "Bread"] Spreads both arrays' items into a new array.

This "copy, don't change" style is how React, Angular signals and most state libraries expect you to update data.

docs.title: References: two names, one object
docs.text:
// Objects and arrays are shared by reference, not copied
const cartA = ["Apple"];
const cartB = cartA;          // the SAME array, two names
cartB.push("Milk");
console.log(cartA);

const cartC = [...cartA];     // a real (shallow) copy
cartC.push("Bread");
console.log(cartA, cartC);

console.log([1, 2] === [1, 2]);   // two different arrays, even with equal contents
Console output
[ 'Apple', 'Milk' ]
[ 'Apple', 'Milk' ] [ 'Apple', 'Milk', 'Bread' ]
false
Code What it does const cartB = cartA; Does not copy. Both names point to the same array, so pushing through cartB changes what cartA sees. const cartC = [...cartA]; A real copy (one level deep: objects inside it are still shared; use structuredClone() for a full copy). [1, 2] === [1, 2] → false === on objects asks "the same object?", not "the same contents?"

docs.title: Map and Set
docs.text:
// Map: key → value, with any type of key, and easy to loop over
const cart = new Map();
cart.set("apple", 2);
cart.set("milk", 1);
cart.set("apple", 3);                 // same key: replaces the value
console.log(cart.get("apple"), cart.size, cart.has("bread"));
for (const [id, qty] of cart) console.log(id, "×", qty);

// Set: a list with no duplicates
const tags = new Set(["fruit", "organic", "fruit"]);
tags.add("seasonal");
console.log(tags.size, [...tags]);
Console output
3 2 false
apple × 3
milk × 1
3 [ 'fruit', 'organic', 'seasonal' ]
Code What it does new Map() A key → value store. Great for a cart: product id → quantity. .set(key, value) / .get(key) / .has(key) / .delete(key) / .size Add or replace, read, check, remove, count. for (const [id, qty] of cart) Loops over [key, value] pairs in the order they were added. new Set([...]) A collection with no duplicates: the second "fruit" is ignored. [...tags] Turn a Set (or Map) into an array.

Use a plain object for a fixed record (product.name); use a Map for a changing lookup table.

docs.title: JSON: data as text
docs.text:
// JSON is how data travels between server and browser: always text
const order = { id: 1042, items: [{ id: "apple", qty: 2 }], paid: false };

const text = JSON.stringify(order);
console.log(text);
console.log(typeof text);

const back = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(back.items[0].qty);

console.log(JSON.stringify(order, null, 2));     // pretty-printed, 2-space indent
Console output
{"id":1042,"items":[{"id":"apple","qty":2}],"paid":false}
string
2
{
  "id": 1042,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "apple",
      "qty": 2
    }
  ],
  "paid": false
}
Code What it does JSON.stringify(order) Object → JSON string, ready to send to a server or save in localStorage. JSON.parse(text) JSON string → a new object you can use again. JSON.stringify(order, null, 2) Pretty-printed with 2-space indentation: handy for debugging.

JSON looks like JavaScript but is stricter: keys and strings need double quotes, and there are no comments, functions or undefined.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create an array of 3 product objects (name, pricePaise, category). Print the name of the second one and the category of the last one using .at(-1).
  2. Write withPrice(product, newPaise) that returns a new product object with the changed price, using spread. Check the original is unchanged.
  3. Save a Map cart to a JSON string and load it back: JSON.stringify([...cart]) and new Map(JSON.parse(text)).

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

1. Second name, last category 
const products = [
  { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900, category: "fruits" },
  { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800, category: "dairy" },
  { name: "Whole Wheat Bread", pricePaise: 5000, category: "bakery" },
];

console.log(products[1].name);
console.log(products.at(-1).category);
Console output
Full Cream Milk
bakery
2. withPrice with spread 
function withPrice(product, newPaise) {
  return { ...product, pricePaise: newPaise };
}

const milk = { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800 };
const dearerMilk = withPrice(milk, 7200);

console.log(milk);          // unchanged
console.log(dearerMilk);    // a new object
console.log(milk === dearerMilk);
Console output
{ name: 'Full Cream Milk', pricePaise: 6800 }
{ name: 'Full Cream Milk', pricePaise: 7200 }
false

The original keeps ₹68 and the two are different objects. Code that receives a product can't be surprised by it changing later.

3. Map → JSON → Map 
const cart = new Map([
  ["apple", 2],
  ["milk", 1],
]);

const text = JSON.stringify([...cart]);   // a Map can't be stringified directly; turn it into [key, value] pairs first
console.log(text);

const loaded = new Map(JSON.parse(text)); // pairs → Map again
console.log(loaded.get("apple"), loaded.size);
Console output
[["apple",2],["milk",1]]
2 2

JSON.stringify(cart) on the Map itself would give "{}": Maps aren't plain objects. Spreading turns it into an array of [key, value] pairs, which JSON can hold, and new Map(pairs) turns it back. FreshCart uses exactly this to keep the cart after a refresh.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• fruits[3] on a 3-item array: indexes start at 0, so it's undefined.
  • Thinking const b = a copies an array or object. It doesn't.
  • Changing an object you received as a parameter and accidentally changing the caller's data. Return a copy instead.
  • Comparing objects with === to check if they have the same contents.

docs.title: 5. Loops & Array Methods
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

A loop repeats code: for every product, for every cart item, until stock runs out. Modern JavaScript mostly uses for…of and array methods (map, filter, reduce) instead of counting by hand.

docs.title: The classic for loop
docs.text:
// Classic for: start; keep going while; step
for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  console.log(`Slot ${i}: ${6 + i}:00`);
}
Console output
Slot 1: 7:00
Slot 2: 8:00
Slot 3: 9:00
Part What it does let i = 1; Runs once, before the loop starts: create a counter. i <= 3; Checked before every round. When it's false, the loop ends. i++ Runs after every round: add 1 to the counter. { … } The body: runs once per round.

Use it when you need a counter. To go through an array, prefer for…of.

docs.title: for…of: each value in a list
docs.text:
const basket = ["Apple", "Milk", "Bread"];

for (const item of basket) {           // for…of: each VALUE of an array (or string, Map, Set)
  console.log("Packing", item);
}

for (const [index, item] of basket.entries()) {   // when you also need the position
  console.log(index + 1, item);
}

const stock = { apple: 12, milk: 0 };
for (const [id, qty] of Object.entries(stock)) {  // loop over an object's key/value pairs
  console.log(id, qty > 0 ? "in stock" : "sold out");
}
Console output
Packing Apple
Packing Milk
Packing Bread
1 Apple
2 Milk
3 Bread
apple in stock
milk sold out
Code What it does for (const item of basket) Each round, item is the next value. No index maths, no off-by-one errors. basket.entries() + [index, item] When you also need the position. Object.entries(stock) Turns an object into [key, value] pairs so you can loop over it.

for…in is different

for (const key in obj) loops over an object's keys, and on an array it gives you the indexes as strings. Use for…of for arrays and Object.entries() for objects.

docs.title: while, break and continue
docs.text:
let stockLeft = 5;
let orders = 0;
while (stockLeft >= 2) {               // repeat while the condition is true
  stockLeft -= 2;
  orders++;
}
console.log(`${orders} orders of 2, ${stockLeft} left`);

for (const n of [3, 8, 1, 9]) {
  if (n === 1) continue;              // skip this one, go to the next
  if (n === 9) break;                 // stop the loop completely
  console.log(n);
}
Console output
2 orders of 2, 1 left
3
8
Code What it does while (stockLeft >= 2) { … } Repeats as long as the condition is true. Make sure something in the body eventually makes it false, or the page freezes. continue Skip the rest of this round and go to the next one. break Leave the loop completely.

docs.title: Array methods: say what, not how
docs.text:
These take a callback (lesson 3) and call it once for every item.

const products = [
  { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900, category: "fruits", deal: true },
  { name: "Robusta Banana", pricePaise: 4900, category: "fruits", deal: false },
  { name: "Fresh Tomato", pricePaise: 3200, category: "vegetables", deal: true },
  { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800, category: "dairy", deal: false },
  { name: "Brown Eggs", pricePaise: 8400, category: "dairy", deal: true },
];

// map: turn every item into something else (same length)
const names = products.map((p) => p.name);
console.log(names);

// filter: keep only the items that pass a test
const dairy = products.filter((p) => p.category === "dairy");
console.log(dairy.map((p) => p.name));

// find: the FIRST item that passes, or undefined
console.log(products.find((p) => p.pricePaise < 5000));

// some / every: does any / do all pass?
console.log(products.some((p) => p.deal), products.every((p) => p.deal));

// reduce: boil the whole array down to one value
const total = products.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.pricePaise, 0);
console.log(total);

// chain them: names of discounted items under ₹100, cheapest first
const cheapDeals = products
  .filter((p) => p.deal && p.pricePaise < 10000)
  .toSorted((a, b) => a.pricePaise - b.pricePaise)
  .map((p) => `${p.name} ₹${p.pricePaise / 100}`);
console.log(cheapDeals);
Console output
[
  'Shimla Apple',
  'Robusta Banana',
  'Fresh Tomato',
  'Full Cream Milk',
  'Brown Eggs'
]
[ 'Full Cream Milk', 'Brown Eggs' ]
{
  name: 'Robusta Banana',
  pricePaise: 4900,
  category: 'fruits',
  deal: false
}
true false
42200
[ 'Fresh Tomato ₹32', 'Brown Eggs ₹84' ]
Method Returns Use it to… .map((p) => p.name) A new array, same length Turn every item into something else (objects → names, data → <li> elements). .filter((p) => p.category === "dairy") A new array, maybe shorter Keep only the items that pass a test. .find((p) => p.pricePaise < 5000) One item, or undefined Get the first match. (.findIndex gives its position.) .some(…) / .every(…) true / false "Is there at least one…?" / "Are all of them…?" .reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.pricePaise, 0) One value Add up or combine everything. sum starts at 0 and carries the running result. chained .filter().toSorted().map() Each method returns a new array, so you can line them up like a pipeline. Read it top to bottom.

map, filter, find, some, every and reduce never change the original array.

docs.title: How reduce works, step by step
docs.text: Round sum (before) p.pricePaise returns 1 0 (the start value) 18900 18900 2 18900 4900 23800 3 23800 3200 27000 4 27000 6800 33800 5 33800 8400 42200

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
const prices = [4900, 18900, 3200, 6800];

console.log([...prices].sort());                   // default sort compares as TEXT
console.log([...prices].sort((a, b) => a - b));    // numbers, low → high
console.log([...prices].sort((a, b) => b - a));    // high → low
console.log(prices.toSorted((a, b) => a - b));     // toSorted() returns a new array
console.log(prices);                               // the original was never changed

const names = ["banana", "Apple", "cherry"];
console.log(names.toSorted((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)));   // alphabetical, ignoring case
Console output
[ 18900, 3200, 4900, 6800 ]
[ 3200, 4900, 6800, 18900 ]
[ 18900, 6800, 4900, 3200 ]
[ 3200, 4900, 6800, 18900 ]
[ 4900, 18900, 3200, 6800 ]
[ 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry' ]
Code What it does .sort() with no function Compares items as text, so "18900" comes before "3200" (because "1" < "3"). Always pass a compare function for numbers. (a, b) => a - b A negative result puts a first. Low → high. Swap to b - a for high → low. .sort() vs .toSorted() sort() changes the original array. toSorted() returns a sorted copy. Prefer toSorted(), or [...arr].sort(). a.localeCompare(b) Correct alphabetical order for words, ignoring case and handling accents.

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text:
const items = [
  { name: "Apple", category: "fruits" },
  { name: "Milk", category: "dairy" },
  { name: "Banana", category: "fruits" },
];
