const byCategory = Object.groupBy(items, (item) => item.category);
console.log(byCategory.fruits.map((i) => i.name));
console.log(Object.keys(byCategory));
Console output
[ 'Apple', 'Banana' ]
[ 'fruits', 'dairy' ]

Object.groupBy(items, callback) puts items into buckets by whatever the callback returns: perfect for "products by category" sections. (Supported in all current browsers since 2024.)

docs.title: Putting it together: a cart bill
docs.text:
// Putting it together: the bill for a cart
const catalogue = new Map([
  ["apple", { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900 }],
  ["milk", { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800 }],
  ["bread", { name: "Whole Wheat Bread", pricePaise: 5000 }],
]);
const cart = [
  { id: "apple", qty: 2 },
  { id: "bread", qty: 1 },
];

const lines = cart.map(({ id, qty }) => {
  const { name, pricePaise } = catalogue.get(id);
  return { name, qty, linePaise: pricePaise * qty };
});
const subtotal = lines.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.linePaise, 0);
const delivery = subtotal >= 19900 ? 0 : 2500;

const rupees = (paise) => `₹${(paise / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
for (const line of lines) console.log(`${line.name.padEnd(18)} × ${line.qty}  ${rupees(line.linePaise)}`);
console.log(`Delivery: ${delivery ? rupees(delivery) : "FREE"}`);
console.log(`To pay:   ${rupees(subtotal + delivery)}`);
Console output
Shimla Apple       × 2  ₹378.00
Whole Wheat Bread  × 1  ₹50.00
Delivery: FREE
To pay:   ₹428.00
Code What it does new Map([[id, product], …]) A catalogue to look products up by id. cart.map(({ id, qty }) => { … }) For each cart line: destructure, look up the product, return a line with its total. lines.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.linePaise, 0) Add all the line totals. subtotal >= 19900 ? 0 : 2500 Free delivery from ₹199. `${line.name.padEnd(18)} …` padEnd lines up the columns.

This is the same logic as the FreshCart cart drawer in E-commerce lesson 6.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. From the products array, make an array of strings like "Shimla Apple: ₹189" with map.
  2. Count how many products are deals with filter(...).length, then do it again with reduce.
  3. Sort the products by name, A to Z, without changing the original array.
  4. Find the most expensive product with reduce (hint: keep the bigger of best and p each round).

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

1. Labels with map 
const products = [
  { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900, category: "fruits", deal: true },
  { name: "Robusta Banana", pricePaise: 4900, category: "fruits", deal: false },
  { name: "Fresh Tomato", pricePaise: 3200, category: "vegetables", deal: true },
  { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800, category: "dairy", deal: false },
  { name: "Brown Eggs", pricePaise: 8400, category: "dairy", deal: true },
];

const labels = products.map((p) => `${p.name}: ₹${p.pricePaise / 100}`);
console.log(labels);
Console output
[
  'Shimla Apple: ₹189',
  'Robusta Banana: ₹49',
  'Fresh Tomato: ₹32',
  'Full Cream Milk: ₹68',
  'Brown Eggs: ₹84'
]
2. Counting deals two ways 
const products = [
  { name: "Shimla Apple", deal: true },
  { name: "Robusta Banana", deal: false },
  { name: "Fresh Tomato", deal: true },
  { name: "Full Cream Milk", deal: false },
  { name: "Brown Eggs", deal: true },
];

console.log(products.filter((p) => p.deal).length);
console.log(products.reduce((count, p) => (p.deal ? count + 1 : count), 0));
Console output
3
3

filter(...).length is easier to read; reduce avoids building a temporary array, which only matters for very large lists.

3. Sort by name without changing the original 
const products = [
  { name: "Shimla Apple" },
  { name: "Robusta Banana" },
  { name: "Fresh Tomato" },
  { name: "Full Cream Milk" },
  { name: "Brown Eggs" },
];

const byName = products.toSorted((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
console.log(byName.map((p) => p.name));
console.log(products[0].name);   // the original order is untouched
Console output
[
  'Brown Eggs',
  'Fresh Tomato',
  'Full Cream Milk',
  'Robusta Banana',
  'Shimla Apple'
]
Shimla Apple
4. Most expensive with reduce 
const products = [
  { name: "Robusta Banana", pricePaise: 4900 },
  { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900 },
  { name: "Fresh Tomato", pricePaise: 3200 },
  { name: "Brown Eggs", pricePaise: 8400 },
];

const mostExpensive = products.reduce((best, p) => (p.pricePaise > best.pricePaise ? p : best));
console.log(mostExpensive.name);
Console output
Shimla Apple

With no start value, reduce uses the first item as best and starts from the second. That's fine here, but it throws a TypeError on an empty array, so check products.length first in real code.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• .sort() on numbers without a compare function.
  • Using map just to loop (ignoring the array it returns). Use for…of or forEach for side effects.
  • Forgetting the start value in reduce (0): on an empty array it throws an error.
  • Changing the array while looping over it. Build a new one with filter instead.

docs.title: 6. The DOM: Changing the Page
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

When the browser reads your HTML, it builds a tree of objects called the DOM (Document Object Model). Each tag becomes an object you can find, read and change from JavaScript. Change the DOM and the browser redraws the page.

flowchart TD doc["document"] --> html["html"] html --> head["head"] html --> body["body"] body --> h1["h1#title<br/>'Today's products'"] body --> p["p.subtitle"] body --> div["div.controls"] div --> b1["button#rename"] div --> b2["button#highlight"] div --> b3["button#add"] body --> ul["ul#product-list"] ul --> li1["li (made by JS)"] ul --> li2["li (made by JS)"]

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: Click the three buttons. Open it full-size: 06-dom.html, then press F12 and look at the Elements panel: the <li>s aren't in the HTML file; JavaScript created them.

docs.title: The HTML
docs.text:
<h1 id="title">Today's products</h1>
<p class="subtitle">Loaded from a JavaScript array.</p>

<div class="controls">
  <button type="button" id="rename">Change the heading</button>
  <button type="button" id="highlight">Highlight cheap items</button>
  <button type="button" id="add">Add a product</button>
</div>

<ul id="product-list"></ul>

The list <ul id="product-list"> is empty. JavaScript fills it from an array: the same way a real store fills its pages from data sent by the server.

docs.title: 1. Find elements
docs.text:
// 1. Find elements
const title = document.querySelector("#title");          // first match for a CSS selector
const list = document.querySelector("#product-list");
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll(".controls button");   // ALL matches (a NodeList)
console.log(buttons.length);                               // 3
Code What it does document The whole page. The starting point for everything. document.querySelector("#title") Finds the first element matching a CSS selector (#id, .class, tag, [data-x], nav a…). Gives null if nothing matches. document.querySelectorAll(".controls button") Finds all matches, as a NodeList. You can loop over it with for…of; use [...list] for array methods like map. buttons.length How many were found: 3.

You can also search inside an element: list.querySelectorAll("li") only looks within the list.

docs.title: 2. Build elements from data
docs.text:
// 2. Build elements from data
const products = [
  { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900 },
  { name: "Robusta Banana", pricePaise: 4900 },
  { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800 },
];

function renderProduct(product) {
  const li = document.createElement("li");                 // a new, empty <li> (not on the page yet)
  li.dataset.price = product.pricePaise;                   // sets data-price="18900"

  const name = document.createElement("span");
  name.textContent = product.name;                         // textContent: safe, never runs HTML

  const price = document.createElement("span");
  price.className = "price";
  price.textContent = `₹${product.pricePaise / 100}`;

  li.append(name, price);                                  // put the spans inside the <li>
  return li;
}

list.append(...products.map(renderProduct));               // put every <li> on the page in one go
Code What it does const products = [ … ]; The data, as an array of objects (lesson 4). function renderProduct(product) A small function: one product in, one <li> out. Reusable for the first render and for adding later. document.createElement("li") Makes a new, empty <li>. It isn't on the page until you insert it. li.dataset.price = product.pricePaise; Sets data-price="18900". dataset.someName ↔ data-some-name. name.textContent = product.name; Sets the text. textContent treats everything as plain text, so data can never inject HTML. price.className = "price"; Sets the class attribute (for the CSS rule .price { font-weight: 700 }). li.append(name, price); Puts both spans inside the <li>, in order. list.append(...products.map(renderProduct)); map turns 3 products into 3 <li>s; spread passes them all to append in one go. One DOM update is faster than three.

innerHTML with data is a security hole

li.innerHTML = product.name would run any HTML inside the name. If a name ever came from a user or a server, someone could insert <img src=x onerror="stealCookies()">. This is called XSS (cross-site scripting). Use textContent for data, and keep innerHTML for fixed markup you wrote yourself.

docs.title: 3. Change what's on the page
docs.text:
// 3. Change what's on the page
document.querySelector("#rename").addEventListener("click", () => {
  title.textContent = "Fresh picks for you";               // change text
  title.style.color = "#0c831f";                           // change one style (prefer classes)
});

document.querySelector("#highlight").addEventListener("click", () => {
  for (const li of list.querySelectorAll("li")) {
    const cheap = Number(li.dataset.price) < 10000;
    li.classList.toggle("highlight", cheap);               // add the class if cheap, remove it if not
  }
});

document.querySelector("#add").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  list.prepend(renderProduct({ name: "Brown Eggs", pricePaise: 8400 }));   // add at the top
  event.currentTarget.disabled = true;                     // the button that was clicked
  event.currentTarget.textContent = "Added";
});
Code What it does addEventListener("click", () => { … }) Run this function when the button is clicked (lesson 7 covers events). title.textContent = "Fresh picks for you"; Replaces the heading's text. title.style.color = "#0c831f"; Sets one inline style. Fine for one-offs; for anything bigger, toggle a class and keep the styling in CSS. list.querySelectorAll("li") Only the <li>s inside the list. Number(li.dataset.price) < 10000 Data attributes are strings; convert before comparing (lesson 1). li.classList.toggle("highlight", cheap) Adds the class when cheap is true, removes it when false. Also: classList.add(), .remove(), .contains(). list.prepend(…) Inserts at the start of the list (append = end; before/after = next to an element). event.currentTarget The element the listener is attached to: here, the clicked button. .disabled = true Many attributes have matching properties: disabled, hidden, value, checked, href. For any other attribute use setAttribute("aria-label", "…") / getAttribute(…).

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: Task Code Find one / all document.querySelector(sel) / document.querySelectorAll(sel) Nearest ancestor matching el.closest(".product-card") Read / change text el.textContent Read an input input.value (always a string) Classes el.classList.add / remove / toggle / contains("name") Attributes el.getAttribute("x"), el.setAttribute("x", "y"), el.removeAttribute("x") Data attributes el.dataset.productId ↔ data-product-id Show / hide el.hidden = true / false Create document.createElement("li") Insert parent.append(child), parent.prepend(child), el.before(x), el.after(x) Replace all children parent.replaceChildren(...newChildren) Remove el.remove()

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Add a fourth button "Sort by price" that re-appends the <li>s in price order (hint: [...list.children], toSorted, list.append(...)).
  2. Give each <li> a "×" button that removes it.
  3. Show the total of all prices in a <p> under the list, and update it when a product is added.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

All three solutions together, live (the code below is included from this file):

1. Sort by price 
<button type="button" id="sort">Sort by price</button>

// Exercise 1: re-append the <li>s in price order. append() MOVES existing elements, so nothing is re-created.
document.querySelector("#sort").addEventListener("click", () => {
  const rows = [...list.children].toSorted((a, b) => Number(a.dataset.price) - Number(b.dataset.price));
  list.append(...rows);
});

list.children is a live HTMLCollection (no array methods), so spread it first. append() moves elements that are already on the page; nothing is copied or re-created.

2. A × button on every row

Build the button inside renderProduct, so every row, including ones added later, gets one:

const remove = document.createElement("button");         // Exercise 2: a × button in every row
remove.type = "button";
remove.className = "remove";
remove.textContent = "×";
remove.setAttribute("aria-label", `Remove ${product.name}`);

li.append(name, price, remove);

Then one listener on the list removes the right row (event delegation, lesson 7):

// Exercise 2: one listener on the list removes whichever row's × was clicked (event delegation, lesson 7)
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest(".remove");
  if (!button) return;
  button.closest("li").remove();
  updateTotal();
});
3. A total that stays in sync 
<p id="total"></p>

// Exercise 3: the total of every price on the list, recalculated from the DOM whenever it changes
const totalText = document.querySelector("#total");
function updateTotal() {
  const prices = [...list.querySelectorAll("li")].map((li) => Number(li.dataset.price));
  const totalPaise = prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
  totalText.textContent = `Total: ₹${totalPaise / 100}`;
}
updateTotal();

Then call updateTotal() after every change: adding a product and removing one. Forgetting one of those calls is exactly the kind of bug that the "change state, then render everything" pattern (used by the FreshCart cart) avoids.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running the script before the HTML exists, so querySelector returns null. Use <script defer> or put the script at the end of <body>.
  • querySelector("product-list") without # or .: that searches for a <product-list> tag.
  • Calling .forEach or .map on something that isn't an array. querySelectorAll has forEach but not map: spread it first.
  • Building HTML strings with data and innerHTML (XSS).

docs.title: 7. Events: Reacting to Users
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

An event is something that happens on the page: a click, a key press, typing, a form being submitted, the page being scrolled. You tell the browser "when this happens to that element, run this function". That's addEventListener.

element.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  // runs every time element is clicked
});

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: Try all four. Open it full-size: 07-events.html.

docs.title: 1. Click: a quantity counter
docs.text:
<section>
  <h2>1. Click: a quantity counter</h2>
  <button type="button" id="minus" aria-label="Remove one">−</button>
  <output id="qty">0</output>
  <button type="button" id="plus" aria-label="Add one">+</button>
</section>

const qtyOutput = document.querySelector("#qty");
let qty = 0;

function setQty(newQty) {
  qty = Math.max(0, newQty);            // never below 0
  qtyOutput.textContent = qty;
}

document.querySelector("#plus").addEventListener("click", () => setQty(qty + 1));
document.querySelector("#minus").addEventListener("click", () => setQty(qty - 1));
Code What it does let qty = 0; The state: the one true quantity. function setQty(newQty) The only place that changes the state, and it always updates the screen too. Math.max(0, newQty) The bigger of 0 and the new value, so it can never go negative. qtyOutput.textContent = qty; Show the new number. addEventListener("click", () => setQty(qty + 1)) On each click, call setQty with one more. Note we pass a function (() => …), not the result of calling one.

click also fires when a keyboard user presses Enter or Space on a <button>. That's one reason to always use real buttons.

docs.title: 2. Input: live search
docs.text:
<section>
  <h2>2. Input: live search</h2>
  <label for="search">Search</label>
  <input id="search" type="search" placeholder="Try “ba”">
  <ul id="results">
    <li>Apple</li><li>Banana</li><li>Bread</li><li>Butter</li><li>Milk</li>
  </ul>
</section>

const search = document.querySelector("#search");
const items = document.querySelectorAll("#results li");

search.addEventListener("input", (event) => {           // fires on every keystroke, paste or clear
  const text = event.target.value.trim().toLowerCase();
  for (const li of items) {
    li.hidden = !li.textContent.toLowerCase().includes(text);
  }
});
Code What it does "input" Fires on every change to the field: typing, pasting, deleting, the × clear button. ("change" only fires when you leave the field.) (event) => { … } The browser passes an event object describing what happened. event.target.value target is the element the event happened on; .value is the text in it (always a string). .trim().toLowerCase() Ignore extra spaces and capital letters, so "BA " still matches "Banana". li.hidden = !….includes(text) Hide items that don't contain the search text.

A bug the automated test caught

The first version of this demo didn't hide anything. The CSS rule li { display: flex } overrides the hidden attribute, because hidden only works through the browser's own display: none. The fix is one line of CSS that every project should have:

[hidden] { display: none !important; }

docs.title: 3. Submit: validating a form
docs.text:
<section>
  <h2>3. Submit: a pincode form</h2>
  <form id="pincode-form" novalidate>
    <label for="pincode">Delivery pincode</label>
    <input id="pincode" name="pincode" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="postal-code" aria-describedby="pincode-msg">
    <button type="submit">Check</button>
    <p class="error" id="pincode-msg" aria-live="polite"></p>
  </form>
</section>

const form = document.querySelector("#pincode-form");
const pincode = form.elements.pincode;                   // form.elements gives inputs by name
const message = document.querySelector("#pincode-msg");

form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                                // stop the browser reloading the page

  const value = pincode.value.trim();
  const valid = /^\d{6}$/.test(value);                   // exactly 6 digits
  pincode.setAttribute("aria-invalid", String(!valid));
  message.className = valid ? "ok" : "error";
  message.textContent = valid
    ? `Great, we deliver to ${value} in 10 minutes.`
    : "Enter a 6-digit pincode, e.g. 560001.";
  if (!valid) pincode.focus();
});
Code What it does <form id="pincode-form" novalidate> novalidate turns off the browser's own error bubbles so we can show our own message. inputmode="numeric" Shows a number keypad on phones. aria-describedby="pincode-msg" Screen readers read the error message along with the input. form.addEventListener("submit", …) Listen on the form, not the button: submit fires for a button click and for Enter in a field. event.preventDefault(); Stops the browser's default action: sending the form and reloading the page. Without it, your JavaScript's work is wiped out. form.elements.pincode Inputs by their name. /^\d{6}$/.test(value) A regular expression: ^ start, \d{6} exactly six digits, $ end. .test() gives true/false. setAttribute("aria-invalid", …) Tells assistive tech the field is invalid; the CSS colours the border red from the same attribute. message.textContent = valid ? … : …; A ternary picks the success or error text. The <p aria-live="polite"> announces it. if (!valid) pincode.focus(); Put the cursor back in the field so the user can fix it straight away.

docs.title: 4. Event delegation: one listener, many buttons
docs.text:
<section>
  <h2>4. Event delegation: one listener, many buttons</h2>
  <ul id="cart">
    <li>Apple <button type="button" data-remove>Remove</button></li>
    <li>Milk <button type="button" data-remove>Remove</button></li>
    <li>Bread <button type="button" data-remove>Remove</button></li>
  </ul>
</section>

const cart = document.querySelector("#cart");

cart.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("[data-remove]");  // did the click land on (or in) a Remove button?
  if (!button) return;
  button.closest("li").remove();
});
Code What it does cart.addEventListener("click", …) One listener on the list, not one per button. How it works A click on a button bubbles up: it fires on the button, then its <li>, then the <ul>, then body… So the list hears every click inside it. event.target.closest("[data-remove]") target is what was actually clicked (maybe text inside the button). closest walks up to the nearest matching ancestor, or gives null. if (!button) return; The click wasn't on a Remove button: ignore it. button.closest("li").remove(); Remove the row that contains the button.

Delegation is faster for long lists and keeps working for items added later, because the listener is on the parent. FreshCart's product grid uses exactly this.

docs.title: Bonus: keyboard
docs.text:
document.addEventListener("keydown", (event) => {
  if (event.key === "Escape" && document.activeElement === search) {
    search.value = "";
    search.dispatchEvent(new Event("input"));            // re-run the search listener
  }
});
Code What it does document.addEventListener("keydown", …) Listen for key presses anywhere on the page. event.key === "Escape" event.key is the key's name: "Enter", "Escape", "ArrowDown", "a"… document.activeElement === search Only when the search box has focus. search.dispatchEvent(new Event("input")) Fires an input event by code, so the search listener runs and shows every item again.

docs.title: Common events
docs.text: Event Fires when click Clicked, tapped, or Enter/Space on a button input The value of an input, select or textarea changes change The value is committed (leaving a text field, ticking a checkbox, choosing an option) submit A form is submitted (on the <form>) keydown A key is pressed focus / blur An element gains / loses focus (focusin/focusout bubble) scroll, resize The page scrolls / the window changes size (throttle these: Coding Interview #9) DOMContentLoaded The HTML has been parsed (not needed with defer)

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Make the counter's − button disabled when the quantity is 0.
  2. Show "No results" under the search list when every item is hidden.
  3. Add an "Add item" form that appends a new <li> with a Remove button to the cart list. Check that Remove works on the new items without adding any listener (delegation!).

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

All three solutions together, live:

1. Disable − at zero 
const minus = document.querySelector("#minus");

function setQty(newQty) {
  qty = Math.max(0, newQty);            // never below 0
  qtyOutput.textContent = qty;
  minus.disabled = qty === 0;           // Exercise 1: nothing to remove at 0
}
setQty(0);                              // run once at the start, so − begins disabled

Updating disabled inside setQty means it can't get out of sync, and calling setQty(0) once at the start sets the initial state from the same code.

2. “No results” 
<p id="no-results" hidden>No results</p>

At the end of the input listener:

// Exercise 2: show the message when every item is hidden
const anyVisible = [...items].some((li) => !li.hidden);
document.querySelector("#no-results").hidden = anyVisible;
3. An “Add item” form 
<form id="add-form">
  <label for="new-item">New item</label>
  <input id="new-item" name="itemName" required>
  <button type="submit">Add item</button>
</form>

// Exercise 3: add rows. The delegated listener above already handles their Remove buttons.
const addForm = document.querySelector("#add-form");
addForm.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const name = addForm.elements.itemName.value.trim();
  if (!name) return;

  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.append(name + " ");                       // append() accepts plain text too (safe: never parsed as HTML)
  const remove = document.createElement("button");
  remove.type = "button";
  remove.dataset.remove = "";                  // the same data-remove hook as the HTML rows
  remove.textContent = "Remove";
  li.append(remove);
  cart.append(li);

  addForm.reset();
  addForm.elements.itemName.focus();
});

New rows' Remove buttons work with no new listener, because the click bubbles up to the list's delegated listener.

Another bug the tests caught: don't name an input item

The first version used name="item", and form.elements.item.value crashed with Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim'). form.elements already has a built-in method called item(), and it wins over an input with that name. The same goes for names like length, submit or action on forms. Choose specific names such as itemName.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• addEventListener("click", doThing()): calls doThing now and passes its result. Pass doThing (no brackets).
  • Forgetting event.preventDefault() on a form submit, so the page reloads and everything resets.
  • Listening for click on the submit button instead of submit on the form, so Enter doesn't work.
  • Adding a listener to every row of a long list (and forgetting rows added later). Use delegation.
  • Making clickable <div>s: no keyboard, no focus. Use <button>.

docs.title: 8. Async: Timers, Promises & fetch
docs.text:
Intermediate

Some things take time: loading products from a server, waiting for payment, a timer. JavaScript doesn't stop and wait; it carries on and runs your code later, when the result is ready. This is called asynchronous code.

docs.title: JavaScript doesn't wait
docs.text:
console.log("1. Order button clicked");
setTimeout(() => console.log("3. Payment confirmed (after 200 ms)"), 200);
setTimeout(() => console.log("2. Packing started (after 100 ms)"), 100);
console.log("0. JavaScript doesn't wait: this line runs straight away");
Console output
1. Order button clicked
0. JavaScript doesn't wait: this line runs straight away
2. Packing started (after 100 ms)
3. Payment confirmed (after 200 ms)
Code What it does setTimeout(fn, 200) "Call fn in about 200 ms." It schedules and returns immediately. The printed order 1, then 0 (the next line runs at once), then 2 after 100 ms, then 3 after 200 ms. The order you write isn't the order things happen.

The browser has a single main thread. If JavaScript waited for every network request, the page would freeze. Instead, slow work happens in the background and your function is queued to run when it's done.

docs.title: Promises
docs.text:
// A Promise is a value that will arrive later: it ends up "fulfilled" (a result) or "rejected" (an error)
function checkStock(productId) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (productId === "apple") resolve({ productId, available: 12 });
      else reject(new Error(`Unknown product: ${productId}`));
    }, 50);
  });
}

checkStock("apple")
  .then((result) => console.log("In stock:", result.available))
  .catch((err) => console.log("Failed:", err.message));

checkStock("dragonfruit")
  .then((result) => console.log("In stock:", result.available))
  .catch((err) => console.log("Failed:", err.message));
Console output
In stock: 12
Failed: Unknown product: dragonfruit
Code What it does new Promise((resolve, reject) => { … }) A promise is an object for a value that will arrive later. You get it straight away; the value comes later. resolve(value) "It worked, here's the result." The promise becomes fulfilled. reject(new Error(…)) "It failed." The promise becomes rejected. .then((result) => …) Runs when it's fulfilled. .catch((err) => …) Runs when it's rejected. Always handle failures.

You'll rarely write new Promise yourself. fetch() and most browser APIs return promises; your job is to use them.

docs.title: async / await: async code that reads top to bottom
docs.text:
const wait = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function placeOrder() {
  console.log("Placing order…");
  await wait(50);                       // pause THIS function until the promise settles
  console.log("Payment done");
  await wait(50);
  console.log("Order confirmed");
  return 1042;                          // an async function always returns a promise
}

const orderId = await placeOrder();     // await works at the top level of modules and the console
console.log("Order id:", orderId);
Console output
Placing order…
Payment done
Order confirmed
Order id: 1042
Code What it does async function placeOrder() Marks the function as asynchronous. It always returns a promise. await wait(50); Pauses this function until the promise settles, then continues. The rest of the page keeps working meanwhile. return 1042; The promise returned by placeOrder() resolves to 1042. const orderId = await placeOrder(); Wait for the result. await is allowed inside async functions, in <script type="module"> and in the console.

async/await is the same promises as .then(), written so it reads like normal step-by-step code.

docs.title: Handling errors: try / catch / finally
docs.text:
async function fetchPrice(productId) {
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20));
  if (productId !== "milk") throw new Error("Price service is down");
  return 6800;
}

async function showPrice(productId) {
  try {
    const price = await fetchPrice(productId);
    console.log(`${productId}: ₹${price / 100}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`Could not load ${productId}: ${err.message}`);   // show a friendly message, keep the app running
  } finally {
    console.log("(hide the loading spinner)");                    // runs whether it worked or not
  }
}

await showPrice("milk");
await showPrice("bread");
Console output
milk: ₹68
(hide the loading spinner)
Could not load bread: Price service is down
(hide the loading spinner)
Code What it does throw new Error("Price service is down") Inside an async function, throw rejects its promise. try { … } Run this code… catch (err) { … } …and if anything inside try throws (or an awaited promise rejects), jump here instead of crashing. err.message is the text. finally { … } Runs either way: the place to hide a loading spinner or re-enable a button.

docs.title: Doing things at the same time
docs.text:
const fakeApi = (name, ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve(name), ms));

let start = Date.now();
const a = await fakeApi("products", 100);
const b = await fakeApi("offers", 100);
const about = (ms) => (ms >= 150 ? "about 200 ms" : "about 100 ms");
console.log("one after another:", a, b, about(Date.now() - start));

start = Date.now();
const [c, d] = await Promise.all([fakeApi("products", 100), fakeApi("offers", 100)]);
console.log("at the same time: ", c, d, about(Date.now() - start));
Console output
one after another: products offers about 200 ms
at the same time:  products offers about 100 ms
Code What it does await a; await b; One after another: the second request doesn't start until the first has finished. 100 + 100 ms. await Promise.all([a, b]) Both start immediately; wait until all are done. About 100 ms total. Results come back in the same order as the array.

If one promise in Promise.all rejects, the whole thing rejects. Use Promise.allSettled when you want every result, even failures. (Build both yourself in Coding Interview #10.)

docs.title: fetch: loading data from a server
docs.text:
// What fetch() code looks like. Here fetch is faked so the example runs anywhere;
// the live demo on this page calls the real fetch().
const fetch = async (url) => ({
  ok: url.endsWith("products.json"),
  status: url.endsWith("products.json") ? 200 : 404,
  json: async () => [{ name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900 }],
});

async function loadProducts(url) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);   // fetch does NOT reject on 404/500
  return response.json();
}

console.log(await loadProducts("/api/products.json"));
try {
  await loadProducts("/api/missing.json");
} catch (err) {
  console.log("Error:", err.message);
}
Console output
[ { name: 'Shimla Apple', pricePaise: 18900 } ]
Error: HTTP 404
Code What it does const response = await fetch(url); Sends an HTTP request and waits for the headers of the response. if (!response.ok) throw … Important: fetch only rejects on network failure (offline, DNS). A 404 or 500 is still a "successful" response, so check response.ok (status 200–299) yourself. return response.json(); Reads the body and parses it from JSON into objects. This is also a promise.

docs.title: Live demo: loading, success and error states
docs.text:
This demo really calls fetch("products.json"), a file next to it. Click both buttons. Open it full-size: 08-fetch.html.

<div class="controls">
  <button type="button" id="load">Load products</button>
  <button type="button" class="secondary" id="broken">Load from a broken URL</button>
</div>
<p id="status" role="status"></p>
<ul id="grid"></ul>

const statusText = document.querySelector("#status");
const grid = document.querySelector("#grid");
const buttons = document.querySelectorAll(".controls button");
const wait = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function loadProducts(url) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`The server answered ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();                                  // parse the JSON body (also async)
}

function showLoading(isLoading) {
  for (const button of buttons) button.disabled = isLoading;
  if (isLoading) {
    statusText.className = "";
    statusText.textContent = "Loading…";
    grid.replaceChildren();                                // clear old results
  }
}

async function show(url) {
  showLoading(true);
  try {
    await wait(400);                                       // pretend the network is slow, so you can see "Loading…"
    const products = await loadProducts(url);
    grid.replaceChildren(
      ...products.map((p) => {
        const li = document.createElement("li");
        li.innerHTML = "<span></span><strong></strong><div></div>";
        li.querySelector("span").textContent = p.emoji;
        li.querySelector("strong").textContent = p.name;
        li.querySelector("div").textContent = `₹${p.pricePaise / 100}`;
        return li;
      }),
    );
    statusText.textContent = `${products.length} products loaded.`;
  } catch (err) {
    statusText.className = "error";
    statusText.textContent = `Sorry, we couldn't load products (${err.message}). Please try again.`;
  } finally {
    showLoading(false);
  }
}

document.querySelector("#load").addEventListener("click", () => show("products.json"));
document.querySelector("#broken").addEventListener("click", () => show("no-such-file.json"));
Code What it does <script type="module"> A module script: deferred automatically, strict mode, and allowed to use import and top-level await. <p id="status" role="status"> A live region: screen readers announce "Loading…", "4 products loaded." and the error. function showLoading(isLoading) One function for the loading state: disables both buttons (no double-clicks), shows "Loading…" and clears old results. await wait(400); Fake slowness, only so you can see the loading state. Remove it in real code. const products = await loadProducts(url); Fetch and parse. If anything fails, we jump to catch. grid.replaceChildren(...products.map(…)) Build one <li> per product (lesson 6) and swap them in. li.innerHTML = "<span></span>…" then textContent Fixed markup via innerHTML; the data goes in through textContent (safe from XSS). catch (err) { … } Show a friendly message. Never leave the user staring at "Loading…" forever. finally { showLoading(false); } Re-enable the buttons whether it worked or not.

Every data-loading UI needs these three states: loading, success and error (and often a fourth: empty).

Why not open this file by double-clicking?

Browsers block fetch() from pages opened as file://. Use VS Code's Live Server, or run python3 -m http.server in the folder and open http://localhost:8000/08-fetch.html.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Add a "Retry" button to the error message that calls show("products.json") again.
  2. Show "No products found" when the JSON is an empty array [].
  3. Load products.json and a second file (e.g. offers.json) at the same time with Promise.all.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

All three solutions together, live (a third button loads an empty list):

1. A Retry button 
// Exercise 1: the error message gets a Retry button that loads the good URL
statusText.className = "error";
statusText.textContent = `Sorry, we couldn't load products (${err.message}). `;
const retry = document.createElement("button");
retry.type = "button";
retry.className = "secondary";
retry.textContent = "Retry";
retry.addEventListener("click", () => show("products.json"));
statusText.append(retry);

The button is created with createElement, not innerHTML, so the error text (err.message) never gets parsed as HTML.

2. “No products found” 
// Exercise 2: an empty list is a success, but it needs its own message
if (products.length === 0) {
  statusText.textContent = "No products found.";
  return;                                              // finally still runs
}

An empty array is a successful response, so it's not an error, but it still needs its own message. return inside try still runs finally, so the buttons are re-enabled.

3. Two files at once with Promise.all 
// Exercise 3: both files at the same time; total wait ≈ the slower one, not the sum
const [products, offers] = await Promise.all([loadProducts(url), loadProducts("offers.json")]);
document.querySelector("#offers").textContent = offers.map((o) => o.title).join(" · ");

Both requests start immediately, and the destructuring [products, offers] matches the order of the array, not the order the responses arrive in. If either request fails, Promise.all rejects and the catch shows the error. (See the offers file.)

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting await: you get a Promise object instead of the data (console.log shows Promise {<pending>}).
  • Not checking response.ok, then trying to parse an HTML 404 page as JSON.
  • No try/catch around await: one failed request breaks the whole feature, silently.
  • Awaiting independent requests one by one when Promise.all could run them together.
  • Using await inside forEach (it doesn't wait). Use for…of or Promise.all(array.map(…)).

docs.title: 9. Errors, Debugging & Good Habits
docs.text:
Beginner Intermediate

Every developer writes bugs every day. What makes you fast is reading the error, finding the line, and checking your assumptions with the console and DevTools. This lesson also covers modules (splitting code into files) and the habits that keep code readable.

docs.title: Reading an error message
docs.text:
const cart = undefined;
console.log("Before the crash");
console.log(cart.items);           // TypeError: reading a property of undefined
console.log("This line never runs");
Console output
Before the crash
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')

In the browser, an uncaught error looks like this:

Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')
    at app.js:3:18
Part Meaning Uncaught Nothing caught it with try/catch, so the script stopped. Nothing after this line ran. TypeError The kind of error (see the table below). Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items') What went wrong: you wrote something.items, and something was undefined. app.js:3:18 Where: file, line 3, column 18. Click it in DevTools to jump to the exact spot.

Read the message, then go to the line. Most bugs are explained right there.

docs.title: The errors you'll see most
docs.text:
const examples = [
  () => totl + 1,                                // a typo in a variable name
  () => { const a = 1; a = 2; },                 // reassigning a const
  () => null.length,                             // a property of null
  () => "apple".toUppercase(),                   // a method that doesn't exist (case matters)
  () => JSON.parse("{name: 'Apple'}"),           // JSON needs double quotes around keys and strings
];
for (const run of examples) {
  try {
    run();
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`${err.name}: ${err.message}`);
  }
}
Console output
ReferenceError: totl is not defined
TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'length')
TypeError: "apple".toUppercase is not a function
SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)
Error Usual cause Fix ReferenceError: totl is not defined A typo, or a variable used outside its scope Check the spelling and where it was declared TypeError: Assignment to constant variable Reassigning a const Use let if it really changes TypeError: Cannot read properties of null querySelector found nothing, or data was missing Check the selector; use ?. for optional data TypeError: … is not a function A typo in a method name (case matters), or the value isn't what you think console.log the value and its typeof SyntaxError: … in JSON Invalid JSON (single quotes, trailing commas, an HTML error page instead of JSON) Check response.ok and the raw text

docs.title: Throwing your own errors
docs.text:
function setQuantity(qty) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(qty) || qty < 0) {
    throw new RangeError(`Quantity must be a whole number ≥ 0, got ${qty}`);
  }
  return qty;
}

for (const value of [2, -1, 1.5]) {
  try {
    console.log("OK:", setQuantity(value));
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`${err.name}: ${err.message}`);
  }
}
Console output
OK: 2
RangeError: Quantity must be a whole number ≥ 0, got -1
RangeError: Quantity must be a whole number ≥ 0, got 1.5
Code What it does Number.isInteger(qty) true only for whole numbers. throw new RangeError(…) Stops the function and hands the error to the nearest catch. RangeError (value out of range) and TypeError (wrong type) are good built-in choices; Error for everything else. try { … } catch (err) { … } Catches it, so the loop carries on with the next value.

Throw early with a clear message ("Quantity must be a whole number ≥ 0, got -1") instead of letting bad data cause a confusing error three functions later.

docs.title: Console tricks
docs.text:
const product = { id: "apple", pricePaise: 18900 };
console.log("plain log", product);
console.info("info: same as log, different icon in the browser");
console.warn("warn: yellow in the browser");
console.error("error: red in the browser, with a stack trace");
console.log({ product });           // wrap in { } to print the variable's NAME too
Console output
plain log { id: 'apple', pricePaise: 18900 }
info: same as log, different icon in the browser
warn: yellow in the browser
error: red in the browser, with a stack trace
{ product: { id: 'apple', pricePaise: 18900 } }

In the browser, warn shows yellow, error shows red with a stack trace, and the console's filter buttons show one level at a time. console.log({ product }) prints the name of the variable along with its value. Also handy: console.table(array) draws an array of objects as a table.

docs.title: Debugging in DevTools (step by step)
docs.text:
console.log is fine for quick checks. For anything harder, pause the code and look around:

  1. Open DevTools (F12) → Sources (Chrome/Edge) or Debugger (Firefox).
  2. Open your .js file (Ctrl+P / Cmd+P and type its name).
  3. Click a line number to set a breakpoint (a blue marker).
  4. Do the thing that runs that code (click ADD). The page freezes on that line.
  5. Hover over any variable to see its value, or read them all in the Scope panel.
  6. Step through: F10 next line · F11 into a function · F8 continue.
  7. Add debugger; to your code to pause there whenever DevTools is open.

For the full tour (Styles, Computed, Grid overlays, every kind of breakpoint, Network status codes) and a page of planted bugs to practise on, see Debugging with DevTools and the Bug Lab.

Other DevTools panels you'll use daily: Elements (see and edit the live DOM and CSS), Network (every request, its status and its response: the first place to look when fetch fails), Application (localStorage, cookies).

docs.title: Modules: splitting code into files
docs.text:
Once a script grows past a couple of hundred lines, split it. Modules let each file export what others may use and import what it needs.

js/money.js
export const FREE_DELIVERY_FROM = 19900;

export function formatPaise(paise) {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(paise / 100);
}
js/cart.js
import { formatPaise, FREE_DELIVERY_FROM } from "./money.js";

const cart = new Map();

export function addToCart(id, pricePaise) {
  const line = cart.get(id) ?? { qty: 0, pricePaise };
  cart.set(id, { ...line, qty: line.qty + 1 });
}

export function total() {
  let paise = 0;
  for (const line of cart.values()) paise += line.qty * line.pricePaise;
  return formatPaise(paise);
}
index.html
<script type="module" src="js/app.js"></script>
js/app.js
import { addToCart, total } from "./cart.js";

addToCart("apple", 18900);
console.log(total());   // ₹189.00
Code What it does export function … / export const … Makes it available to other files. Anything not exported stays private to the file (like cart above). import { a, b } from "./money.js"; Brings in named exports. The path is relative and needs the .js extension in the browser. <script type="module"> Required for import/export in the browser. Modules are deferred automatically and run in strict mode.

Like fetch, modules don't load from file://: use Live Server or python3 -m http.server. Angular, React and Vite projects use exactly this syntax; the build tool bundles the files for you.

docs.title: Habits that make code easy to read
docs.text:
// 1. const by default, let only when the value changes, never var
// 2. === not ==
// 3. Name things for what they ARE: cartTotalPaise, not x or data2
// 4. Small functions that do one thing
// 5. Return early instead of nesting if inside if

// Nested (hard to read)
function canCheckout1(cart, user) {
  if (cart.length > 0) {
    if (user) {
      if (user.address) {
        return true;
      }
    }
  }
  return false;
}

// Early returns (easy to read)
function canCheckout2(cart, user) {
  if (cart.length === 0) return false;
  if (!user) return false;
  return Boolean(user.address);
}

const user = { name: "Asha", address: "21 MG Road" };
console.log(canCheckout1(["apple"], user), canCheckout2(["apple"], user));
console.log(canCheckout1([], user), canCheckout2([], user));
Console output
true true
false false

Both functions give the same answers, but canCheckout2 is far easier to read and change. The checklist:

  • const by default, let when it changes, never var.
  • ===, never ==.
  • Names say what the value is: cartTotalPaise, isLoggedIn, renderProduct().
  • Small functions that do one thing; return early instead of nesting.
  • Keep data (state) separate from the DOM; change the state, then render.
  • Use textContent for data, never innerHTML.
  • Handle the failure path of every await.
  • Use a formatter (Prettier) and a linter (ESLint) so style is never a discussion.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Open the store demo, set a breakpoint inside setQty in store.js, click ADD and step through render(). Watch count and subtotal change in the Scope panel.
  2. Break something on purpose (misspell a variable), read the error, click the file link, and fix it.
  3. Split lesson 5's cart-bill example into money.js, cart.js and app.js modules.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
Try each exercise yourself first, then open its solution to compare.

1. Step through the store with a breakpoint

What you should see, in order:

  1. Click ADD on Shimla Apple: the page freezes on your breakpoint in setQty. The Scope panel shows card (the <article>), and qty = 1.
  2. F10 over the const { id, name, price } = card.dataset; line: id = "apple", name = "Shimla Apple", and price = "18900", a string (data attributes always are).
  3. Step into render() with F11. In the for…of loop, watch count go 0 → 1 and subtotal 0 → 18900.
  4. F8 to continue: the card shows the − 1 + stepper and the badge shows 1.
2. Read and fix an error

For example, change cart.set(id, …) to crat.set(id, …) in store.js and click ADD. Chrome's console shows (captured from a real run; the file paths are shortened):

Uncaught ReferenceError: crat is not defined
    at setQty (store.js:25:7)
    at <anonymous> (store.js:40:48)

The first line names the problem: a variable that doesn't exist. The at … lines are the stack trace, newest call first: the error happened inside setQty, which was called from the anonymous click listener on line 40. Click the store.js link to jump to the code (Chrome points at the start of the if/else statement that contains the typo), fix it, and reload.

3. Split the cart bill into modules

Three files, each with one job. money.js knows about paise and currencies:

money.js
// money.js: everything about prices. No other file needs to know about paise or currency formats.
export const FREE_DELIVERY_FROM = 19900; // ₹199
export const DELIVERY_FEE = 2500;        // ₹25

export function rupees(paise) {
  return `₹${(paise / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
}

export function deliveryFee(subtotalPaise) {
  return subtotalPaise >= FREE_DELIVERY_FROM ? 0 : DELIVERY_FEE;
}

cart.js builds the bill and imports only what it needs:

cart.js
// cart.js: turns a catalogue + a cart into bill lines. It imports only what it needs from money.js.
import { deliveryFee } from "./money.js";

export function billFor(catalogue, cart) {
  const lines = cart.map(({ id, qty }) => {
    const { name, pricePaise } = catalogue.get(id);
    return { name, qty, linePaise: pricePaise * qty };
  });
  const subtotal = lines.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.linePaise, 0);
  const delivery = deliveryFee(subtotal);
  return { lines, delivery, total: subtotal + delivery };
}

app.js is the entry point that wires them together:

app.js
// app.js: the entry point. Load it with <script type="module" src="app.js"></script>, or run `node app.js`.
import { rupees } from "./money.js";
import { billFor } from "./cart.js";

const catalogue = new Map([
  ["apple", { name: "Shimla Apple", pricePaise: 18900 }],
  ["milk", { name: "Full Cream Milk", pricePaise: 6800 }],
  ["bread", { name: "Whole Wheat Bread", pricePaise: 5000 }],
]);
const cart = [
  { id: "apple", qty: 2 },
  { id: "bread", qty: 1 },
];

const { lines, delivery, total } = billFor(catalogue, cart);
for (const line of lines) console.log(`${line.name.padEnd(18)} × ${line.qty}  ${rupees(line.linePaise)}`);
console.log(`Delivery: ${delivery ? rupees(delivery) : "FREE"}`);
console.log(`To pay:   ${rupees(total)}`);
Console output
Shimla Apple       × 2  ₹378.00
Whole Wheat Bread  × 1  ₹50.00
Delivery: FREE
To pay:   ₹428.00

Exactly the same bill as lesson 5, but now rupees() and deliveryFee() can be reused by any other file, and cart.js can be tested without a page. This output comes from running node app.js (Node 22 understands import/export directly).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Ignoring the red error and changing random things. Read the message and go to the line first.
  • Leaving console.log and debugger lines in finished code.
  • Catching errors and doing nothing (catch (err) {}): the bug is still there, now silent.
  • Forgetting type="module", then getting Cannot use import statement outside a module.

docs.title: Layout: Choosing the Right Tool
docs.text:
CSS has four layout systems. Picking the right one is half the job.

flowchart TD Q1{"Is it text and simple<br/>blocks stacked top to bottom?"} -- Yes --> F["Normal flow<br/>(no layout CSS needed)"] Q1 -- No --> Q2{"Do you control rows AND<br/>columns at the same time?"} Q2 -- "Yes (2-D)" --> G["CSS Grid"] Q2 -- "No, one direction (1-D)" --> Q3{"Should item sizes come<br/>from their content?"} Q3 -- Yes --> FX["Flexbox"] Q3 -- "No, strict columns" --> G Q1 -- "It overlaps / floats<br/>on top of something" --> P["position: absolute / fixed / sticky<br/>or the top layer (dialog, popover)"] Flexbox Grid Dimensions 1-D: a row or a column 2-D: rows and columns Sizing comes from Content outward: items decide their size, the container distributes leftovers Layout inward: the container defines tracks, items are placed into them Great for Navbars, toolbars, button groups, centering, media objects, tag lists Page layouts, card grids, dashboards, forms, galleries, overlapping elements Wrapping Each wrapped line is independent (items in row 2 don't align with row 1) Items align to columns across every row

The honest rule of thumb

Use Grid for the overall page and for anything that should line up in columns. Use Flexbox for components inside that grid, and whenever you'd say "put these things in a row and space them out". Most real UIs nest both.

docs.title: The same UI, two ways
docs.text:
/* A row of 3 equal cards */
.flex { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
.flex > * { flex: 1; }

.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 1rem; }

flex

ShortA much longer item that wrapsMid

grid

ShortA much longer item that wrapsMid

They look the same here. The difference shows up when they wrap:

flex-wrap: the last row stretches, columns don't line up

12345

grid auto-fill: every item stays in a column

12345

docs.title: Flexbox (complete reference)
docs.text: Flexbox lays items out along one axis. In every demo, the dashed orange box is the flex container and the coloured boxes are flex items.

docs.title: The two axes Beginner
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph "flex-direction: row" direction LR A[item 1] --> B[item 2] --> C[item 3] end
  • Main axis: the direction items flow (row = left→right; column = top→bottom). justify-content works on this axis.
  • Cross axis: perpendicular to it. align-items works on this axis.

When you switch to flex-direction: column, the axes swap, so justify-content becomes vertical.

docs.title: display: flex Beginner
docs.text:
<div class="container">
  <div>1</div><div>2</div><div>3</div>
</div>

.container { display: flex; }
123

Children become flex items: they sit in a row, shrink to fit their content, and stretch to the container's height. display: inline-flex does the same but the container itself flows inline.

docs.title: flex-direction Beginner
docs.text:
flex-direction: row;            /* default */
flex-direction: row-reverse;
flex-direction: column;
flex-direction: column-reverse;
row123 row-reverse123 column123 column-reverse123

Accessibility · 🟠 Advanced

*-reverse and order change only the visual order. Keyboard tab order and screen readers still follow the HTML source order. If the visual and DOM orders disagree, keyboard users see focus jump around. Change the HTML order instead when the order matters.

docs.title: flex-wrap Beginner
docs.text:
flex-wrap: nowrap;        /* default: items shrink, then overflow */
flex-wrap: wrap;          /* items move to new lines */
flex-wrap: wrap-reverse;  /* new lines go above */
nowrap 1234 wrap 1234 wrap-reverse 1234

(The nowrap demo uses flex-shrink: 0 so you can see the overflow.)

flex-flow: row wrap; is the shorthand for flex-direction + flex-wrap.

docs.title: justify-content (main axis) Beginner
docs.text:
justify-content: flex-start;    /* default */
justify-content: center;
justify-content: flex-end;
justify-content: space-between; /* first & last at the edges, equal space between */
justify-content: space-around;  /* equal space around each item (half at edges) */
justify-content: space-evenly;  /* exactly equal spaces, including edges */
flex-start123 center123 flex-end123 space-between123 space-around123 space-evenly123

docs.title: align-items (cross axis) Beginner
docs.text:
align-items: stretch;     /* default: items fill the container's height */
align-items: flex-start;
align-items: center;
align-items: flex-end;
align-items: baseline;    /* text baselines line up */
stretch123 flex-start123 center123 flex-end123 baselinesmallBigmid

docs.title: align-content (multiple lines) Intermediate
docs.text:
Only has an effect when items wrap onto several lines and the container has spare cross-axis space. Same values as justify-content, plus stretch.

.container { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; height: 200px; align-content: space-between; }
stretch (default)1234 flex-start1234 center1234 space-between1234

docs.title: gap Beginner
docs.text:
gap: 1rem;          /* row-gap and column-gap */
gap: 2rem 0.5rem;   /* row-gap column-gap */
12345

Always prefer gap over margins on items: no "remove the margin from the last item" hacks.

docs.title: flex-grow Beginner
docs.text:
How much of the leftover space an item takes, as a proportion.

.a { flex-grow: 0; }   /* default: don't grow */
.b { flex-grow: 1; }   /* takes 1 share */
.c { flex-grow: 2; }   /* takes 2 shares */
grow 0grow 1grow 2

Item 3 gets twice as much of the extra space as item 2. It's not twice as wide overall; the shares are added on top of each item's base size.

docs.title: flex-shrink Intermediate
docs.text:
How much an item gives up when there isn't enough space. Default 1 (all shrink equally, weighted by size). 0 = never shrink.

.logo   { flex-shrink: 0; }   /* never squash the logo */
.title  { flex-shrink: 1; }
shrink 0 (160px)shrink 1shrink 3

docs.title: flex-basis Beginner
docs.text:
The item's starting size before growing or shrinking. auto (default) = use width or content size. 0 = ignore content size, so space is split purely by flex-grow.

flex: 1 1 auto: extra space shared, but long content stays wider AA longer itemB flex: 1 1 0: equal widths regardless of content AA longer itemB

docs.title: flex shorthand Beginner
docs.text:
Always use the shorthand. It sets sensible values for all three.

Shorthand = grow shrink basis Meaning flex: initial 0 1 auto Default. Content-sized, can shrink, won't grow flex: auto 1 1 auto Content-sized, then grows/shrinks flex: none 0 0 auto Rigid: exactly its content/width size flex: 1 1 1 0% Equal share of all space ("make columns equal") flex: 2 2 1 0% Double share flex: 0 0 200px Fixed 200px, never changes flex: 1 1 250px Prefer 250px, wrap when there's no room: the responsive card pattern

docs.title: align-self Beginner
docs.text:
Override align-items for one item.

.container { align-items: flex-start; }
.special   { align-self: flex-end; }
startself: centerself: endself: stretch

docs.title: order Intermediate
docs.text:
Change visual order. Default 0; lower numbers come first. (See the accessibility warning above.)

.first { order: -1; }
1 (order 0)2 (order 0)3 (order -1)

docs.title: Perfect centering Beginner
docs.text:
.center { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; min-height: 200px; }
Centered

docs.title: Push items apart with margin-*: auto Beginner
docs.text:
An auto margin in a flex container absorbs all the free space on that side.

<nav class="bar">
  <a>Logo</a><a>Docs</a><a>Blog</a>
  <a class="push">Sign in</a>
</nav>

.bar  { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
.push { margin-inline-start: auto; }   /* pushes itself (and anything after) to the end */
LogoDocsBlogSign in

docs.title: Sticky footer (card) Beginner
docs.text:
.card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
.card .actions { margin-top: auto; }   /* buttons always at the bottom */
TitleShortButton TitleLonger text that takes two linesButton

docs.title: The min-width: 0 bug Intermediate
docs.text:
Flex items default to min-width: auto, which means they won't shrink below their content's width. A long URL or a white-space: nowrap child will blow out the layout.

.item { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }   /* allow it to shrink; let text-overflow kick in */
without min-width: 0 (overflows) Icona-very-long-filename-that-refuses-to-shrink.pdf with min-width: 0 (truncates) Icona-very-long-filename-that-refuses-to-shrink.pdf

docs.title: Responsive without media queries Intermediate
docs.text:
.cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.cards > * { flex: 1 1 220px; }    /* each card wants 220px; wraps when it can't fit */
CardCardCardCard

Resize the browser: 4 per row → 2 → 1, with no breakpoints.

docs.title: Flexbox interview cheat sheet Advanced
docs.text: Question Answer Difference between justify-content and align-items? Main axis vs cross axis. They swap meaning with flex-direction: column. Why do my flex items overflow instead of shrinking? min-width: auto on flex items. Set min-width: 0 (or overflow: hidden). flex: 1 vs flex: auto? 1 = basis 0, equal widths. auto = basis auto, content-weighted widths. Do margins collapse in flex? No. float on a flex item? Ignored. How does flex-shrink distribute? Proportional to flex-shrink × flex-basis, so big items shrink more. Does vertical-align work? No; use align-items / align-self.

docs.title: CSS Grid (complete reference)
docs.text: Grid lays items out in rows and columns at the same time. In every demo, the dashed orange box is the grid container and the coloured boxes are grid items.

docs.title: Vocabulary Beginner
docs.text: Term Meaning Grid line The dividing lines, numbered from 1 (and from -1 at the end) Track A row or a column (the space between two lines) Cell One row × one column Area A rectangle of one or more cells Gap / gutter Space between tracks Explicit grid Tracks you define with grid-template-* Implicit grid Tracks the browser creates when items don't fit (grid-auto-*)

docs.title: display: grid + columns Beginner
docs.text:
.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 2fr;
  gap: 1rem;
}
120px1fr2fr120px1fr2fr

docs.title: The fr unit Beginner
docs.text:
fr = a fraction of the free space left after fixed tracks and gaps. 1fr 2fr splits leftovers 1:2.

1fr is really minmax(auto, 1fr)

A 1fr column won't shrink below its content's minimum width, the same "won't shrink" behaviour as flex items. If a long word or a wide table blows out your grid, use minmax(0, 1fr).

docs.title: repeat() Beginner
docs.text:
grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);              /* 4 equal columns */
grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 100px 1fr);        /* 100px 1fr 100px 1fr */
grid-template-columns: 250px repeat(3, 1fr);        /* sidebar + 3 equal */
grid-template-columns: repeat(12, minmax(0, 1fr));  /* 12-column system */
12345678

docs.title: minmax() Intermediate
docs.text:
grid-template-columns: minmax(150px, 300px) 1fr;  /* first col between 150 and 300px */
grid-auto-rows: minmax(80px, auto);               /* rows at least 80px, grow with content */

docs.title: auto-fill vs auto-fit: responsive with zero media queries Beginner
docs.text:
The single most useful line of CSS layout ("RAM": Repeat, Auto, Minmax):

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(200px, 100%), 1fr));
  gap: 1rem;
}

"Fit as many columns as possible, each at least 200px, then stretch them to fill the row." The min(200px, 100%) stops overflow on screens narrower than 200px.

auto-fill: keeps empty column slots 12 auto-fit: collapses empty slots, items stretch 12

With few items, auto-fill leaves empty columns and auto-fit stretches the items. With many items, they behave the same.

docs.title: Rows Beginner
docs.text:
grid-template-rows: 80px auto 60px;   /* explicit rows */
grid-auto-rows: 100px;                /* size for any extra (implicit) rows */
grid-auto-rows: minmax(100px, auto);
row 1 (40px)11row 2 (80px)22implicit (30px)33

docs.title: Placing items by line number Beginner
docs.text:
.hero   { grid-column: 1 / 4; }       /* from line 1 to line 4 = 3 columns */
.wide   { grid-column: span 2; }      /* span 2 columns from wherever it lands */
.full   { grid-column: 1 / -1; }      /* first line to last line = full width */
.tall   { grid-row: 1 / 3; }          /* 2 rows */
.box    { grid-area: 2 / 1 / 4 / 3; } /* row-start / col-start / row-end / col-end */
1 / -1 (full width) span 2 rows span 2 cols · · · ·

docs.title: grid-template-areas: draw your layout Beginner
docs.text:
Name areas, then draw the layout as ASCII art. . is an empty cell.

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar main"
    "footer footer";
  min-height: 100dvh;
}
header { grid-area: header; }
aside  { grid-area: sidebar; }
main   { grid-area: main; }
footer { grid-area: footer; }

/* Mobile: just redraw the map */
@media (width < 700px) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 1fr;
    grid-template-areas: "header" "main" "sidebar" "footer";
  }
}
header sidebar main footer

Rules: every row string must have the same number of cells, and each named area must be a rectangle.

docs.title: Named lines Advanced
docs.text:
.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns:
    [full-start] minmax(1rem, 1fr)
    [content-start] minmax(0, 60rem) [content-end]
    minmax(1rem, 1fr) [full-end];
}
.layout > *     { grid-column: content; }   /* centred content column */
.layout > .full { grid-column: full; }      /* full-bleed images, banners */

This "full-bleed" layout is covered in Layout Patterns.

docs.title: Implicit grid and grid-auto-flow Intermediate
docs.text:
grid-auto-flow: row;          /* default: fill row by row */
grid-auto-flow: column;       /* fill column by column */
grid-auto-flow: row dense;    /* backfill holes with later small items */
row (holes left by the wide items) 12 wide3 wide45 row dense (holes backfilled; visual order ≠ DOM order) 12 wide3 wide45

docs.title: Alignment Beginner → Intermediate
The one-line centre Beginner
docs.text:
.center { display: grid; place-items: center; }
Centered with 2 properties

docs.title: Overlapping items Intermediate
docs.text:
Grid lets several items occupy the same cell: an alternative to position: absolute that keeps everything in flow.

.hero { display: grid; }
.hero > * { grid-area: 1 / 1; }        /* everything in the same cell */
.hero .text { place-self: end start; z-index: 1; }
Text stacked on the image, no absolute positioning

docs.title: Subgrid Advanced
docs.text: See Modern CSS → Subgrid for a live demo. grid-template-columns: subgrid or grid-template-rows: subgrid lets nested elements align to the parent grid's tracks.

docs.title: Masonry Expert
docs.text: A native masonry layout (Pinterest-style) is being standardised as CSS Grid Lanes (display: grid-lanes), with an earlier experimental syntax grid-template-rows: masonry in Firefox and Safari Technology Preview. It isn't Baseline yet. Until it is, use CSS multi-column (columns: 3 220px, ordered top-to-bottom per column) or a JS library. See Layout Patterns → Masonry.

docs.title: Grid cheat sheet Advanced
docs.text: You want Write N equal columns grid-template-columns: repeat(N, 1fr) Responsive cards repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(250px, 100%), 1fr)) Sidebar + content grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr (or minmax(200px, 25%) 1fr) Full width item grid-column: 1 / -1 Centre one thing display: grid; place-items: center Stack things on top of each other grid-area: 1 / 1 on every child Columns that don't blow out minmax(0, 1fr) instead of 1fr Equal-height rows of cards grid-auto-rows: 1fr Fill gaps from wide items grid-auto-flow: dense (watch out for reading order)

docs.title: Layout Patterns
docs.text:
Real-world layouts you'll build again and again. Each has the code and a live, responsive output. Most demos react to your browser width; resize to see them adapt.

All of them, plus extra ones, are also on the standalone Layout Gallery page.

docs.title: 1. Centering: six ways
docs.text:
Beginner

/* 1. Grid: the shortest */
.a { display: grid; place-items: center; }

/* 2. Flexbox */
.b { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }

/* 3. Flex/grid parent + margin auto on the child */
.c { display: flex; }  .c > * { margin: auto; }

/* 4. Absolute + translate (works anywhere, e.g. over an image) */
.d { position: relative; }  .d > * { position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; translate: -50% -50%; }

/* 5. Absolute + inset + margin auto (child needs a size) */
.e > * { position: absolute; inset: 0; margin: auto; width: fit-content; height: fit-content; }

/* 6. Horizontal only: a block with a width */
.f > * { max-width: 40rem; margin-inline: auto; }

/* Text only */
.g { text-align: center; }
grid flex margin auto translate inset 0

docs.title: 2. Holy grail layout
docs.text:
Beginner Header, footer, main content between two sidebars. Stacks on mobile.

<div class="holy">
  <header>Header</header>
  <nav>Nav</nav>
  <main>Main</main>
  <aside>Aside</aside>
  <footer>Footer</footer>
</div>

.holy {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  grid-template: auto 1fr auto / 1fr;        /* rows / columns */
  grid-template-areas: "header" "nav" "main" "aside" "footer";
  min-height: 100dvh;
}
@media (width >= 48em) {
  .holy {
    grid-template-columns: 180px 1fr 180px;
    grid-template-areas:
      "header header header"
      "nav    main   aside"
      "footer footer footer";
  }
}
.holy > header { grid-area: header; }
.holy > nav    { grid-area: nav; }
.holy > main   { grid-area: main; }
.holy > aside  { grid-area: aside; }
.holy > footer { grid-area: footer; }
HeaderNavMainAsideFooter

docs.title: 3. Sidebar + content (intrinsic, no media query)
docs.text:
Intermediate The sidebar sits beside the content when there's room and wraps above it when there isn't.

.with-sidebar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.with-sidebar > :first-child { flex: 1 1 200px; }          /* sidebar: ideal 200px */
.with-sidebar > :last-child  { flex: 999 1 0; min-inline-size: 60%; }  /* content takes the rest; wraps under 60% */
SidebarContent: grows to fill; when it would get narrower than 60%, the sidebar wraps above.

docs.title: 4. Pancake stack + sticky footer
docs.text:
Beginner Header and footer take their natural height; main fills the rest, so the footer is always at the bottom even on short pages.

body { display: grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; min-height: 100dvh; }
Header (auto)Main (1fr: fills the space)Footer (auto, pinned to the bottom)

docs.title: 5. Responsive card grid (RAM)
docs.text:
Beginner

.cards {
  display: grid;

}
123456

docs.text:
Beginner Image on one side, text on the other: comments, notifications, list rows.

<div class="media">

Beginner Two equal halves (login pages, landing heroes). Stacks on mobile.

docs.text:
Intermediate The classic design-system grid (Bootstrap, Material). Items span a number of columns.

.row { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(12, minmax(0, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }

Intermediate The 2024–2026 favourite for feature sections: tiles of different sizes in a tight grid.

.bento {

Intermediate Pinterest-style columns of uneven heights. Until native masonry is Baseline, CSS multi-column is the simplest no-JS approach (items flow top-to-bottom, then into the next column).

.masonry { columns: 3 180px; column-gap: 1rem; }
.masonry > * { break-inside: avoid; margin-bottom: 1rem; }

Advanced Readable text column, with some elements (images, quotes) breaking out to the full width.

.article {
  display: grid;

    [full-start] minmax(1rem, 1fr)

Full-bleed image

Intermediate Sidebar navigation, a top bar, KPI tiles and panels.

Intermediate Text and image alternate sides down the page: the eye zig-zags.
